Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment years 2017-18 to 2020-21 - Whether amounts paid by resident Indian end-users/distributions to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software, and thus, same does not give rise to any income taxable in India - Held, yes [Para 23] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of OECD Model Convention - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Whether amounts paid by resident Indian end-users/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software, and same does not give rise to any income taxable in India - Held, yes [Paras 10 to 12] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Amounts paid by resident Indian end-users/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software, and same does not give rise to any income taxable in India

I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and China - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty/Fees for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Assessee, a US based company, received certain amount of consideration towards rendering usage of Microsoft license services to its Indian subsidiary for execution of sub-contract with Tower India - Assessing Officer treated aforesaid services offered as royalty in terms of article 12 of India-USA DTAA and held that same were liable to be taxed in India - It was observed that license for usage of copyrighted products were with Microsoft only and assessee had acquired global right and transferred said licenses to its group entities based on requirements - Whether since no vestige of copyright was at all transferred either to assessee or to end user, said services would not fall in category of royalty or copyrights - Held, yes [Paras 14 and 16] [In favour of assessee]  II. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 5 and 7 of the India-USA DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Business Profits - Others) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Assessee, a US based company, provided service desk facility to employees of TW group entities to monitor IT enabled glitch for execution of sub-contract with TW India - It had received certain amount of consideration for same from Indian subsidiary - Assessing Officer held that said payment was in nature of royalty as well as fee for technical services (FTS) - It was observed that services provided by assessee to group entity were separate and nothing to do with separate sub-contract awarded to Indian subsidiary, which was independent contract - Further, service desk services were provided to all group entities to enable common services provided to TW group employees and there was nothing on record to indicate any independent service provided to Indian subsidiary or IT enabled services which gave knowledge made available to Indian subsidiary - Whether since services provided by assessee was separate and it only collected related cost to maintain service desk, it was a receipt which would fall under article 7 of India-US DTAA as business profits and, hence, addition made by Assessing Officer was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 18] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9, read with sections 90 and 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA and OECD Model Commentary - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India - Assessment years 2000-01 to 2003-04 - Whether as per India-USA DTAA, royalty in respect of subject-matter of a copyright includes only payments for use, i.e., exploitation of copyright of such literary/artistic or scientific work - Held, yes - Whether therefore, in order to be classified as royalty, right of person in possession of subject-matter of a copyright should be to utilize such copyright in manner which is otherwise protected by respective copyright law in favour of owner of copyright - Held, yes - Whether as per clause 13.1 of OECD model commentary, payment can constitute royalty only if transferor grants to transferee right to use copyright of product - Held, yes - Assessee was engaged in business of providing networking solutions to its customers - Said activity of assessee included sale of software packages to customers - For purpose of its business, assessee had imported readymade software packages from one ‘H’ of USA and sold same to its customers in packed condition - Whether payment made by assessee to ‘H’ for import of software packages was in nature of royalty - Held, no - Whether said payment was commercial income which is subject-matter of article 7 of India-USA DTAA but, since ‘H’ did not have permanent establishment in India, assessee had no obligation to deduct tax at source on payment made to ‘H’ - Held, yes

II. Section 9 , read with sections 195 and 40(a)(i), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of OECD Model convention - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee-company was engaged in profession of software development services to its AE - Assessee claimed to have incurred expenses for purchase of software - Assessing Officer made addition on ground that assessee had failed to comply with provisions of section 195 - It was found that no license had been issued by AEs in favour of assessee for transfer of copyrights but assessee had merely paid consideration for transfer of copyrighted article in form of software and as such, exclusive right had not been transferred in favour of assessee qua software purchased by it rather assessee's right was restricted to use copyrighted product for internal business purpose - Whether Assessing Officer/DRP had erred in treating acquisition of software under head 'fee for technical services/royalty' requiring assessee to pay tax on same - Held, yes [Paras 28 to 30] [In favour of assessee]

I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2019-20 - Assessee, a tax resident of USA, had entered into a Software Licensing Agreement for supply of software license in connection with its telecommunication business to its Indian customers and received licence fee - Whether revenue earned from supply of software by assessee on a non-transferable, non-exclusive basis to Indian customers was not taxable as royalty income under provisions of article 12 of India-USA DTAA as same was consideration for sale of a copyrighted software and not for use of any copyright - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Revenue earned from supply of software by assessee, a tax resident of USA, on a non-transferable, non-exclusive basis to Indian customers was not taxable as royalty income under provisions of article 12 of India-USA DTAA as same was consideration for sale of a copyrighted software and not for use of any copyright  INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where receipts from annual maintenance contract was inextricably linked to licence granted by assessee to its licensees and no human intervention was required in provision of AMC services, said receipts were not taxable as FTS in India, same were business profits of assessee not taxable in India in absence of a permanent establishment (PE) of assessee in India

facts.text:
The assessee was a marketing and development company of an international group, owned by its holding company incorporated outside India. The said group was a leader in civil engineering software and had developed a software called Mx, which was used for civil engineering works in various countries throughout the world. Based on the market position and business potential of the said software and related products in India, a branch office of the group was established in India after obtaining necessary approval, mainly for import and supply of software and also to provide support services including system related services such as, installation of software; interface to peripherals; uninstallation; imparting of training on the application of software, etc. For the relevant assessment year, the assessee filed the return of income showing the receipts from sale/licensing of the software. It claimed that it was entitled to deduction of purchase cost of software, as well as other related expenses from the aforesaid receipts and the net profit so arrived at alone could be taxed as its business profit as per Article 7 of the DTAA. The Assessing Officer rejected its claim holding that the entire amount received by the assessee-company from transfer of software as well as other incidental services, such as installation of software; imparting of training, etc., was in the nature of royalty under section 9(1)(vi) and such royalty income having been accrued or arisen to the assessee-company through its PE in the form of its branch office in India, the same was chargeable to tax in India as per Article 13(6) of the DTAA. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The assessee, a tax resident of USA, was engaged in the business of developing and marketing of telecommunication equipments and related software. The assessee had entered into agreements with certain India telecommunication companies, such as, Bharti, Tata and Reliance for supply of basic telecom infrastructure equipment software and assisting them to set up telecommunication network. The assessee had a branch office in India.

The Assessing Officer noticed that though the assessee had receipts from certain Indian companies, however, the assessee had not offered such receipts to tax.

The assessee submitted that it had sold the software along with hardware (equipments) on outright sale. The assessee submitted that the software sold by the assessee was embedded in the hardware and only for the purpose of operating hardware. Therefore, it could be treated as royalty.

Referring to agreements entered with various Indian telecommunication companies, such as, Bharti, Tata, and Reliance, the Assessing Officer concluded that the receipts from transfer of right to use the software were in the nature of royalty and the assessee had a branch office in India and as the agreements with the Indian telecommunication companies had been signed in India by an employee of the branch office, the royalty income was connected to the branch office, which constituted permanent establishment (PE) of the assessee in India. Thus, he held that the receipts would be taxable in India, as royalty income, both under section 9(1)(vi), read with section 115A/44D as well as under the India-USA DTAA, since, the assessee had a PE in India in terms of article 5. He further observed, even assuming assessee's claim that the receipts were not in the nature of royalty income was correct, still they would be taxable as business profits under article 7(1) of the treaty, as, the assessee had a PE in India.

The Commissioner (Appeals) held that insofar as receipts from Bharti and Tata were concerned, since the assessee had transferred limited, non-transferable, non-exclusive right to use the software solely in the operation of telecommunication equipments purchased by them, such receipts could not be treated as royalty income. However, he observed, since, the agreement with Reliance was, differently worded, in the sense, that a perpetual, irrevocable, exclusive, unrestricted licence had been granted, the receipts from Reliance would be taxable as royalty income and receipts from supply of software as business profit were taxable as business profit under article 7 of India-USA DTAA as the assessee had a PE in India and such receipts were integrally connected to the PE.

The assessee was a company incorporated in USA. It entered into an agreement with a software company, Oracle, in terms of which it obtained non-exclusive user right of a software owned by said company.

The assessee had two subsidiaries in India namely, CIL and CDS. It agreed to grant those companies user rights of software acquired from Oracle.

The assessee claimed that fees received from CIL and CDS for granting right to use software in question could not be treated as royalty or fee for technical services.

The assessee thus treated said income as business profit under Article 7 of the DTAA between India and USA and since it did not have PE in India income in question was claimed as exempt.

The Assessing Officer, however, opined that the payments received were royalty covered under section 9(1)(vi) and same was taxable in the hands of the assessee in India.

The Assessing Officer also examined the Articles of DTAA between India and USA and held that the amount of fee partook the character of the royalty within the meaning of Article 12(3) of the DTAA and, thus, it was taxable in the source country i.e. India.

The DRP confirmed the order passed by Assessing Officer.

On appeal:

The assessee, viz. Qad Europe B.V., was a company incorporated in Netherlands. It was also a tax resident of Netherlands. The assessee entered into a software licence agreement with an Indian company namely HLL. In pursuance to the agreement entered into with HLL, ERP software was sold by the assessee-company to HLL. Income arising from the said transaction was treated as business income by the assessee-company, and in absence of any PE in India, the same was not offered to tax in India.

According to the Assessing Officer, the payment received by the assessee-company on account of sale of ERP software product to HLL amounted to 'Royalty' and, therefore, it was taxable in India in the hands of the assessee-company under section 9(1)(vi).

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal:

The assessee-company had purchased software primarily consisting of software AMC's from third-party vendors outside India for and on behalf of all of its group companies, including AI. Out of the software charges paid by the assessee to the vendors, it had allocated certain amount towards charges recoverable from AI and claimed the same as reimbursement on an 'at-cost' basis and without any profit element. Therefore, the same was not offered for tax in the return of income filed by the assessee.

The Assessing Officer treated reimbursement of software charges as income from royalty under section 9(1)(vi) and article 12 of the DTAA based on the facts that the assessee had made payments for the software charges directly to the third-party vendors outside India.

The DRP also upheld the order passed by the Assessing Officer.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee-company purchased different types of software from residents of different countries for its business of oil and gas exploration. It made payment but did not deduct TDS from said payments.

The Assessing Officer, however, observed that the assessee had only got a license to use the software and that no other title or interest in the software was transferred to the payer/assessee, hence, there was no question of sale of software per se. He, further, observed that if at all there was an element of sale, it was only in respect of career media, i.e., CD (Compact Disk) in which the software was transacted/loaded. He held that what the assessee was given was the license to use software and that the payments made for the import of software were in the shape of royalty and as per the provisions of section 9(1)(vi), the income in respect of the same was deemed to have accrued in India and, thus, the assessee was liable to deduct the tax at source under section 40(a)(i) in respect of such payments.

The Commissioner (Appeals) relying upon the definition of 'royalty' as provided under the DTAA held that the payment made by the assessee for purchase of software did not amount to royalty. He held that vide the agreement in question, assessee got the right to use the software for its internal business purpose only and not for commercial exploitation. That the assessee did not receive any copyright over the software. Since the foreign company did not have any PE (Permanent Establishment) in India, its business profits were not taxable in India as per articles 5 & 7.

On appeal:

The assessee company claimed Rs. 93.63 lakhs towards Software expenses paid to its parent company, Atmel Corporation, USA, however it had not deducted TDS on ground that mere reimbursement of expenses on cost to cost basis without any mark-up did not attract TDS under section 195.

The Assessing Officer considered the assessee's explanation and found that it was not correct for the reason that the software expenses were in the nature of royalty as per provisions of section 9(1)(vi). Since the software was used in India for the purpose of business or profession carried on by the assessee in India, he invoked the provisions of section 195 and disallowed the expenditure since there was no deduction of TDS under section 40(a)(i).

The DRP observed that the reimbursement of software expenses on a cost to cost basis without any mark-up would not constitute income chargeable to tax in India in the hands of Atmel US. Accordingly, assessee shall not be liable to withhold any tax under the provisions of the section 195 on such reimbursement. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer made addition of Rs. 93.63 lakhs.

On appeal to the Tribunal the assessee contended that provisions of the section 195 could not be applied as the payment made to non-resident was not chargeable to tax under the Act and there was no question of withholding any tax.

The assessee was a company incorporated in Israel and was a tax resident of that country. It had entered into a contract with ‘R’ for the supply and license of software for the wireless network of ‘R’ in India. The Assessing Officer examined the software license agreement which provided that the assessee had granted ‘R’ a perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive, royalty-free, worldwide license to install and operate the software and the documentation licensed under the agreement for implementation, operation, management and maintenance of wireless network within India. The assessee had claimed that the payment received for supply of software was business income and in the absence of PE in India such business profit was not taxable in India. The Assessing Officer, however, held that the payment made for the supply of software was royalty within the meaning of article 12 of the DTAA and also section 9(1)(vi). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) found out that the agreement did not give any title to the software or any trademark or copyright in it to ‘R’. It was also found that the software license could not be sold, transferred, assigned, sub-licensed or used by any outsourcee of ‘R’ without the consent of the assessee. In view of the aforesaid findings, the Commissioner (Appeals) concluded that payment in question was made only for purchase of copyrighted article and did not amount to royalty within the meaning of article 12(3). Accordingly, impugned addition made by the Assessing Officer was deleted.

On revenue’s appeal :

The assessee, a company incorporated in the United States and resident of USA for taxation purposes, was a leading provider of information solutions. The company operated globally through the presence of subsidiaries in other countries. In India, it entered into joint venture company with 'NIPL' which acted as a distributor for the company and imported certain software from the assessee and duplicated and sold or sometimes resold the same in the Indian sub-continent. It was noticed by the Assessing Officer that in the relevant assessment year, the assessee received royalty as per the distribution agreement amounting to Rs. 1.76 crore towards sales made by NIPL which was offered by the assessee as royalty income. The Assessing Officer accepted the said amount as royalty income and taxed it accordingly. The assessee was also found to have received a sum of Rs. 58.29 lakhs from NIPL towards the direct sale of software, which were subsequently resold by NIPL to its end customers. The assessee claimed such amount from sale of software as business income and in the absence of it having permanent establishment in India as per article 5 of India-USA treaty, not chargeable to tax.

The A.O. held that a sum of Rs. 58.29 lakh declared by the assessee as business income from the sale proceeds of software also represented royalty income covered under article 12(3) of the DTAA. In his opinion there was no difference between two situations viz., firstly, in which the NIPL acquired the right to duplicate for which the assessee received income of Rs. 1.76 crore and; secondly in which NIPL acquired software as such from the assessee for a sale consideration of Rs. 58.29 lakh. He, therefore, treated the entire amount of Rs. 2.34 crore as royalty income and charged tax accordingly. The Commissioner (Appeals) echoed the assessment order.

On second appeal:

The assessee was a tax resident of the USA and was a developer, marketer and seller of robotic process automation (RPA) technology and related products and services. During the year under consideration, the assessee company received certain receipts from its Indian clients. There was a subsidiary of the assessee company which had been appointed by the assessee under inter-company agreement to provide services to AA Inc. in the nature of Developing Robotic Process Automation (RPA) related software development.

The Assessing Officer proceeded to hold that the assessee had a PE in India in form of subsidiary and attributed 25 per cent of receipts on account of the software license fees as attributable to the PE and, consequently, taxable in India as business income.

On appeal, the assessee had objected to the attribution of profit in respect of the PE of the assessee in India.

■

The assessee, a US company, was engaged in providing localization and translation solutions. It had entered into agreements titled 'Contract Localization Services' with its group entities including with its Indian entity. As per the said agreement, back office support work was outsourced to its Indian subsidiary, the Indian entity. The assessee was also stated to have entered into multiple user master agreements with third parties such as Microsoft, Adobe and Dell for use of programs and software such as Microsoft Windows, Outlook, MS Office and others and the software so procured was stated to have been thereafter deployed on the system of users of its group entities by third parties. The aforesaid software was to be used by the group entities for their internal use and who in turn were liable to reimburse the assessee for the cost of such programs and softwares on the basis of the number of users of such programs/licenses of the concerned entity.

■

The assessee filed application for Nil withholding tax certificate under section 197.

■

Meanwhile, the assessee’s return was selected for scrutiny and the Assessing Officer passed the draft assessment order holding that since assessee had purchased software and installed same in premises of its group entities, assessee had been charging its subsidiaries in India as well as across globe ‘in lieu of provision of usage of infrastructure in place’ and, thus, receipts towards reimbursement of cost was in nature of royalty.

■

In view of the above and resting its decision on the draft assessment order , the revenue proposed the tax withholding certificate under section 197 being issued at rate of 9.99 per cent .

■

On writ :

The assessee was carrying on the business of development of software package and agency software products. In the relevant assessment year, it claimed deduction under section 37 in respect of royalty expenses. It also claimed that it had made the said payments towards royalty for 'duplicating' the software by the name of 'Ingres' in India and supplying the same to the end users and that the ownership of the said software was retained by Ingress Corporation which is an American based multi-national company; and that for each copy, which stood duplicated and sold to the customers in India, the assessee had paid royalty to the American Corporation based on its sale value and, thus, such payment towards royalty formed part of the expenditure incurred by it in making the sales. The Assessing Officer held that only one-sixth of the amount was allowable in view of section 35AB and, accordingly, after allowing the benefit under section 35AB, he made disallowance of the balance amount, which was added back to the income of the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner(Appeals) deleted the addition which view was confirmed by the Tribunal. The High Court refused to entertain the revenue's appeal.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

Microsoft Corporation (MS Corp) a US based company, had directly entered into agreements with various Indian distributors for sale of Microsoft products being ‘off the shelf’/‘shrink wrapped’ software, on principal to principal basis. The Indian Distributors, in turn, sold these Microsoft products to re-sellers/consumers. The above business model continued up to 31-12-1998. From 1-1-1999, the Microsoft products were sold by Microsoft Regional Sales Corporation [MRSC], USA, to Indian distributors, through its branch office in Singapore. The business model with effect from 1-1-1999 onwards was as follows:- (ia) MS Corp entered into agreement on 1-1-1999 with assessee, i.e., Gracemac Corporation, USA, a hundred per cent subsidiary, to grant an exclusive licence, to manufacture in the retail territory the MS retail software products including all updates as developed from time to time and to distribute such MS retail software products manufactured by its subsidiary or so manufactured by a sub-licensee or sub-contractor of subsidiary, in accordance with terms of the license agreement or the previous licenses. (ib) MS Corp also granted an exclusive right to license any third party in the retail territory to grant directly to customers the right to reproduce the software portion of MS retail products for internal use. (ii) Gracemac, in turn, entered into a license agreement with Microsoft Operations Pte. Ltd. (‘MO’), Singapore, under which ‘MO’ was granted non-exclusive license to manufacture (reproduce) Microsoft software in Singapore; non-exclusive license to distribute the software products so manufactured to retailers or to MS Corp or to subsidiaries of MS Corp; and non-exclusive right to license or sub-license the right to reproduce Microsoft software to certain end users (large account customers) for their internal use. (iii) MO, in turn, entered into a non-exclusive distribution and inter-company services agreement (distribution agreement) with MRSC, Singapore, for appointing MRSC as a distributor for selling the copies of Microsoft software which were reproduced/manufactured by MO. (iv) MO sold all the software copies to MRSC in Singapore. MRSC, in turn, had entered into agreements with various distributors in various countries including India. The distributors had a right to distribute the copies of software in their respective countries. (v) The Microsoft software copies were delivered by MRSC to the Indian Distributors "Ex-warehouse" in Singapore. The distributor sold the products to the re-sellers in India which, in turn, sold them to the end users. (vi) MS Corp entered into agreement with end users to use the software products licenced to them as per terms of agreement.

The Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had granted the right to MO for manufacture and distribution of software in India. The assessee’s source (of income) was MO which was distributing software in India through another group concern, i.e., MRSC. The agreement clearly stated that the assessee was getting royalty out of licensing of software carried out in India. The Assessing Officer referring to provisions of article 12(3) of the Indo-US Treaty noted that royalty and fee for included services would be deemed to arise in a Contracting State when payer was a resident of that State. The Assessing Officer was of the view that the payment was for the right to use the copyright in the programme, i.e., the software and not for manufacturing of tangible products. According to the Assessing Officer, there was no dispute to the fact that as per article 12(2), the royalty was to be taxed in India if it was arising in India. Since the payment of royalty was directly related to source in India, the Assessing Officer treated the sale as taxable in India. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the stand taken by the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal:

■

The assessee, a tax resident of USA , was engaged in healthcare business for the General Electric (GE) group, and was a global medical device provider. In the assessment year under dispute, the assessee received an amount as reimbursement of software licence fee cross charged to its affiliates in India which was not offered to tax in India by the assessee. The assessee explained that the amount received, being in the nature of business income under article 7 of India - USA DTAA, was not taxable in India in absence of a Permanent Establishment (PE).

■

The Assessing Officer, however, did not accept the claim of the assessee and proceeded to frame the draft assessment order by holding that the reimbursement of software licence fee was to be treated as income from other sources under section 56(1) and article 23(3) of the tax treaty.

■

The Dispute Resolution Panel upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

The assessee provided off-the-shelf software and related support services to its associates in India. The said amount was claimed as exempt being reimbursement of expenses.

The Assessing Officer as well as the DRP held same as royalty chargeable to tax in India under section 9(1)(vi).

On the assessee's appeal before the Tribunal:

■

On the basis of the information appearing on the Insight Portal of non-filing monitoring system, the revenue noticed that various payments were made to the assessee in respect of which tax had been deducted at source by various entities and issued notice under section 148A(b) on ground that as assessee had not filed return , said income remained unexplained and appeared to have escaped assessment.

■

The assessee submitted that it was a foreign company and was engaged in the supply of software and it procured software from its vendors on a principal-to-principal basis for purposes of sale/resale to its customers situate across the globe including India and in the course of that sale no right to reproduce, sub-licence, modify or translate any software was transferred. Thus, the assessee took a stand that monies received from the sale/resale of shrink-wrapped software would not amount to royalty so as to be taxable and even if the income so generated were to be viewed as business income, the same would not be taxable in the absence of a Permanent Establishment (PE) of the assessee existing in India and, hence, the question of unexplained income did not arise in the case at hand.

■

The Assessing Officer passed the order under section 148A(d) observing that though the assessee had claimed that the income was exempt but since the assessee had not filed ITR and end user licence agreement between parties, income could not be claimed as exempt.

■

On writ:

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of manufacturing, trading and sale of pharmaceutical products as well as manufacturing of ready-to-eat food products. The assessee claimed that its Netherlands based associated enterprise had purchased software on licence from a company named Microsoft for use by all its group entities and licence fees paid by said fee for software to Microsoft was apportioned at actuals to all Group entities and share of the assessee was reimbursed to its AE on the basis of actuals. Said amount, thus, represented purely reimbursement of expenses to AE and, thus, the assessee claimed that it was not liable to deduct tax at source on said payment.

The Assessing Officer observed that the said amount was paid by the assessee for the use of software and since it was taxable as royalty as per the provisions of the Act as well as the DTAA between India and USA, the assessee was required to deduct tax at source under section 195. As the assessee had failed to comply with the said requirement, the Assessing Officer invoked section 40(a)(i) and disallowed the same.

The Commissioner (Appeals) agreed with the view taken by the Assessing Officer.

The assessee contended that the same issue had already been decided by the Tribunal in assessee's case in favour of the assessee in earlier year.

The assessee, a US based company, was engaged in the business of supply, installation and commissioning, maintenance, consultancy and training of softwares which were used in connection with the prospecting for production exploration and extraction of mineral oils.

Assessee had supplied its software to various Indian companies. The assessee had also rendered services in relation to installation and commissioning and providing training to the employees of the Indian companies to use the software.

The assessee claimed that it did not have PE in India and, thus, income arising from sale of software was not taxable in India.

The Assessing Officer opined that the title of goods (being software) was to pass outside India. However, owing to the fact that the installation and commissioning of the software was required to be carried in India, it was held that a part of the income from supply of software along with income from installation and training from software (calculated on notional basis) was taxable in India.

The Commissioner (Appeals) found that the assessee did not have any office in India and that its activities were not covered by the deeming fiction of article 5(2) of India-US DTAA. Accordingly, it was held by the Commissioner (Appeals) that in the absence of PE, the business profits from sale of software could not be brought to tax in India.

Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition made by Assessing Officer

On revenue's appeal:

The assessee, a US based company, was engaged in the manufacture and production of business support software. It had a wholly owned subsidiary in India, namely, OIPL.

The assessee entered into a 'Software Duplication and Distribution License Agreement' with OIPL pursuant to which OIPL sub-licensed software products to various customers in India. The assessee offered the royalty received under the aforesaid agreement to tax in its return of income.

In the course of assessment, the Assessing Officer accepted that the ordinary course of business of OIPL was replication and licensing of software and therefore, amount received by assessee was to be taxed as royalty in accordance with article 12 of the India-US DTAA.

Subsequently, the Assessing Officer took a view that royalty payable to the assessee by OIPL was linked to its PE in India and by applying the principle of 'force of attraction', the said royalty would be taxable as business profits and not as royalty under article 12 of DTAA.

He thus issued notice under section 148 seeking to reopen the assessment.

The assessee filed instant petition contending that since there was no failure on its part to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for assessment, initiation of reassessment proceedings merely on basis of change of opinion was not permissible in law.

The assessee-company had incurred expenses in foreign currency for purchase of software from Singapore company (QAD).

The case of the assessee was that it had not purchased any copyright in the software rather, it had purchased only a copyrighted article named as 'MFG Pro Software'.

The Assessing Officer, however, observed that the assessee had purchased the right to use the software and the software was used for the business purpose in India. He, therefore, held that the same was liable for deduction of tax at source under section 195 in view of the provisions of section 9.

Before the DRP, the assessee adduced evidence in the form of invoice and other documents/material in respect of the software purchased to prove that the said software had been standard software and that the payment made by the assessee for the said software was a one time payment and not a recurring payment for use of software. It was also explained by the assessee that what it had purchased as a 'copyrighted article' and not the 'copyright', itself, so as to classify it as royalty or fees for technical services.

The DRP had held that the software purchased was a one 'off the shelf' product. However, the DRP further observed that the software was not sold but a license was given to the assessee to use it in a particular manner in consideration of the license fee. Even after obtaining a copy of the software, the assessee required permission to use the software by way of activation on a certified machine. Therefore, payment made by the end user was towards license to use copyright in software and not for sale of software. The DRP, therefore, held that the license to use the software would fall under the purview of royalty.

On appeal:

0

The assessee, Financial Software and Systems Private Limited (FSS), was an Indian company. It was engaged in providing software and related services in Banking and Financial Service Sector. The assessee company had made payments to two non-resident entities. They were ACI Singapore and IRPL Australia. The former company, ACI Singapore was a resident of Singapore and the latter company, IRPL Australia was a resident of Australia.

The assessee company had made payments to these two non-resident companies towards procurement of standard software. The assessee company operates under a distribution model, wherein software products were procured from the two non-resident companies namely, ACI Singapore and IRPL Australia and in turn, supply those software products to various customers in India. But while making payment it did not deduct tax at source. It stated that distribution model did not generate taxable income for the non-resident companies in India and therefore, there was no necessity to deduct tax at source while making the payments.

The Assessing Officer was of the view that the payments made by the assessee company to the non-resident companies were in the nature of Royalty. Royalty generates taxable income in the hands of the non-resident companies, in India. Therefore, he held that the assessee was under an obligation to deduct tax at source, while making the payments, and as no such TDS had been made, the assessee is liable for the consequence of provisions of section 40(a)(i). Accordingly, the Assessing Officer disallowed those payments incurred for procurement of software claimed by the assessee company as expenditure, while computing its taxable income.

It was also considered by the Assessing Officer that even otherwise the assessee was liable for deducting tax at source under section 195 on the ground that the assessee company being a distributor of software products of the non-resident companies, had to be treated as a Permanent Establishment (PE) of the non-resident companies. He held that the assessee was bound to deduct tax at source as the non-resident companies had a PE in India.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal, to the Tribunal the assessee submitted that the assessee company purchases software products from non-resident vendors and re-sells such products to its customers in India. It was a pure trading transaction therefore, no withholding tax would be required. Software products purchased were only copyrighted articles and the assessee did not have any right to copy the products purchased from ACI Singapore and IRPL Australia. The relationship between the assessee company and the non-resident companies was on a principal-to-principal basis.

The assessee, engaged in the business of providing services of internet advertising and marketing services, including e-commerce, showed purchases of online advertisement space and reimbursement of expenses for use of software license to its holding company (associate enterprise), 'K' of USA. The assessee claimed that 'K' did not have a Permanent Establishment (PE) in India and the remittance was towards the invoices raised by K; which was doing independent business. Therefore, the remittance was claimed to be towards the business income of parent company, and as per article 7 of Indo-US DTAA, business income of non-resident company is taxable in India only if it has a PE in India. Thus, it was contended by the assessee that in the absence of a PE in India, the business income of parent company was not taxable, and therefore, there was no question of withholding tax in respect of remittance made by the assessee. The Assessing Officer did not accept the contention of the assessee and held that the assessee was a PE of its parent company in India through which the parent company was doing its business on ground that one of the directors was common in both companies and that both were engaged in similar kind of business activities. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer treated the assessee as an agency PE of 'K' and held that the assessee was required to withhold the tax in making payment to its AE, and consequently, the expenditure claimed towards purchase of online space and reimbursement expenses for use of software license was disallowed under section 40(a)(i).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition by holding that the assessee and parent company were independent parties transacting on arm's length, and therefore, the assessee did not constitute a PE to 'K'. As regards the reimbursement of expenses for use of software license, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the said payment was pure reimbursement and would not constitute a reward or compensation paid for the service rendered. Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that there was no requirement as per law to deduct tax under section 195.

The assessee-Swedish company was providing limited user rights in the software related to Lotus Notes and MS Office to its Associated Enterprise (AE).

On appeal:

The assessee US company developed shrink wrap software and sold the same to its customers in India through distributors. The Assessing Officer held that the payment received on account of supply of software by the assessee was in the nature of royalty and he accordingly, brought the same to tax. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), held that the said payment was not in the nature of royalty and was payment for purchase of copyrighted article.

The Tribunal on identical facts had already taken a view that the sums received by the Assessee for supply of software was not in the nature of royalty within the meaning of Article 12(3) of the DTAA between India and USA and was in the nature of business income and since the assessee did not have a Permanent Establishment (PE) in India the receipts were not taxable in India.

The Tribunal further held that sale of software by the assessee to the distributor or end user did not involve any transfer of copyright either in part or in whole; therefore, consideration paid by the distributor cannot be said to be a payment for right of use copyright or transfer of use of copyright. It has been uniformly held in several decisions of the ITAT that sale of shrink wrap software does not involve receipt of consideration which can be said to be royalty. End user of the software in the case of shrink-wrap software does not have any access to source code. He has only right to use the software for his personal or business use. Therefore, payment received would not in the nature of royalty and could not, therefore, be brought to tax.

Despite the aforesaid orders of the Tribunal on identical facts, the revenue submitted that the decision of the Tribunal required reconsideration and made the submissions that the assessee distributed its software to the end user through its distributors and sub-distributors in India. The Distribution Agreement contained terms and conditions subject to which the software distributor was to distribute the software to the end user. The distribution agreement also contained an end users licence agreement (EULA). The revenue submitted that the end user was granted only a license (EULA) to use the software, which provided for a security mechanism being embedded in the software to ensure that the terms of the license were not violated. The revenue submitted that the assessee had complete control over the use of the software and, therefore, to say that the software was a copyrighted article and not use of software was not correct. Even the distributor got only a license and, therefore, there could be no sale of a copyrighted article as had been held in the earlier assessment years. The revenue principally based on the decision of the Karnataka High Court in the case of CIT (International Taxation) v. Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. [2011] 203 Taxman 477/ 16 taxmann.com 141.

On the other hand, the assessee relied on the decision of the Delhi High Court in the case of DIT v. Ericsson A.B., [2012] 204 Taxman 192 /[2011] 16 taxmann.com 371. However, the submission of the revenue was that the decision rendered by the Delhi High Court was in respect of use of software embedded in an equipment supplied and, therefore, the same should not be applied to the case of shrink wrap software.

Being dissatisfied with the explanation furnished by the assessee in this regard, in the order of assessment the disallowance of Rs. 17.10 crores was made by the Assessing Officer under section 92, read with section 37(1) on account of payment of royalty beyond 30 per cent of the sub-licensing fee earned by the assessee. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee would be entitled to get the deduction in respect of entire amount paid by it to parent company by way of royalty. The order of the Tribunal further revealed that according to it, pre-condition for invoking the provisions of section 92, viz., there was no profit or less than ordinary profit accruing to the resident assessee on account of business connection between the resident and non-resident had not been established. Therefore, section 92 would have no application to the facts of the case. The Tribunal concluded that since the assessee itself had declared profits of amount of Rs. 1227.40 lakhs in the return for the income for this year, it was not the case of no profit. The Tribunal also answered another facet of section 92, viz. , as to whether it could be said that the profits earned by the assessee were less than the ordinary by holding that the Assessing Officer did not bring on record any comparable case as to what was the ordinary profit in this type of business. The case of the assessee was that all these reimbursements had been received in the immediately following year. The case of the assessee was that no element of profit was involved in the reimbursements. Therefore, nothing was taxable either in this or in the succeeding year.

The Assessing Officer held that the assessee had offered to tax all sums received from India as royalty/FTS under the DTAA. However, there were certain amounts from CSC which had not been offered for taxation, not in any year till date. By way of example, it is stated that the amount for grant of software license as per form no. 3CEB of CSC and as per assessee's statement was Rs. 62,22,779; however, the assessee had offered to tax a sum of Rs. 61,81,410. It was further mentioned that the assessee had probably accounted for the amount net of tax deducted at source, but the difference may be due to some other reason also. CSC had claimed deduction of Rs. 62,22,779. There was difference of Rs. 41,369 on this account. There were payments by CSC, which pertain to the current year; however, the income had been deferred to the next year. The accounting for of the income was pending in some cases for two to three years from the date of the transaction. This might be due to fault in the recording of the transactions in the books by the assessee. The difference in the amounts was claimed by CSC and offered to tax by the assessee has been included in the income of the assessee. On this basis, the income of this year had been enhanced.

Two main questions were involved in this case (i) whether, reimbursement of expenses in respect of SAP licenses, RAS charges and travelling etc. are liable to be included in the receipts as royalties/FTS, and (ii) whether, royalty is taxable in the year of accrual or in the year of receipt?

The assessee purchased the software called 'Small World Software' from the Dutch company and bundled it with its own software and, thus, customized it and sold it to its own customers, both in India and abroad.

As the payment was made to a non-resident company, the Assessing Officer held that the payment represented, not the purchase price of the software but, actually, royalty payment to the Dutch company. As the tax was not deducted at source on the alleged royalty payment under section 195(1), the Assessing Officer invoked the provisions of section 40(a)(i) and disallowed the expenditure.

The DRP rejected assessee's objections to such disallowance.

On appeal:

Lionbridge, US had entered into an agreement with Microsoft for the purchase of standard off the shelves software to be used by its group entities across the globe. Lionbridge US had made the payment for the purchase of software, which in turn was reimbursed by the various group entities using the software. The assessee being one of the group entities made the payments to Lionbridge USA as reimbursement of the cost of the software. The assessee's stand was that the acquisition of the software for the use of software did not give rise to 'royalty' or 'income' in the hands of the recipient, because it was purchased off shelf and was merely a reimbursement of cost.

The Assessing Officer held that the assessee should have withheld the tax on the amount remitted to Lionbridge US, as such payment amounted to payment towards 'royalty'. Accordingly, he treated the assessee as 'assessee-in-default' under section 201(1).

The Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal:

■

The assessee, a US company engaged in development and licensing of software products, had a wholly owned Indian subsidiary, Oracle India Pvt. Ltd. (OIPL), carrying out software development activities in India.

■

Revenue authorities alleged that OIPL constituted assessee’s permanent establishment in India under articles 5(1), 5(2), 5(4) and 5(5) of India-USA DTAA and attributed business profits to such alleged PE.

■

For assessment years 2006-07 to 2012-13, Assessing Officer treated OIPL as fixed place PE, service PE and agency PE and computed profits attributable to alleged PE; such findings were sustained by Commissioner (Appeals)/Dispute Resolution Panel.

■

On appeal to Tribunal

The assessee, a non-resident company, was operating airlines services worldwide. A notice was issued to the assessee asking it to submit the name of the reservation system used by it with the name of Company Owning it. In response to said notice, the assessee replied that they were using AXESS system of reservation belonging to it. The Assessing Officer informed the assessee that the income earned by it on account of the use of AXESS reservation system (software) was taxable in India. The assessee replied that it did not earn any income by the use of AXESS as the same was owned by it and it was for self use only and was not given to any one for use. The Assessing Officer was not convinced by the explanation of the assessee and was of the view that the assessee had been non-co-operative in its attitude as well as had been misrepresenting the facts before him. He observed that the assessee had entered into agreements with several airlines by virtue of which those airlines or any travel agent could access the software owned by it for which the assessee was to receive certain payments through IATA clearance house. As per the agreement, the assessee was to maintain and operate the AXESS system and provide standard functionalities specified in the schedule to the agreement. The Assessing Officer, therefore, inferred that the payment received by the assessee was covered under the term 'royalty' as provided in the DTAA and levied tax.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) took note of the communication sent out by the assessee to various airlines informing them that with effect from 1-4-1994, the AXESS Airlines Participation Agreement was assigned to its subsidiary AXESS International Network Inc. and came to conclusion that with effect from 1-4-1994, AXESS did not belong to assessee and there was no question of accrual of any income to the assessee in India.

On appeal:

The assessee was a subsidiary of a German company, engaged in the business of supply of assemblies/sub-assemblies of metallurgical equipment, provisions of consultancy and technical services in design and engineering to ferrous and non-ferrous sectors.

During relevant year, assessee made payments of SAP charges to AE for use of licensed software as intranet without deducting tax at source.

The Assessing Officer took a view that said payment amounted to royalty under section 9(1)(vi) as well as under article 12(3) of India-Germany DTAA, liable to tax in India. He thus disallowed payments in question on account of non-deduction of tax at source.

The Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the said disallowance.

The assessee filed the instant appeal contending that it was a case of reimbursement of expenses and therefore, no tax was required to be deducted thereon.

On second appeal:

The applicant, an Indian company, entered into an agreement with a non-resident American company for securing license of a particular software, which the applicant is entitled to use. The applicant has to pay license fee for the same to the American company. According to the applicant, the said company does not have any establishment/office in India and, therefore, the payments received by it from the applicant, for allowing it to download and use the software, are covered under article 7 of the DTAA, i.e., business profits, which are not chargeable to tax in India. On these facts, the applicant sought ruling of the Authority as regards the question as to whether periodical payments made by it to the American company in connection with the use of software developed by it on internet are subject to tax deduction at source under DTAA with USA. The jurisdictional Commissioner submitted his comments stating, inter alia, that as per Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi), the use of software falls under the category of 'royalty' and, consequently, payments would be covered under article 12 of the DTAA and the applicant is liable to deduct tax at source while making payment to that non-resident person.

■

The assessee is a non-resident company having a wholly owned subsidiary in India, OIPL, which performed software development/support activities in India under inter-company arrangements.

■

The AO held that OIPL constituted the assessee’s Permanent Establishment in India as a fixed place PE, service PE and agency PE within the meaning of Articles 5(1), 5(2), 5(4) and 5(5) of the India–USA DTAA, and attributed business profits to the alleged PE. While attributing profits, the AO, inter alia, estimated a portion of global profits to India, restricted deduction under section 44C to 5% of net profits, and did not allow reduction of revenues taxed in OIPL’s hands for software development services.

■

The CIT(A)/DRP, as applicable for the respective years, affirmed the AO’s findings on existence of PE and the profit attribution methodology.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal for AYs 2006-07 to 2012-13.

held.text:
Pattern of invoices from the companies indicates that a specific number of licenses of each software product were purchased by the assessee without acquiring any copyright therein and it was allowed user of such licenses by its group entities including India for which it got reimbursement of cost. Thus it is obvious that the licensors permitted the assessee only to install, operate and use their software products to the extent of copies purchased by it. [Para 6]

The primary contention of the assessee has been that the receipt is in the nature of reimbursement and hence not taxable. In principle, chargeability is attracted on the income element embedded in a revenue receipt. A receipt de hors profit element, which is only Reimbursement, is not taxable. However, it needs to be examined from the facts if it is really a case of Reimbursement. The assessee made factual submission before the DRP to the effect that: 'Husco USA centrally negotiates and procures standardized software from third party vendors, without any customization or modification, for the use of self and for use by Husco group entities globally and distributes the same to the group/affiliate companies as per their requirement'. When the DRP sent the relevant material to the Assessing Officer for his comments, the Assessing Officer, did not approve the contention of Reimbursement. The assessee in response to the Assessing Officer's comments, stated that the appellant had paid such amount to third parties for expenses incurred on behalf of the Indian group entity which was later on cross-charged at actual cost basis to the Indian group entity. From the stand of the assessee taken before the Assessing Officer/DRP, it is evident that it set up a case that it purchased certain number of licenses of different software and charged, inter alia, the Indian entity for the licenses issued to the latter. However, the written submissions before the Tribunal narrates a different story. It demonstrates that the costs incurred by the assessee on all the software products purchased from PTC Inc. and two other vendors were aggregated and such total invoice value was allocated between five entities including the assessee itself on the basis of number of employees of each entity. A fortiori, it is a case of 'allocation' of the aggregated costs on the basis of number of employees and not 'reimbursement'. The patent reason is the missing of one-to-one link between the cost of purchase of the software for the Indian entity and its, as such, recovery, which is a condition precedent for 'reimbursement'. Had it been a case of the assessee purchasing a particular number of software licenses from the vendors and then transferring them at the identical price to the Indian entity, it would have amounted to reimbursement. The manner of charging done by the assessee runs contrary to the concept of reimbursement. The contention of the assessee that it cross-charged all the entities without any markup does not advance the case any further. In so far as the Indian taxability of a non-resident is concerned, it is only the amount of revenue from India which matters and not what the non-resident earns from its group entities situated in other countries. Even if allocation of combined cost is without any mark-up, it need not necessarily be reimbursement qua each participant individually. [Para 7]

It is not a case of identical recovery of the exact cost of the designated number of software purchased and transferred to the Indian entity. The very fact that the Indian entity has been charged on the basis of number of employees, divorced from the actual number of software products transferred to it, amply proves that there is no one-to-one correlation between the outgo and income of the assessee on this score, thereby jeopardising the concept of Reimbursement. If the Indian entity is charged higher or lower than what is actually due from it with the corresponding downward or upward adjustment in the share of allocation to the entities situated in other foreign destinations, the dented share of revenue from the Indian entity will affect the Indian income tax due from the non-resident assessee notwithstanding the fact that its overall cost recharge remains without any mark-up. For the foregoing reasons, the contention of 'Reimbursement' is hereby repelled. [Para 8]
