Section 9(6)(b) defines 'royalty' to include consideration for the use or right to use any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment. Since the foreign company provides capital goods, equipment, or tooling and retains ownership, while the Indian manufacturer uses them, any consideration paid by the Indian manufacturer for this arrangement would squarely fall within the definition of 'royalty' under section 9(6)(b). The income is deemed to accrue or arise in India as it is payable by a resident of India, and the equipment is used in India.

Most DTAAs between India and other countries define 'royalties' to include payments for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial, or scientific equipment. If the specific DTAA between India and the country of which the foreign country is a resident includes 'payments for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment' in its definition of royalty, then the income would be classified as royalty under the DTAA. In such a case, the income would be taxable in India at the rate specified in the DTAA, provided the foreign company is the beneficial owner and the income is not effectively connected to a PE in India. If the DTAA does not include such payments in its royalty definition (under the OECD Model), the income would be treated as business profits and taxable in India only if the foreign company has a PE in India and the profits are attributable to that PE.

8.5-11d Classification as FTS - Section 9(7)(a) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 9(1)(vii) of the ITA 1961) deems income by way of fees for technical services (FTS) to accrue or arise in India. Section 9(7)(b) defines 'fees for technical services' as any consideration for the rendering of any managerial, technical or consultancy services (including the provision of services of technical or other personnel). Where the foreign company also provides the installation and training services for the capital goods, equipment, or tooling to the Indian manufacturer to use them, any fees paid by the Indian manufacturer for these services would squarely fall within the definition of FTS under section 9(7)(b). The income is deemed to accrue or arise in India as it is payable by a resident of India.

Most DTAAs have a specific article on FTS (Fees for Included Services). These articles may include a 'make available' clause, meaning the services must not only be technical but also 'make available' technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how, or processes to the recipient. If the foreign company is merely providing equipment and not imparting any technical knowledge or skills to the Indian manufacturer that enable the latter to apply the technology independently, the 'make available' test (if present in the DTAA) would not be met. In such a situation, the FTS will not be taxable in India. If the DTAA does not explicitly contain a 'make available' clause, then any service of a managerial, technical, or consultancy nature will be taxable as FTS.

8.5-11e Computation of taxable income - The taxable income arising to the foreign company, for which the exemption under this entry is not available, will depend on the two factors:

(a)

Whether the foreign company has a PE in India

(b)

Whether the income is such that the presumptive scheme as specified in Section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 applies (corresponding to Section 44BBD of the ITA 1961) (Business of providing services or technology in India, for the purposes of setting up an electronics manufacturing facility).

The taxable income, taking these factors into account, will be as follows.

Business income connected to PE in India

If the foreign company has a PE in India, and the business income earned in India is connected to such PE, the tax liability in such a case shall be computed as per the ITA. If the conditions of section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 is fulfilled; the taxable business income shall be computed on a presumptive basis at the rate of 25% of the specified amount. If conditions are not fulfilled, the actual business income shall be computed as per the general provisions.

Business income not connected to PE in India

If the non-resident does not have a PE in India, the business income earned by him in India shall not be taxable in India. In such a situation, the presumptive scheme of section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 will have no relevance.

The ITA 2025 has combined both provisions of Explanation 1(a) and the third proviso to Explanation 2A of section 9(1)(i) into section 9(9)(f). Sub-clauses (i) and (ii) of section 9(9)(f) correspond to Explanation 1(a) and the third proviso to Explanation 2A, respectively. The deliberate inclusion of 'reasonably' in the ITA 2025 in the SEP context suggests a legislative intent for a potentially more nuanced or proportionate allocation based on overall business functions, assets, and risks. As a result, income attribution under SEP will no longer be distinct from attribution under ordinary business connection cases. Both will now be governed by the overarching principle of reasonable attribution, ensuring consistency and reducing the scope for disproportionate taxation.

3.4-3 Purchase of goods in India for export [Section 9(8)(c)(ii)(A) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Explanation 1(b) to Section 9(1)(i) of the ITA 1961)]

Explanation 1(b) to section 9(1)(i) of the ITA 1961 provides that in the case of a non-resident, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to him through or from operations which are confined to the purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export. In the corresponding section 9(9)(c)(ii) of the ITA 2025, the words used are "purchase of goods in India for the purposes of export out of India".

On a strict literal interpretation, the addition of "out of India" might seem redundant, since "export" universally means sending goods out of the country. However, the expression "export out of India" would primarily serve to explicitly remove any remote ambiguity. It could prevent an interpretation where "export" might be construed to include movement to a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) within India (which is treated as foreign territory for certain purposes but is geographically within India) or other domestic transfers that are deemed exports for other regulatory purposes but do not involve physical exit from India's customs territory. It would clarify that the exemption applies only when goods physically leave the Indian customs territory.

3.4-4 'Transfer of all or any rights' v. 'Transfer or grant of all or any rights' [Section 9(6)(b) & 9(6)(c)(i) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Explanations 2 & 4 to Section 9(1)(vi) of the ITA 1961)]

Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(vi) defines the meaning of 'royalty' which includes "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence) in respect of a patent, invention, model, design, secret formula or process or trade mark or similar property", and Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi) clarified that the transfer of any right, property or information shall include transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

Under the ITA 1961, the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…" was used in Explanation 2(i) & 2(v) to section 9(1)(vi), whereas the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights" was used in Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi). However, under the ITA 2025, the former phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…", and the latter phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights". The corresponding provisions under the ITA 2025 are sub-clauses (i) and (vi) of section 9(6)(b) and sub-clause (i) of section 9(6)(c), respectively.

(a)

(b)

Transaction in respect of goods, services or property,—

(i)

On a literal reading, the transaction could cover both sale as well as purchase transactions. (ii)

On a plain reading, the goods could be physical goods and property could include intangible property .

Judicially, the term "software" is explained as follows:

(i)

Software is nothing but another word for computer programmes, i.e., instructions, that make the hardware work. Software is broadly of two types, i.e., the systems software, which is also known as the operating system which controls the working of the computer; while the other being applications such as word processing programs, spread sheets and database which perform the tasks for which people use computers. Besides these there are two other categories of software, these being: network software and language software. The network software enables groups of computers to communicate with each other, while language software provides with tools required to write programmes. Service PE

The CIT(A) held that the payments under the technical services agreement for the employees visiting India to provide training were covered as FIS under Article 12 of the India US tax treaty and accordingly, no service PE was created. The tax department did not appeal against this conclusion of the CIT(A).

The Tribunal decision on the issue of Fixed Place PE highlights the need to closely analyse arrangements where employees of the foreign entity visit India. However, with respect, the decision has made certain important conclusions without a detailed reasoning of the factual matrix and without establishing that CIS had made available certain designated space to CMG. There is no reference in the ruling to the decision of the Delhi Special Bench in the case of Motorola Inc. v. Dy. CIT7 wherein it was observed that merely because the Indian company allowed the visiting employees of the foreign company to use certain facilities occasionally, it could not be said that the foreign company had at its disposal, as matter of right, certain space which could be characterized as a fixed place of business in terms of Article 5(1) of the tax treaty.It does not appear to examine the relationship between the service-level activities of CMG and those of CIS to determine whether the business of CMG could actually be said to be carried on from the premises of CIS. Further, it upholds the order of the CIT(A) in general but is silent as to whether the presence of employees seconded to CIS had a bearing on the Tribunal's conclusion. It also does not clarify whether economic dependence on the parent company, as observed by the CIT(A), could result into establishing a Fixed Place PE. Lastly, it does not throw light on how provision of certain free of cost hardware and software could lead to the conclusion that CMG has a PE in India.

All said and done, one would definitely worry as the decision could prove to be a dangerous weapon in the hands of the tax authorities who may allege the existence of a PE in case the Indian entity receives support and guidance from its foreign affiliates. It would be hard to find a situation where a subsidiary, especially a captive, does not receive support and guidance and hence the precedent is all the more worrisome.

Whether one agrees with the conclusion or not, it becomes more imperative to take a re-look at the specific roles of the visiting employees vis-à-vis the functioning and overall profile of the Indian entity (whether by way of dependence on the foreign entity or significance in the value chain) and view the same in a holistic manner. Employees expected to perform functions which are more than stewardship activities would typically be present in India for longer durations and hence, steps should be taken to shift the economic employment of the employees to the Indian entity so as to mitigate the PE exposure.

Attribution of profits to the PE

To attribute profits to the PE, the AO adopted a method which involved apportioning the total revenue earned by CMG from global operations based on the number of employees during the year in CMG and CIS.

The CIT(A) held that Profit Split Method was most suitable for determining the arm's length profit attributable to the PE. The approach applied by the CIT(A) entailed calculation based on the revenue from Indian operations. Further, substantial portion of the expenses were disallowed on various counts.

CMG inter alia put forth that, in the case of CIS, the transfer pricing officer made an upward adjustment to the mark-up charged by CIS to CMG by considering comparables as companies which assume normal business risk. Thus, there would be double taxation as on the one hand, profits had been attributed to the alleged PE of CMG and at the same time a transfer pricing adjustment was made in the hands of CIS.

The Tribunal held that no attribution of profits was required to be made on account of entrepreneurial services to manage risk related to service delivery. Also, that there could be no disallowance of expenditure for non-deduction of tax8 as the same is not in accordance with Article 7(3) of the tax treaty9.

The Tribunal observed that attribution of profits should be made in accordance with transfer pricing principles. As the charge for employees visiting India and those seconded to India was subsumed in the transfer pricing analysis of CIS, the Tribunal concluded that attribution was required to be made on account of free of cost assets and software provided by CMG to CIS.

2.8.1 Amendments Explanations 4, 5 and 6 have been inserted in section 9(1)(vi) with retrospective effect from 1-4-1976 so as to clarify that—

(i) the transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred (Explanation 4).

(ii) royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not (a) the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer; (b) such right, property or information is used directly by the payer; (c) the location of such right, property or information is in India (Explanation 5).

(iii) the expression 'process' includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-linking of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret (Explanation 6).

2.8.2 Object

The objective of the amendments as explained in the Memorandum explaining the provisions of Finance Bill, 2012 is as follows:

"II. Section 9(1)(vi) provides that any income payable by way of royalty in respect of any right, property or information is deemed to be accruing or arising in India. The term "royalty" has been defined in Explanation 2 which means consideration received or receivable for transfer of all or any right in respect of certain rights, property or information. Some judicial decisions have interpreted this definition in a manner which has raised doubts as to whether consideration for use of computer software is royalty or not; whether the right, property or information has to be used directly by the payer or is to be located in India or control or possession of it has to be with the payer. Similarly, doubts have been raised regarding the meaning of the term processed.

Considering the conflicting decisions of various courts in respect of income in nature of royalty and to restate the legislative intent, it is further proposed to amend the Income-tax Act in following manner:-

(i) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that the consideration for use or right to use of computer software is royalty by clarifying that transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information as mentioned in Explanation 2, includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

(ii) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not

(a) the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer;

(b) such right, property or information is used directly by the payer;

(c) the location of such right, property or information is in India.

(iii) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that the term "process" includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-linking of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret.

These amendments will take effect retrospectively from 1st June, 1976 and will accordingly apply in relation to the assessment year 1977-78 and subsequent assessment years."

/off-the-shelf software should typically attract sales tax and since no element of service is involved, service tax cannot be levied. However, this argument is bound to fail in view of the very specific provisions under service tax laws. The Hon'ble Madras High Court in the case of Infotech Software Dealers Association has held that transaction in relation to canned/off-the-shelf software can be service in case the developer of software retains the copyright while right to use of software is given to the subscriber. The scenario has become grave for the dealers who prior to introduction of service tax were charging only sales tax on the value of software. Now in view of the specific category under service tax, they need to charge both sales tax and service tax. Since the sales tax and service tax are indirect taxes and to avoid litigation, the dealers tend to charge both the taxes and it is only the end - consumer who has to suffer in view of multiplicity of taxes.

As regards the customized/uncanned software, the contract for development of such software perhaps at the best may be viewed as a service contract. The customized software means software developed for a specific customer to meet his specific requirements. The software industry prior to the introduction of new category of taxable service in the name of 'Information Technology Software Service' was at an advantageous position, as no indirect taxes were applicable on the development of customized software treating it as a service contract. However, the advantageous position got diluted after the introduction of new category as above, as now development of customized software attracts service tax. The dilution has further been deepened after the judgment of the Hon'ble Madras High Court in the case of Infosys Technologies Ltd. in which it has been held that even customized software may qualify as goods.

The sales tax authorities after taking recourse to the judgment of the Hon'ble Madras High Court are issuing notices demanding tax on the transaction involving development of software. The judgment has opened a Pandora's Box of litigations in relation to customized/uncanned software.

Another area of litigation concerning software is supply of software through electronic downloads. In such a scenario, service tax gets attracted in view of the specific language of the taxable service under the category of 'Information Technology Software Service'. However, whether sales tax is also payable is another point where litigation surrounds the software industry. The Hon'ble Karnataka High Court recently in the case of Sasken Communication Technologies Ltd. has observed that intellectual property once put on a medium becomes goods and when transferred is leviable to sales tax. After this judgment, the industry players can hope that the sales tax authorities do not litigate on this issue.

The menace of double taxation is detrimental to the interests of users of goods/services as it results into high procurement costs, especially in those cases where credit of input taxes paid cannot be taken by the users. The domestic users only take a hit as the exporters of software generally enjoy the tax free status and, accordingly, no taxes are charged on the value of goods/services exported from India. Presently, the sales tax (local VAT) rate for software is either at 4% or at 5% and service tax rate is at 10%, which can significantly enhance the costs of procurements in case software suffers double taxation, specifically in cases where the credit of input taxes is not available either in full or in part.

Though the laws on sales tax and service tax are on the statute books for good number of years now, yet the provisions of these laws need alignment, which seems to be an uphill task in view of the fact that the Governments desire to garner more and more revenue and sometimes it happens by introducing provisions which put the taxpayer in a situation where he has no alternative but to resort to litigation.

2.2 Issues regarding Classification - Another controversy that surrounds the software revolves around its classification, especially in those cases where the software is not embedded in the hardware and is procured separately from the vendor of the hardware. The problem is generally faced by the importers of telecom equipments.

At present, the rate of customs duty on telecom equipments is generally at around 15% and on software it is at around 10% in case it is imported say on CD. Due to the difference in the rate of customs duty, the customs authorities always litigate on the genuineness of the imports and try to include the value of software in the value of hardware and, accordingly, make the value of software suffer higher rate of customs duty. This particular issue of telecom industry is yet to test the scrutiny of judiciary but apparently, both hardware and software are classifiable into different customs tariff classifications and different customs duty structure is also justifiable.

2.3 Issues regarding Withholding Tax - Another issue that hovers around software is whether the payments remitted by a resident to a non-resident for software can be said to be one for use of copyright or can be categorised as one for copyrighted article. The issue has over a period of time been interpreted differently by the Appellate Tribunals across India. In case, the amount is categorised as royalty, the Indian entity making the payment is required to do withholding of tax under section 195 of the Income-tax Act.

The Mumbai Tribunal in the case of Novel Inc. v. Dy. DIT [2011] 16 taxmann.com 186 has held that payments made by the Indian distributors to a non-resident for procuring rights to further sell the software to customers in India would not amount to royalty.

Revenue contended that the protocol appended to the subject DTAA showed that the benefit of the lower rate of withholding tax would be available only if the country with which India entered into a DTAA were a member of the OECD at the time of the execution of the subject DTAA. None of the aforesaid countries, i.e., Slovenia, Lithuania, and Columbia, were members of the OECD on the date DTAAs was signed with India.Thus, clause IV(2) of the protocol appended to the subject DTAA would have no applicability.

On writ, Delhi High Court held that a bare perusal of Clause IV(2) of the protocol appended to the subject DTAA shows that it incorporates the principle of parity between the subject DTAA and the DTAAs executed thereafter. Such parity is available qua the rate of withholding tax or the scope of the conventions in respect of items of income concerning dividends, interest, royalties, fees for technical services, or payments for the use of equipment.

However, the principle of parity kicks-in, only if the third State with whom India enters into a DTAA is a member of the OECD. Further, India should have, in its DTAA, executed with the third State, limited its withholding tax rate, on subject remittances, at a rate lower or a scope more restricted, than the rate or scope provided in the subject DTAA.

Once the aforementioned conditions are fulfilled, then, from the date on which the DTAA between India and a third State comes into force, the same rate of withholding tax or scope as provided in the DTAA executed between India and the third State would necessarily have to apply to the subject DTAA.

Therefore, the beneficial withholding tax rate of 5% in India-Slovenia DTAA will apply from the date when Slovenia became an OECD member, i.e., from August 2010. However, India - Slovenia DTAA came into force in February 2005.

5. Income from cloud hosting and its ancillary services neither royalty nor FTS : ITAT

Racksapce US, Inc. v. Dy. CIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 92 (Mum. - Trib.)

The assessee was a tax resident of the USA. Assessee earned income from cloud services, including cloud hosting and other supporting and ancillary services provided to Indian Customers. The assessee filed the return of income and the notes stating that the cloud hosting services were not taxable as 'royalties' under Article 12 of the India-US tax treaty.

The Mumbai ITAT held that the agreement between the assessee and its customer was for providing hosting and other ancillary services to the customer and not for the use of or leasing of any equipment.

The Data Centre and the Infrastructure therein were used to provide these services belonging to the assessee. The customers do not have physical control or possession over the servers, and right to operate and manage this infrastructure or servers vested solely with the assessee. The agreement was to provide simpliciter hosting services and not give the underlying equipment on hire or lease. The customer did not know any server location in the data centre, webmail, websites, etc.

Thus, the income from cloud hosting services had erroneously been held as royalty within the meaning of Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi) as well as article 12(3)(b) of the India-USA DTAA by AO and DRP.

Unlike trade in goods, services do not cross the border or pass the frontier and, therefore, hard to regulate at that point. A ‘service’ is an intangible product and can be supplied easily by using information technology such as calls, fax and e-mail. The important characteristics of services are:—

(a) Services are process.

(b)Transaction in services may require personal contact between providers and consumers.

(c)Some services may have to be regulated.

Where ‘services’ itself moves without the provider or recipient having to travel to another country is referred to in terms as ‘Cross Border Provision of Services’5; whereas when the recipient of the service or ‘consumers’ moves to the country where service provider is established is known as ‘Consumption abroad’ or ‘Movement of consumer’6. Lastly, when the business itself moves to the country where services are to be provided it is considered to be commercial presence which is commonly referred as Permanent Establishment.

OUTSOURCING SERVICES IN INDIA

3. Of late, the outsourcing industry around the world has been confronted with the contentious question of whether outsourced services provided by companies — particularly by captive service providers/manufacturers — would lead to a Permanent Establishment (PE) of the non-resident service recipient to come into existence under the terms of the relevant tax treaty. India has been a major beneficiary in the outsourcing boom, and, hence, if Indian tax authorities were to hold that such activities are tantamount to a PE, the global profits attributable to the PE would be taxable in India at the rate of 42.23 per cent7. Further, the availability of a tax credit in the home jurisdiction for such tax paid in India would be uncertain, potentially leading to double taxation and wiping out the economic advantage of outsourcing to India. On the other hand, if no PE exists, no profits can be subjected to Indian corporate tax.

In India, tax liability is based on the structure of the outsourcing contract and the scope of activities being undertaken. The generally preferred models, like third-party service providers, captive centres set up as wholly owned subsidiaries or outsourcing to transition partners on a BOT basis are taxed differently under Indian tax laws. Companies establishing captive facilities and BOT arrangements have to consider issues relating to transfer pricing and permanent establishment.

The Court took the view that MSCo being an international company was entitled to insist on quality control and confidentiality in the services provided by MSCo. Stewardship activities involve briefing of the MSAS staff to ensure that the output meets the requirements of the MSCo. These activities include monitoring of the outsourcing operations at MSAS. The object is to protect the interest of the MSCo. These stewards are not involved in day-to-day management or in any specific services to be undertaken by MSAS. The stewardship activity is basically to protect the interest of the customer. Hence, contrary to the ruling of the AAR, the stewardship activities would not constitute a service PE under article 5(2)(l).

Moving ahead, the concept of a service PE finds place in the U.N. Convention19. It is constituted if the MNE renders services through its employees in India, provided the services are rendered for a specified period. In cases where the activities of the MNE entail it being responsible for the work of deputationists and the employees continue to be on the payroll of the MNE or they continue to have their lien on their jobs with the MNE, service PE can emerge. Applying the above tests to this case, the Court concluded that the employees deputed by MSCo. retain their lien on their jobs are on the payroll of MSCo. and on completion of tenure of two years repatriate back to his parent job. Hence, so far as the deputationists are concerned, a service PE under article 5(2)(l) does emerge.

Hence, the judgment makes it clear that activities in the nature of preparatory or auxiliary services, though carried out at fixed place, do not qualify as a PE. Similarly, the activities in the nature of back-office operations and inability to enter into or conclude contracts independently, would not give rise to an agency PE.

Whilst pronouncing its judgment, the Supreme Court held that definition of PE, as adopted by India, is an inclusive definition which covers, among others, service PEs, agency PEs, software PEs, etc. In passing such, the Supreme Court made reference to software PEs, where service providers may be required to act according to quality control specifications of their customers. However, this does not assist in determining the scope of software PEs and has, in fact, left room for uncertainty.

The Software Value Chain

A typical software development value chain entails various functions, starting from the Conceptualization and Design phases to Software Development, Testing, Bug fixing etc. and finally the delivery of the software module to the end customer and maintenance of the software after delivering the same. While an independent software entity would be responsible for all the phases, the role of a captive is usually limited to only a few of these phases. Particularly captives in majority of the instances are neither involved in the design or conceptualization phase nor are responsible for the delivery of the final product to the end customer. Their role is restricted to the specific portions of the software development process that is outsourced to them. Many of the GICs would typically receive a steady flow of work from their parent companies and they need not engage in any selling and marketing activities to bid for projects for themselves. Although they are responsible for the quality of services rendered to their related parties, they do not assume the majority of the risks pertaining to the business. In most cases, even if there is any re-work necessary, they are remunerated for the rework costs incurred. The most common compensation model for GIC is a cost plus remuneration model wherein they earn a fixed margin on their total operating costs and they are absolved from majority of the risks. For example in case of turmoil in the market condition, GICs would continue to earn a consistent margin.

Unlike the GICs, full-fledged software developers undertake all the functions, bear all the risks and might own/develop intangibles in the course of its business. This helps them to command a better price and earn higher profits in the market or losses depending on the market conditions such as demand vs. supply, type of market they are operating, economic conditions, etc. In contrast a typical GIC's functions would not involve the development or usage of any non-routine intangible that allows it to earn high profits for itself. Similarly, as GICs do not bear any entrepreneurial or business risk, even if the parent company is facing losses, GIC's margins will not be affected.In a nutshell, the business of a typical GIC does not witness much fluctuation and is insulated by a good measure from the risks and challenges that plagues a full-fledged software developer.

Hence, going by the economic rationale that higher risks would be compensated with higher expected return over a time period and vice versa, a full-fledged software developer would earn higher expected return in the long run, when compared to a typical GIC. However this fact has not been appreciated by the income tax authorities in India, as is evident from the several rounds of transfer pricing audits so far. The revenue authorities have compared low risk GICs with software developer who owns intangibles and are placed high in the value chain. GIC are limited risk bearers who need to be differentiated from full-fledged software development companies.

The Indian Transfer Pricing Audit Experience: Challenges

The GICs have been constantly under the scanner of the transfer pricing authorities. Over the years, they have faced extensive audit from both the Assessing Officers and Transfer Pricing Officers and have been questioned over their business model and profitability. As India continues its foray into the globalized world economy, transfer pricing will become a key concern area both from the perspective of investors and the Indian revenue authorities alike. Globally, transfer pricing authorities across economies have become more aggressive in a bid to protect their tax base and revenue. MNCs with cross border operations are thus facing increasing transfer pricing challenges from multiple geographical locations.

However, it is possible that the non-resident entity may have a business connection with the resident Indian entity. In such a case, the resident Indian entity could be treated as the Permanent Establishment of the non-resident entity. The tax treatment of the Permanent Establishment in such a case is under consideration in this circular. During the last decade or so, India has seen a steady growth of outsourcing of business processes by non-residents or foreign companies to IT-enabled entities in India. Such entities are either branches or associated enterprises of the foreign enterprise or an independent Indian enterprise. Their activities range from mere procurement of orders for sale of goods or provision of services and answering sales related queries, to the provision of services itself like software maintenance service, debt collection service, software development service, credit card/mobile telephone related service, etc. The non-resident entity or the foreign company will be liable to tax in India only if the IT-enabled BPO unit in India constitutes its Permanent Establishment. The extent to which the profit of the non-resident enterprise is to be attributed to the activities of such Permanent Establishment in India has been under consideration of the Board.

A non-resident or a foreign company is treated as having a Permanent Establishment in India under Article 5 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements entered into by India with different countries if the said non-resident or foreign company carries on business in India through a branch, sales office etc. or through an agent (other than an independent agent) who habitually exercises an authority to conclude contracts or regularly delivers goods or merchandise or habitually secures orders on behalf of the non-resident principal. In such a case, the profits of the non-resident or foreign company attributable to the business activities carried out in India by the Permanent Establishment become taxable in India under Article 7 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement.

Paragraph 1 of Article 7 of Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements provides that if a foreign enterprise carries on business in another country through a Permanent Establishment situated therein, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other country but only so much of them as are attributable to the Permanent Establishment. Paragraph 2 of the same Article provides that subject to the provisions of Paragraph 3, there shall in each contracting State be attributed to that Permanent Establishment the profits which it might be expected to make if it were a distinct and separate enterprise engaged in the same or similar activities under the same or similar conditions and dealing wholly independently with the enterprise of which it is a Permanent Establishment. Paragraph 3 of the Article provides that in determining the profits of a Permanent Establishment there shall be allowed as deduction expenses which are incurred for the purposes of the Permanent Establishment including executive and general administrative expenses so incurred, whether in the State in which the Permanent Establishment is situated or elsewhere. What are the expenses that are deductible would have to be determined in accordance with the accepted principles of accountancy and the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

Paragraph 2 contains the central directive on which the allocation of profits to a Permanent Establishment is intended to be based. The paragraph incorporates the view that the profits to be attributed to a Permanent Establishment are those which that Permanent Establishment would have made if, instead of dealing with its Head Office, it had been dealing with an entirely separate enterprise under conditions and at prices prevailing in the ordinary market. This corresponds to the "arm’s length principle". Paragraph 3 only provides a rule applicable for the determination of the profits of the Permanent Establishment, while paragraph 2 requires that the profits so determined correspond to the profits that a separate and independent enterprise would have made. Hence, in determining the profits attributable to an IT-enabled BPO unit constituting a Permanent Establishment, it will be necessary to determine the price of the services rendered by the Permanent Establishment to the Head Office or by the Head Office to the Permanent Establishment on the basis of "arm’s length principle".

"Arm’s length price" would have the same meaning as in the definition in section 92F(iii) of the Income-tax Act. The arm’s length price would have to be determined in accordance with the provisions of sections 92 to 92F of the Act.

The CBDT Circular No. 1/2004, dated 2nd January, 2004 is hereby withdrawn with immediate effect.

Arm’s length price

Royalties in general means the payment made to the owners of certain types of rights by those who are permitted by the owners to exercise the rights. The term originated from the fact that in Great Britain for centuries gold and silver mines were the property of the Crown and such 'royal' metals could be mined only if a payment ("Royalty") were made to the Crown.

Royalties thus reflect usage-based payments made by one party (the "licensee") to another (the "licensor") for ongoing use of intangible or tangible assets. Intangible assets are defined as identifiable non-monetary assets that cannot be seen, touched or physically measured, which are created through time and/or effort and that are identifiable as a separate asset. There are two primary forms of intangibles - legal intangibles (such as trade secrets (e.g., customer lists), copyrights, patents, trademarks, and goodwill) and competitive intangibles (such as knowledge activities (know-how, knowledge, collaboration activities, leverage activities, and structural activities). Royalties can be determined as a percentage of gross or net sales derived from use of the asset or a fixed price per unit sold. Further, there also exist other modes and metrics of compensation.

The first leg of the controversy relates to the taxability of the foreign entity, granting the rights. When the user of the right, property or information is resident in one country say India and pays royalties to the owner thereof who is resident in another country say the USA, the amount paid by the user is generally subject to withholding tax in India, the source country. The basic challenge, which is pending before courts relates the characterisation of the certain payments. While the taxpayer contends that the payment received is in lieu of services and not grant of rights, the Revenue Authorities contends otherwise. The most talked about controversy here relates to transmission of data through undersea cables, satellites etc. Other could be where the taxpayer contends that there is transfer of rights in perpetuity and hence the transaction qualifies a sale. The most talked about controversy here relates to usage of off the shelf software products.

The second leg of controversy relates to the treatment of the cost incurred in the hands of the Indian user entity. For the purposes of this article, we are limiting the discussion to the transfer pricing challenges, which arise when the transaction is between two related entities of the group.

Take a simple scenario, a manufacturing enterprise or an inventor may have incurred substantial sums on the development of the property generating the royalties. However, the work of research and testing involves considerable capital outlays and does not always yield successful results. The issue lies in determining an appropriate arm's length return for using such property, which is rather complex. The Revenue Authorities generally raise the challenge from a variety of perspectives, such as (a) why user entity per se has taken up the right; (b) what is the technology granted and how it has benefited the Indian entity; and (c) how to determine the arm's length price.

In this article, we have taken a deep dive into these controversies.

CONTROVERSIES DISSECTED

One of the typical situations giving rise to the transfer pricing controversy involves a Foreign Multinational Group licensing technology/know-how to its Indian affiliate and charging a bundled Royalty. The Indian affiliate would deploy the technology in the manufacturing process and; thereafter would undertake selling and distribution function selling goods under the brand name of the Foreign Multinational Group. In lieu of the rights granted, Indian affiliate would pay a Royalty charge, of say 5%, which will be computed on its net sales. The entities would document their understanding through a written agreement.

The Revenue Authorities generally makes the following assertions upon encountering the above situation:

(a)

The taxpayer has not been able to provide substantial evidence of any tangible benefit arising from the use of such rights and as to why it entered into such an arrangement;

(b)

The taxpayer have not been able to demonstrate that its profits have increased, by use of technology or brand name and no cost benefit analysis was furnished;

(c)

The taxpayer has used Regulatory guidelines to justify the royalty rate and such treatment lacks judicial approval;

(d)

The taxpayer has failed to produce contemporary data, justifying the rate of royalty payout.

With the aid of some or all the assertions, Revenue Authorities at times adjudicate that value of such royalty payment charge is NIL.

In terms of paragraph 1 of article 7 of the subject treaty, the business profits of an enterprise of USA are taxable in India, only if it carries on business through a ‘Permanent Establishment’ (PE) in India. For this purpose, the meaning of ‘PE’ has to be found in the special inclusive definition in the treaty. The profits of the PE so taxable are the profits attributable to the said PE and arrived at by taking into account the deductible expenses in accordance with paragraph 3. As provided in paragraph 2, the profits attributable to the PE are required to be in accordance with the arms length principle.

To put it differently, if in a given case the profits of the PE have been determined, even in the normal course of the business, in accordance with the arms length principle, the question of the Assessing Officer carrying out a separate exercise in this regard does not at all arise; also not envisaged in the subject treaty.

Further, the methodology as per the TPR for determining the taxable profits is basically different; in that, it provides for applying the ‘arms length price’ to the gross income/receipts and to the expenses, separately, and determining the taxable profits on that basis.

The subtle but crucial distinction between the above referred two methodologies (that is, the one as envisaged in the treaty and the other as per the TPR under the Act) will be better appreciated if one bears in mind the old section 92 (which provided for adjustment of profits), which was substituted by sections 92 to 92F with effect from April 1, 2002 [which now provides for adjustment(s) of transfer price(s)].

As is thus seen, the underlying scheme under the Act of the TPR is not compatible but is inconsistent with the arm’s length principle as embodied in the subject treaty. Accordingly, article 7 lends no scope for invoking and applying the TPR in cases covered therein. In particular, in any view, the TPR cannot be invoked and applied in such cases rigidly or in toto.

According to the available information on international practice, the factual position is broadly as under:—

u There are discrepancies in the specifics of each country’s laws concerning the application of the arm’s length principle.

u Different countries may accept different methods of calculating the transfer price. For example, Japan requires that the three traditional methods (i.e. Comparable Uncontrolled Price method, Cost Plus method, and Resale Price method) be systematically discounted before allowing the use of alternative methods, whereas the US accepts the most appropriate method. Some countries may have immature transfer pricing regimes or apply the arm’s length principle in different ways.

For the foregoing reasons, it appears that, it would not, to put it mildly, in any view, be prudent for the tax authorities in India to proceed on the premise that they could rigorously invoke and apply the TPR as per the Act, without having regard to the treaty provisions, or without consultations and specific concurrence of the treaty partner.

6. Where profits include items of income, which are dealt with separately in other Articles of the Convention, then the provisions of those articles shall not be affected by the provisions of this article.

For the purposes of the Convention, the term ‘business profits’ means income derived from any trade or business including income from the furnishing of services other than included services as defined in article 12 (Royalties and Fees for Included Services) and including income from the rental of tangible personal property other than property described in paragraph 3(b) of article 12 (Royalties and Fees for Included Services)."

In terms of paragraph 1 of article 7 of the subject treaty, the business profits of an enterprise of USA are taxable in India, only if it carries on business through a ‘Permanent Establishment’ (PE) in India. For this purpose, the meaning of ‘PE’ has to be found in the special inclusive definition in the treaty. The profits of the PE so taxable are the profits attributable to the said PE and arrived at by taking into account the deductible expenses in accordance with paragraph 3. As provided in paragraph 2, the profits attributable to the PE are required to be in accordance with the arms length principle.

To put it differently, if in a given case the profits of the PE have been determined, even in the normal course of the business, in accordance with the arms length principle, the question of the Assessing Officer carrying out a separate exercise in this regard does not at all arise; also not envisaged in the subject treaty.

Further, the methodology as per the TPR for determining the taxable profits is basically different; in that, it provides for applying the ‘arms length price’ to the gross income/receipts and to the expenses, separately, and determining the taxable profits on that basis.

The subtle but crucial distinction between the above referred two methodologies (that is, the one as envisaged in the treaty and the other as per the TPR under the Act) will be better appreciated if one bears in mind the old section 92 (which provided for adjustment of profits), which was substituted by sections 92 to 92F with effect from April 1, 2002 [which now provides for adjustment(s) of transfer price(s)].

As is thus seen, the underlying scheme under the Act of the TPR is not compatible but is inconsistent with the arm’s length principle as embodied in the subject treaty. Accordingly, article 7 lends no scope for invoking and applying the TPR in cases covered therein. In particular, in any view, the TPR cannot be invoked and applied in such cases rigidly or in toto.

According to the available information on international practice, the factual position is broadly as under:—

u There are discrepancies in the specifics of each country’s laws concerning the application of the arm’s length principle.

u Different countries may accept different methods of calculating the transfer price. For example, Japan requires that the three traditional methods (i.e. Comparable Uncontrolled Price method, Cost Plus method, and Resale Price method) be systematically discounted before allowing the use of alternative methods, whereas the US accepts the most appropriate method. Some countries may have immature transfer pricing regimes or apply the arm’s length principle in different ways.

As pointed further in this article, by virtue of article 27 of the subject treaty, which provides for the mutual agreement procedure, the above aspect would be required to be negotiated and agreed upon between the two treaty partners.

For the foregoing reasons, it appears that, it would not, to put it mildly, in any view, be prudent for the tax authorities in India to proceed on the premise that they could rigorously invoke and apply the TPR as per the Act, without having regard to the treaty provisions, or without consultations and specific concurrence of the treaty partner.

Are there any transfer pricing implications for an existing Indian manufacturing and distribution company to become a contract manufacturer for its foreign parent entity?

Profit is a reward for the functions undertaken, assets deployed and risks borne (FAR). Thus this requires an analysis of the FAR of the Indian company in its existing operational form vis-à-vis its FAR in the proposed new form. Transfer pricing implications need to be determined for two stages – (i ) one time change stage, and (ii) going forward stage.

In the one time change stage analysis, if it is observed that the Indian company is reducing the scope of its manufacturing and distribution FAR in favour of its foreign parent entity, there is transfer of tangible or intangibles e.g. customers, distribution network, etc. and as a result its profits earning are also expected to reduce, it may require the Indian company to receive an arm’s length compensation (as an exit charge) from the foreign parent company for such change. However, in case of an Indian company where there is a history of operational losses being incurred and / or the future projections reflect possibility of operational losses or very low profits, the determination of arm’s length exit charge compensation may result in a Nil or a minimal amount. Evaluation on the need for, and the amount (if any) of arm’s length exit charge compensation is highly fact dependent and will need to be a specific exercise based on facts of each case.

From a going forward perspective, it is important to determine the arm’s length compensation to be received by the Indian company for acting as a contract manufacturer. The FAR for this purpose also needs to specifically consider what and whose is the source of raw material, source of manpower, source of technology, and other important inputs for the manufacturing process besides considering the level of capacity utilization.

Whether a captive back office service provider (compensated on a cost plus X% basis) should pay for various charges to the Head Quarter, and whether this could lead to round-tripping of costs?

In computing the arm’s length compensation for a captive back office service provider, it is important to include all the operational costs related to the activities and services of the service provider. Unless this is ensured, the cost base of the captive service provider may be artificially under-stated (if certain costs are directly borne by associated enterprises) and thereby artificially lower the arm’s length profit to be earned by it.

Some typical examples of costs borne by associated enterprises are discussed here. Cost of personnel deputed to work for (under the directions of) the captive service provider should be recovered, however cost of personnel visiting as representatives of the associated enterprise (in its role as a customer of services) should not be recovered from the captive service provider. Cost of senior group management visiting for stewardship purposes should not be recovered. Common IT and communication costs, common HR and administrative costs should be recovered if these result in specific benefit to the activities and operations of the captive service provider. Costs of any software provided which will enable the captive service provider to execute the required services should be recovered, however costs of a software platform where the service provider is required to merely deliver (not execute) the performed services may not be recovered.

To some extent this may lead to a round-tripping of costs however this may be necessary evil for appropriate determination of cost base and hence the cost plus X% compensation.

Whether the transfer of shares of an Indian company amongst two non-resident associated enterprises would attract Indian Transfer Pricing compliance?

This issue has been discussed in a recent ruling by the Authority for Advance Ruling (AAR) in the case of Amiantit International Holding Limited. In this Ruling, the AAR has held that while ascertaining Transfer Pricing compliance in India, the first question which has to be answered is whether the income is chargeable to tax in India or not. The Transfer Pricing provisions are not independent charging provisions. They merely mandate that income which is chargeable to tax in India is compliant with the arm’s length principle. Hence, where the income is not chargeable to tax in India, the question of arm’s length compliance does not arise. The Ruling in this case is consistent with the earlier ruling by the AAR in the case of Dana Corporation.

2. Digital economy

Digital economy constitutes a shift of traditional business to online business that are enabled by information and communication technologies such as internet, mobile and sensor networks. Some of the key business activities in this space are enumerated below:

Cloud Computing: A new business model in the technology industry is the development of the virtual world a.k.a "Cloud computing". Cloud computing is a model for enabling convenient, on-demand access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources (e.g., networks, servers, storage, applications, and services) that can be accessed with minimal management effort or service provider interaction.

Online advertising: The latest form of marketing which uses the internet to deliver promotional marketing messages to its consumers.

E-commerce: A trading platform for trading in products or services using computer networks.

Under the Act, no specific regime has been prescribed on taxability of income from above-mentioned business activities. Therefore, both the tax payers and the Indian Revenue authorities are facing challenges in addressing the following tax issues:

-

How do enterprises in the digital economy add value in the value chain and make their profits?

-

Determination of place of accrual of income in the absence of a fixed place of business and consequent allocation of taxing rights to the resident country and the source country;

-

Characterisation of income earned by such enterprises;

-

PE implications and manner of attribution of income to such PE.

The definition of PE under the tax treaties entered into by India typically includes the concept of a fixed place PE. However, in the absence of any fixed place of business for any company operating under the digital economy model, the PE definition based on physical presence needs a re-thinking. Specifically in the context of e-commerce, the Commentary of the OECD states that a mere presence by way of a website cannot constitute a PE. Similarly, the interpretation of PE as per tax treaties also generally does not extend to websites, unless the servers on which websites are hosted are also located in the same jurisdiction. However, India (having an observer status to the OECD) has made a key reservation that a website may constitute a PE in certain circumstances, without elaborating on such instances.

Moreover, with the penetration of internet coupled with increase in confidence of on-line buyers, the trend of online advertising / website hosting have drastically been on the rise. The prima facie difficulty arises in respect of determination of source of income from such online advertising i.e. its "situs" and "place of business". It is pertinent to evaluate if mere presence of a search engine in a particular location other than the location of its effective place of management, through the internet or website can constitute PE? It is interesting to note that the Courts2 while explaining the concept of online advertisement, have held that consideration paid to non-residents for online advertising services qualifies as "business profit" and in the absence of PE of non-resident in India, the income cannot be said to be taxable in India.

For businesses engaged in cloud computing, the location of the server is the key to determine the place of PE. Facts and circumstances of each value chain would need to be determined including location-specific factors that increase the value attributable to the server location.

The OECD as part of its Action 1 of the BEPS project seeks to address the challenges in digital economy by shifting of place of taxation to market economies, rather than the home country where the entity is a resident. On applicability of the new measures, profits would be taxed where economic activities take place and value is created. In this context, the relevant limited recommendations of Action Plan 1 of BEPS are:

Wider definition of the term "PE" by curtailing exemptions for activities erstwhile being classified as "preparatory or auxiliary". Foreign e-commerce business having mere warehouses in India for storage and delivering goods sold online may going forward not be eligible for claiming exclusion from PE.

It also suggests modification in the definition of PE to address artificial arrangements through 'conclusion of contract' arrangements.

The report also suggests some additional safeguards which can be inserted in the domestic laws such as nexus rule in the form of significant digital presence, withholding tax on payment for digital transactions and an equalisation levy.

Status of BPO entity

8. The BPO entity in India carrying on the outsourcing activities for a non-resident company, may be its branch or subsidiary company or an independent company.

A branch connotes a physical presence of the foreign enterprise in India. It is an office with an independent administration. Where a non-resident has an office in India and employs staff to carry on its business, it is its branch. A branch office is not regarded as a separate legal entity. Its profits are the profits of a company owning the branch office. It is different from a subsidiary which has a legal entity of its own - CIT v. Stewarts & Lloyds of India Ltd. [1987] 165 ITR 416 (Cal.)—and which is regarded as a domestic company in the country where it is established. The subsidiary company may be a branch office of a foreign establishment under certain circumstances. If it is engaged in transactions with or on behalf of the foreign enterprise as an agent of the parent company in circumstances pointing out to a trading in a host country, it can be said to be performing functions on behalf of that enterprise in the same way as any could do - Fire Stone Tyre and Rubber Co. Ltd. v. Lewellin 37 TC 111. To that extent the subsidiary is the branch office of the foreign enterprise, in spite of it having independent and own legal status.

BPO entity - Taxability of income

9. For taxability of income attributable to the activities in India, the status of the BPO entity has to be first ascertained, whether it is a branch of the foreign enterprise or an independent entity, and then whether the branch qualifies as permanent establishment (PE) in terms of the Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) between India and the State of which the foreign enterprise is resident, or whether the independent entity has "business connection" in terms of the definition under section 9 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961 where there is no DTA. Between PE and "business connection", there is little distinction. In content they are the same.

Maintenance of branch outside India

10. Explanation 3(b) to section 65B(44) of Finance Act, 1994 introduced w.e.f. 1-7-2012 reads as follows - An establishment of a person in the taxable territory and any of his other establishment in a non-taxable territory shall be treated as establishments of distinct persons.

This Explanation has been given to definition of 'service'. In fact, this Explanation has nothing to do with definition of 'service' and is at a wrong place.

However, this Explanation is creating lot of difficulties (may be mainly because it has been placed at a wrong place). This Explanation is being interpreted to mean that HO in India and branch outside India are two different 'persons'. Hence, if the HO in India remits money to maintain branch outside India, it will be treated as 'import of service' i.e. branch outside India is providing service to Head Office in India.

Really, 'shall be treated as establishment of different persons' does not mean 'shall be treated as two different persons'.

Thus, Branch/office in India and branch/office of same business entity outside India will be treated as different 'establishments' and not 'different persons'.

A branch received service from its other branch outside India will not be subject to service tax under reverse charge mechanism as 'import of service', as they are not different persons.

Similarly, a branch in India cannot 'export' service to its branch outside India.

In any case, it would be export of service and not taxable.

Implications for the revenue 3. A no-nonsense ITO, swearing by the letter of the law, may insist upon knowing the comparable uncontrolled price for the same technology. Suppose the foreign company had simultaneously entered into a technical agreement, say, with an Indonesian company, which is not its associated enterprise, for manufacture of the same type of cars with the same technology but had to settle for a royalty of only three per cent as opposed to five per cent/eight per cent from the Indian company. Now he may insist upon allowing only three per cent of the ex-factory price as royalty expenditure while computing the business income of the Indian company on the ground that five per cent/eight per cent is not the ‘arm’s length’ price and only three per cent can be taken as the ‘arm’s length’ price because that price was arrived at without being influenced by the relationship of associates. Of course this will recoil on the tax administration to some extent because having homed in one benchmark, that is, the ‘arm’s length’ price, the same benchmark must be applied when the foreign company’s income by way of royalty from the Indian company is subjected to tax in India. On balance, however, for the revenue in India, there is an overall gain as would be evident from the following hypothetical figures :

Royalty @ 5 per cent on indigenous turnover : Rs. 100 crore

Royalty @ 8 per cent on export turnover : Rs. 80 crore

Now the Assessing Officer invoking the ‘arm’s length’ rule is going to disallow Rs. 40 crore from the first and Rs. 50 crore from the second as the benchmark rate of royalty zeroed in on by him is only 3 per cent. The aggregate disallowance of Rs. 90 crores, translates into an additional tax of Rs. 31.5 crore, given the corporate tax rate of 35 per cent ignoring surcharge. Let us see what the quantum of tax loss would be while taxing the foreign company. On Rs. 180 crore, the tax payable by the foreign company @ 20 per cent works out to Rs. 36 crore. But now that the ‘arm’s length’ royalty rate is only 3 per cent, the foreign company’s income from royalty would be deemed to be only Rs. 90 crore on which the tax liability works out to only Rs. 18 crore. Thus, when we turn about and assess the foreign company, the revenue stands to lose Rs. 18 crore, thanks to the invocation of the ‘arm’s length’ rule. But its invocation still begets additional net revenue of Rs. 13.5 crore. In other words, the additional revenue is entirely attributable to the differential of fifteen per cent in the two tax rates, that is, the one applicable to the Indian company and the other applicable to the foreign company : 15 per cent of Rs. 90 crore is Rs. 13.5 crore. The Indian company may not take kindly to this tax treatment, and may challenge the course adopted by the Assessing Officer on the ground that he has relied upon a percentage which is not the true benchmark. It may be that auto manufacturers found it difficult to get a foothold on the Indonesian market because of intense competition amongst them and, therefore, settled for a low royalty rate. The foreign company of course will not complain because now it stands to get a tax refund of Rs. 18 crore. There is another imponderable. 6.1 Excise duty on software

The abatement available is at 15% of MRP, i.e., excise duty (and corresponding CVD in case of imported packaged or canned software) is payable on 'value' which will be at 85% of MRP printed on the packaged or canned software.

If appropriate excise duty (in case of software manufactured in India) or customs duty (in case of imported software) is paid on basis of MRP valuation by the manufacturer, duplicator or the person holding the copyright to such software, service tax will not be payable on such packaged or canned software - Notification No. 53/2010-ST dated 21-12-2010 - confirmed in MF(DR) Circular No. 15/2011-Cus, dated 18-3-2011.

The service provider should make a declaration on the invoice relating to such service that no amount in excess of the retail price declared on the said goods has been recovered from the customer [why such unnecessary complication which increases chances of litigation?]

'Appropriate duty of excise or customs' means duty payable after considering Exemption Notification issued under section 5A(1) of the Central Excise Act or section 25(1) of the Customs Act.

6.1.2 Charges for installation, etc. - In case of packaged or canned software, really no amount should be charged except MRP. Therefore, in cases where it is claimed that the income is not chargeable to tax in India as per the provisions of the Act being not deemed to have accrued in India under the provisions of Section – 9, the foreign company shall also require to furnish a declaration, in addition to no-PE declaration, that

It does not have and is not likely to have any 'business connection' or 'significant economic presence' in India as defined in Explanation 2 and 2A to Section 9(1)(i) of the Act respectively during the Financial Year.

The Provisions of DTAA is not applicable – When?

It is important to mention here that the provisions of DTAA shall not apply in the situation where the payee or foreign company which has income chargeable to tax in India but it neither has PAN in India nor it furnishes the prescribed documents as required under the provisions of Rule 37BC of the Rules.

What if non-resident constitutes PE/Business Connection in India?

If the foreign company constitutes PE in India as defined in Article 5 of the respective DTAA or business connection in India as defined in section 9(1)(i) of the Act, then it shall be taxed in India as per the provisions of Article 7 of such DTAA r.w.s 9 of the Act read with rule 10 of the Rules wherein the foreign companies are liable to tax on net basis i.e. on its profits attributable to PE in India.

As per the provisions of section 44DA of the Act, the income by way of royalty or fees for technical services in the case of the foreign companies which carries on business in India through PE situated in India shall be computed under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession' in accordance with the provisions of the Act.

Further, such non-resident shall be required to meet with additional compliances like maintenance of books of accounts, tax audit u/s 44AB of the Act, compliances under other laws applicable in India, e.g., Companies Act, 2013, RBI / FEMA compliances, Goods and Services Tax, etc.

In view thereof, if the foreign company constitutes PE in India and books of accounts are not maintained as required under the provisions of Companies Act then the taxable profits shall be determined as per formulary approach prescribed under new draft rule 10 of the Rules.

Compliances in India under Income Tax Act

Return of Income

As per the provisions of section 139 of the Act, every company is required to file its Return of Income on or before the prescribed due date of filing Return of Income. The due date to file return of income in the case of company including foreign company is the 30th day of September of the assessment year (i.e. immediately succeeding the financial year) unless the company has entered into international transaction (as defined u/s 92B of the Act) with its Associated Enterprises ('AE').

As per the provisions of sec 115A(5) of the Act, the foreign company is not liable to file Return of Income in India if –

(a)

Its income consists of only interest or dividend income and

(b)

The due tax has already been deducted from such income

The foreign company may furnish the belated return of income u/s 139(4) of the Act with a late filing fees as prescribed u/s 234F of the Act till the end of the assessment year.

Transfer Pricing Provisions – Audit Report in Form 3CEB

In addition to the requirement of filing return of income by foreign company as explained above, if the foreign company has entered into international transactions with its AE which gives rise to income of foreign company chargeable to tax in India then it is subject to transfer pricing provisions in India and accordingly it should comply with the arm's length principle u/s 92 of the Act.

Accordingly, as per the provisions of section 92E of the Act, such foreign company who has entered into an international transaction with its AE shall obtain a report in Form 3CEB from a CA and furnish such report along with return of income on or before the due date as prescribed u/s 139(1) of the Act. The due date in such a case where the foreign company is required to furnish a report in Form 3CEB u/s 92E of the Act is 30th day of November of the assessment year.

In such a situation, the Indian entity is required to reimburse the cost of the employee to the foreign entity. Very often, ignoring the practical aspects of such arrangements, the tax authorities take aggressive positions and determine taxability involving one or more of the following: treating the reimbursement as subject to withholding tax in India – resulting into economic double taxation of the same income once as salary in the hands of the employees and then in the hands of the foreign company as fees for providing services;

disallowance of reimbursed salary cost in the hands of the Indian entity in the absence of withholding tax on such reimbursements; or

treating the foreign company as having a taxable presence (Permanent Establishment) in India in the form of its employees.

It is heartening to see how the tax tribunal in a few recent rulings4 has decided the aforesaid issues in favour of the taxpayer recognizing that such reimbursements if made subject to withholding tax would result in double taxation and have allowed reimbursements as business expenditure in the hands of the Indian entity where they were purely reimbursements and not regarded to constitute fee for technical services.

4.4 Provision of technical know- how – Whether contract manufacturing

Another controversial area is arrangements involving provision of technical know-how by a group entity to its Indian group entity enabling the latter to manufacture goods for group entities as well as third parties. Tax authorities tend to treat such arrangements as those of contract manufacturing and thus, disallow royalty pay-outs to the Indian entity treating it as a payment to self. In a few recent tribunal rulings5, the issue was decided in favour of the taxpayer distinguishing such arrangements from contract manufacturing.

5. CONCLUSION

The issues emanating from the aggressive approach adopted by the tax authorities, which adversely impact genuine cases, should be addressed both by the tax administration and the taxpayers, otherwise significant time and effort would go into litigation. It is certainly to be ensured that Indian tax revenue should not be lost due to improper characterization. However, it is most desirable that there is reasonable certainty with regard to taxability of remittances from India and of amounts which are deemed to be regarded as Indian sourced income. It calls for the tax administration to lay down clear and unambiguous rules and guidelines for source rules and where some provisions of law are open to interpretation, judicial precedents on similar issues should be followed. This will go a long way in reducing avoidable litigation and bring the much desired certainty in tax matters for multinational organisations. The taxpayers on their part also need to consciously ensure that their documentation is robust and adequately reflect the actual conduct and intent. There is certainly a need to establish trust and spirit of partnership between taxpayer and tax administration. Chanakya, the master of economics has given the guidelines to tax administration as "tax needs to be collected from people as the honey bee collects honey from flowers – without harming the flower itself".
