2.8 Amendments to section 9(1)(vi)

2.8.1 Amendments Explanations 4, 5 and 6 have been inserted in section 9(1)(vi) with retrospective effect from 1-4-1976 so as to clarify that—

(i) the transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred (Explanation 4).

(ii) royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not (a) the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer; (b) such right, property or information is used directly by the payer; (c) the location of such right, property or information is in India (Explanation 5).

(iii) the expression 'process' includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-linking of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret (Explanation 6).

2.8.2 Object

The objective of the amendments as explained in the Memorandum explaining the provisions of Finance Bill, 2012 is as follows:

"II. Section 9(1)(vi) provides that any income payable by way of royalty in respect of any right, property or information is deemed to be accruing or arising in India. The term "royalty" has been defined in Explanation 2 which means consideration received or receivable for transfer of all or any right in respect of certain rights, property or information. Some judicial decisions have interpreted this definition in a manner which has raised doubts as to whether consideration for use of computer software is royalty or not; whether the right, property or information has to be used directly by the payer or is to be located in India or control or possession of it has to be with the payer. Similarly, doubts have been raised regarding the meaning of the term processed.

Considering the conflicting decisions of various courts in respect of income in nature of royalty and to restate the legislative intent, it is further proposed to amend the Income-tax Act in following manner:-

(i) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that the consideration for use or right to use of computer software is royalty by clarifying that transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information as mentioned in Explanation 2, includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

(ii) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not

(a) the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer;

(b) such right, property or information is used directly by the payer;

(c) the location of such right, property or information is in India.

(iii) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that the term "process" includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-linking of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret.

These amendments will take effect retrospectively from 1st June, 1976 and will accordingly apply in relation to the assessment year 1977-78 and subsequent assessment years."

The assessee, Financial Software and Systems Private Limited (FSS), was an Indian company. It was engaged in providing software and related services in Banking and Financial Service Sector. The assessee company had made payments to two non-resident entities. They were ACI Singapore and IRPL Australia. The former company, ACI Singapore was a resident of Singapore and the latter company, IRPL Australia was a resident of Australia.

The assessee company had made payments to these two non-resident companies towards procurement of standard software. The assessee company operates under a distribution model, wherein software products were procured from the two non-resident companies namely, ACI Singapore and IRPL Australia and in turn, supply those software products to various customers in India. But while making payment it did not deduct tax at source. It stated that distribution model did not generate taxable income for the non-resident companies in India and therefore, there was no necessity to deduct tax at source while making the payments.

The Assessing Officer was of the view that the payments made by the assessee company to the non-resident companies were in the nature of Royalty. Royalty generates taxable income in the hands of the non-resident companies, in India. Therefore, he held that the assessee was under an obligation to deduct tax at source, while making the payments, and as no such TDS had been made, the assessee is liable for the consequence of provisions of section 40(a)(i). Accordingly, the Assessing Officer disallowed those payments incurred for procurement of software claimed by the assessee company as expenditure, while computing its taxable income.

It was also considered by the Assessing Officer that even otherwise the assessee was liable for deducting tax at source under section 195 on the ground that the assessee company being a distributor of software products of the non-resident companies, had to be treated as a Permanent Establishment (PE) of the non-resident companies. He held that the assessee was bound to deduct tax at source as the non-resident companies had a PE in India.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal, to the Tribunal the assessee submitted that the assessee company purchases software products from non-resident vendors and re-sells such products to its customers in India. It was a pure trading transaction therefore, no withholding tax would be required. Software products purchased were only copyrighted articles and the assessee did not have any right to copy the products purchased from ACI Singapore and IRPL Australia. The relationship between the assessee company and the non-resident companies was on a principal-to-principal basis.

The assessee, a resident company, was primarily engaged in providing employment background screening services to its clients, which consisted of checks such as education screening, employment screening, address verification, criminal check/verification, reference check, database verification hiring management services, assessment solution which the clients could choose from. The assessee entered into a reimbursement agreement with an American company 'FDAV-US'. It was agreed between assessee and FADV-US that assessee would reimburse to FADV-US at actual cost (with no profit mark-up) for various purchases/upgrades FADV-US which included data cards, application, support software and OS/OS upgrades amounting to Rs. 83,75,075 for the financial year ended 31-3-2008. The Assessing Officer opined that the purchase/upgrades by FADV US which included data cards, application, support software and OS/OS upgrades were squarely covered under section 9(1)(vi) and, hence, were in the nature of royalty as defined under the Act. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer passed an order under section 195(2) holding payments as royalty under the Act and directing to withhold taxes at 10.56 per cent on gross basis as per section 11(5)(A).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the payment for use of software did not amount to payment of royalty within the meaning of term as defined in India-US DTAA or section 9(1)(vii). Alternative, he held that being pure reimbursement of expenditure, the assessee was not required to deduct tax. The revenue thus filed instant appeal contending that the purchase of software through associate concern i.e. FADV-US could not be considered as reimbursement of expenditure. On the other hand, the assessee's case was that it being a case of sale of copyrighted article, payment in question could not be considered as payment for royalty either under the Act or under the DTAA.

The assessee company was incorporated in Netherland and it was operating in international market for safety, security and efficiency of nautical and air traffic. It was awarded a contract by Airports Authority of India (AAI) for supply, installation, testing & Commissioning (SITC) of Advance Surface Movement Guidance Control System (ASMGC) at various Airports. The contract consisted of supply of equipments besides training charges. The assessee claimed that amount received from offshore supply of equipment could not be brought to tax in India.

The Assessing Officer took a view that the assessee had a PE in India in respect of another project and, thus the revenue from offshore supply of equipment was also liable to be taxed. Applying Section 44DA the Assessing Officer brought to tax 50 per cent of amount received towards offshore supply of hardware.

The DRP accepted the contention of the assessee that the PE of the assessee in India had nothing to do with the contract in question and that the action of the Assessing Officer in treating the receipts as business income was not correct. The DRP nevertheless directed that Assessing Officer to treat the payment made for supply of software and its license embedded in equipment as payment towards royalty under section 9(1)(vi) of the Act.

Nothing could be more clear that the contents of the agreement referred to above to show that PTC is the sole owner of the Pro-E software and GEISA/GEIE only has limited right to use the software subject to the conditions stipulated in the agreement. There is no sale of copyright of software, but the sale is only in respect of the rights to use the software and not the right to the code in itself. When once the transaction is very clear that no copyright of the software is sold but only the rights to use the software were sold without impacting any rights to the source code, merely because the assessee puts it to a particular use, such a usage will not relate back to change the nature of transaction from the sale of product to the sale of copyright.

When once the software is purchased for a particular usage under a non-transferable and non-exclusive grant of license, by no stretch of imagination could be said that any payment made for the usage of software could be royalty. Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. (supra), the Hon'ble Apex Court considered the nature of payments made in cases in which computer software is purchased directly by an end-user, resident in India, from a foreign, non-resident supplier or manufacturer, and held that the amount paid by resident Indian end-user/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreement, is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software, and thus, same does not give rise to any income taxable in India.

12. Facts of the case involved in this matter are squarely covered by the decision of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. (supra). We, therefore, while respectfully following the same hold the issue in favour of the assessee and inasmuch as such payments do not result in any income taxable in India, the person referred to in section 95 of the Act is not liable to deduct any tax under section 195 of the Act. We, therefore, hold that the remittances made by the assessee to GEISA towards use of Pro-E software or Global Web are not royalty income chargeable to tax under the Act as well as under the treaty and consequently the assessee cannot be treated as an 'assessee-in-default' under section 201 of the Act for non-deduction of taxes under section 195 of the Act. Grounds of appeal are accordingly allowed.

A perusal of para 1 of article 7 shows that the profits of an enterprise of a Contracting State shall be taxable only in that State unless the enterprise carries on business in the other Contracting State through a PE situated therein. If the enterprise carries on business as aforesaid, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other State but only so much of them as are attributable, inter alia, to that PE. In other words, with reference to the facts of the instant case, the contents of para (1) would mean that ‘RC’, which is an enterprise of USA, shall be taxable in USA unless it carries on business through a PE situated in India. If ‘RC ’carries on business through a PE as aforesaid, the profits may be taxed in India but only so much of them as are attributable to the PE of ‘RC’ in India. [Para 7]

The expression ‘business profits’ is defined in para 7 of article 7, to mean income derived from any trade or business including income from the furnishing of services other than included services as defined in article 12 (royalties and fees for included services) and including income from the rental of tangible personal property other than described in paragraph 3(b ) of article 12 (royalties and fees for included services). The amount that is being paid by the applicant to ‘RC ’is for repairs of hardware (including replacement of defective parts) and services for repairing. If such services fall within the meaning of ‘included services’ as defined in article 12, the amount cannot be classified as‘business profits’. It would, therefore, be necessary to see whether the amount in question satisfies the requirement of ‘fees for included services’. [Para 9]

A plain reading of para 1 of article 12 discloses that it enables the other Contracting State to tax ‘royalties’ and ‘fees for included services’ arising in a Contracting State and paid to a resident of the other Contracting State. In other words, in terms of para 1, royalties and fees for included services arising in India and paid to ‘RC’, a resident of USA, may be taxed in USA. The term ‘royalties’ is defined in para 3 of article 12. It is clear from the sub-para (a) that payments of any kind received as consideration for the use of, or the right to use, any copyright of a scientific work, any patent, design or model, secret formula or process, or for information concerning industrial, commercial or scientific experience, including gains derived from the alienation of any such right or property are contingent on the productivity, use or disposition thereof. If the payment represents consideration for the use of, or the right to use, any copyright or scientific work of any patent, design or model or process, it would fall within the meaning of ‘royalties’. The expression ‘fee for included services’ as defined in para 4 of article 12 means payments of any kind to any person in consideration for the rendering of any technical consultancy services (including the services of technical or other personnel) if such services are covered under either sub-para (a) or sub-para (b). [Para 10]

Sub-para (a ) of para 7 of article 12 incorporates the source rule; it says that royalties and fees for included services shall be deemed to arise in a Contracting State when the payer is that State itself, a political sub-division, a local authority, or a resident of that State. Inasmuch as the payer in the instant case is State within the meaning of article 12 of the Constitution of India or at any rate a resident of India, the payment if construed as ‘royalties’ and ‘fees for included services’ ,shall be deemed to arise in India. [Para 12]

The agreements clearly reveal that the assessee has supplied telecommunication hardware with software. The software provided are embedded in the hardware and are required to operate the telecommunication network. It is a fact on record that the Commissioner (Appeals) after appreciating the materials placed before him was convinced that the software supplied by the assessee was embedded in the hardware and were required for operating the hardware/equipment. Insofar as agreement with Reliance is concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) has taken a different view by stating that the assessee has transferred a perpetual, irrevocable, exclusive, unrestricted licence. [Para 6]

Thus, from the terms of the agreement, it is very much clear that the embedded software has been provided to Reliance only for the purpose of operating the telecommunication equipments supplied by the assessee for Broadband Access Reliance Network. The software licence agreement puts various restrictions and conditions on Reliance with reference to usage of this software. The terms of the agreement make it clear that Reliance cannot itself make copy or duplicate, or permit anyone else to do so with regard to any part of the software, or create the source programs or any part thereof from the object programs. Reliance cannot make the software accessible to any person other than its employees, contractors etc. only for the purpose of establishing and operating the Broadband Access Network. Reliance cannot directly or indirectly sell, transfer, offer, disclose, rent, lease (as lessor), or license the software to any thirty party, except for right to use the software. Agreement further makes it clear that the assessee has not made any independent supply of software to the Indian telecommunication companies. Rather, the assessee has supplied Digital Loop Carrier System (DLC), which is the hardware along with software to operate the hardware. [Para 7]

This fact becomes more clear from the definition of product, which means all hardware and software components and sub-systems are provided by the assessee. Therefore, it is evident that the hardware and software were supplied together as an integral and inseparable package and the hardware and software cannot be operated without each other. Thus, from the aforesaid facts it is very much clear that the assessee has not transferred use or right to use, a copyright of a literary, artistic or scientific work so as to fall within the definition of royalty under Article 12 of India-USA DTAA. [Para 8]

Thus, applying the ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in case of Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42/281 Taxman 19/432 ITR 471, it has to be held that the receipts from Reliance are not taxable as royalty income, either under the domestic law or India-USA DTAA. More so, when the agreement between the parties made it clear that the ownership rights over the software remained with the licensor, the amount received by the assessee from Reliance is not taxable as royalty income. [Para 10]

As regards the decision of the first appellate authority which held that the PE in India is involved not only in providing marketing and support services, but has also sold part of software to the head office, which in turn, was used by the head office in the final product, the agreement for supply of telecommunication equipment along with software was between the head office and the Indian customers. It is also a fact that the telecommunication equipments along with software were supplied from outside India directly to the Indian customers. The payments were also made directly to the assessee by the Indian customers. Though, there is an allegation by the departmental authorities that the branch office has played a role in respect of such supplies, however, in what manner and to what extent the branch office has played such role is not forthcoming from the observations of the departmental authorities. It appears from record that the branch office has developed a patch of the software, which has been sold to the head office. It may be a fact that the patch of the software developed by the branch office was made part of the complete software, which in turn, got embedded in the hardware supplied to the Indian customers by the head office. However, such sale of patch of software by the branch office to the head office cannot be linked to the supply of telecommunication equipment and software by the assessee to the Indian customers, as, the branch office has a very limited and restricted role of supplying patch of the software. Principal-to-principal transaction - Where assessee (a Finnish company) supplied both hardware and software manufactured in Finland to Indian telecom operators from outside India on a principal-to-principal basis under independent buyer/seller arrangements and installation activities were undertaken by its Indian subsidiary, consideration for supply of software was not taxable as 'royalty' [DIT v. Micro Focus Ltd. [2021] 124 taxmann.com 560/279 Taxman 242 (Delhi), SLP granted inCIT v. Micro Focus Ltd. [2021] 133 taxmann.com 264/[2022] 284 Taxman 444 (SC)].

Reimbursement - Recovery or reimbursement of lease line charges from an Indian company would not classify either as 'royalty' or as income attributable to a PE in India [DIT v. Sale of copyright - In order to constitute 'royalty', what is contemplated is a payment that is dependent upon user of copyright and not a lump sum payment made for acquisition of a copyrighted article [DIT v. Ericsson A. B., New Delhi [2011] 16 taxmann.com 371/[2012] 204 Taxman 192 (Delhi), approved inEngineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42/281 Taxman 19 (SC)].

There is a difference between a transaction of 'sale of a copyrighted article' and one of 'copyright' itself; provisions of section 9(1)(vi), as a whole, would stand attracted in the case of sale of copyright and not in the case of sale of a copyrighted article [CIT v. Vinzas Solutions India (P.) Ltd. [2017] 77 taxmann.com 279/245 Taxman 289 (Mad.)].

Views taken by Courts in taxation matter:

Keeping software development out of the ambit of manufacturing is also disconcerting since over the years, various Courts/Tribunals have held software development activity to be manufacturing under various provisions of the Act. Most recently, the Bangalore bench of Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) in the case of Manhattan Associates (India) Development Centre Pvt. Ltd. vs DCIT (ITA No.150/Bang/2019) allowed deduction under the erstwhile section 80JJAA of the Act in respect of employment of new employees to a taxpayer engaged in the business of rendering software development services. The ITAT relied on a Bombay High Court ruling, in the case of ESI Vs. Reliable Software Systems Pvt. Ltd. (2012) 5 AIR Bom R 795, wherein it was held that development of computer software falls within the definition of manufacturing process as per the Factories Act, 1948.

Conclusion

Clearly, software development is a big market waiting to be tapped. And India has all the required ingredients like highly qualified talent pool of technical graduates, low-cost advantage by being 5-6 times inexpensive than US, among the fastest digitising economy in the world, government's push towards Make in India, etc.

The government should thus, revisit its stance of keeping software development companies out of the ambit of 15% tax rate. Alternatively, rather than keeping the sector in the negative list, the government may attach riders in the Act to ensure that only key players in the sector are able to obtain the benefit of reduced rate. It may be provided that like other provisions under the Act, a company would need to obtain a certificate from a Chartered Accountant (CA) certifying compliance with the specified requirements such as

1.

Minimum prescribed employment by a software company along with provision for yearly growth in employee numbers at a prescribed percentage

2.

Minimum investment threshold at the time of setting up the business – This should cover investment made in computer and peripherals.

To conclude, it would be appropriate to highlight one of the key pointers from the speech by Mr. Rajiv Kumar, Joint secretary to the Electronics & Information Technology Ministry, at the Global Exhibition on Services (GES)-2019 at Bengaluru which is testimony to the potential of India's software development industry

"India has done well in software services and our next big opportunity is in software products. There will be USD one trillion opportunity in the software production by 2025 and India has a great chance to tap it."

The assessee company has entered into agreements with ACI Singapore and IRPL Australia for supply of standard software products, which in turn, are to be sold in India to the customers of the assessee company mainly, Banks and Financial Institutions. The software transmitted to the assessee company is installed on a server with identifying location and machine No. of the customer. As per the terms of agreements, the assessee company do not have any exclusive right to distribute the software products. It obtains orders on its own account for customers in India and thereafter places orders with non-resident companies. When the products are delivered to the assessee, it sells the products to the customers in India. The non-resident companies raise invoices on the assessee company and in turn, the assessee company raises separate invoices on the end users. It is to be seen that the orders are placed by customers and banks in India with the assessee company on a need based arrangement. The supply of the products are made by the non-resident companies only after approving the technicality of the software module and other necessary particulars. The software products are delivered to the assessee on a CD/any other media specified in the invoices. It is seen that the assessee does not have ownership in the copyright supplied by the non-resident companies. It is also to be seen that the assessee does not have any right to make copies of software or use the software anywhere else. The software is carefully marked for that particular customer to whom the assessee has sold the software product. From the above features, it is clear that the relationship subsisted between the assessee company and the non-resident companies was on a principal-to-principal basis. The risk of the failure of the software product is borne by the assessee company. The assessee company does not have any right to make changes in the software supplied by ACI Singapore and IRPL Australia. The assessee company is permitted to make only nominal/cosmetic modifications for the purpose of installing the software and running the software product in the system of customers. The software transferred by the non-resident companies is a standard software. [Para 48]

The services rendered by the assessee in installing the software products in the system of its customers are in the nature of making the software compatible to the environment of the individual customers. The assessee company never becomes the owner of the software. The intellectual property in the software products always remains with the ACI Singapore and IRPL Australia. [Para 49]

[2010] 322 ITR 125/188 Taxman 223 (AAR - New Delhi), CIT v. Dynamic Vertical Software India (P.) Ltd. [2011] 332 ITR 222/201 Taxman 78 (Mag.)/12 taxmann.com 431 (Delhi), DIT v. Ericsson A.B. [2012] 343 ITR 470/204 Taxman 192/[2011] 16 taxmann.com 371 (Delhi), the courts have held that where the assessee is purchasing software from the vendor and selling the same further in Indian market, the consideration paid for such purchase could not be termed as "royalty". It is held that in order to constitute royalty, what is contemplated, is a payment that is depending on user of copyright and not a lump sum paid for the acquisition of copyrighted article. [Para 50]

In the present appeals also, what has been purchased by the assessee from ACI Singapore and IRPL Australia was only copyrighted articles and not copyright, proper. Within the meaning of Indian Copyright Act, 1957, a copyright is an exclusive right to reproduce software including storage of the same in electronic machines with exclusive right to sell it. In the present case, the assessee does not have ownership of the software and does not have right to reproduce the said software. It is in fact only procuring copyrighted software product meant for a particular customer in India. The technical role of the assessee is limited in installing and running the software product in the system of customers in India. Therefore, the assessee is right in its contention that the payments made by the assessee company in the previous year relevant to the assessment years under appeal to non-resident companies are only purchase consideration for procuring copyrighted software products. They were not in the nature of Royalty. [Para 51]

The assessee-company was based in Singapore and it had no presence in India. Its income consisted of receipts from licensing of software to four customers in India. One of the customers was CSC, which was its hundred per cent subsidiary company. Other three customers were unrelated to the assessee.

SAP software was internally used by all the group companies. This software was procured from an unrelated party. The expenditure incurred for the use of the license by the group companies was shared by them on the basis of the extent of user. The whole of the payment was made by the head office. This expenditure pertained to the business of the group companies including the Indian subsidiary company. Therefore, the expenditure was reimbursed on the basis of the bills raised by the head office. This amount was not included in the receipts.

All the group companies also used remote access facilities provided by an unrelated party. In respect of the user, remote access charges 'RAS' charges were paid by the head office. These expenses were also spread over the user-group companies on the basis of actual user. They reimbursed the expenses to head office on the basis of bills raised by it. These amounts were also not includible in the receipts.

The assessee also incurred travel expenses in respect of employees of the head office who came to India for helping the work of the Indian subsidiary company. The expenses were in relation to air-tickets, hotel bills, taxi charges etc. The Indian company had reimbursed these expenses to the head office on cost to cost basis. These amounts were also not included in the receipts.

The case of the assessee was that all these reimbursements had been received in the immediately following year. The case of the assessee was that no element of profit was involved in the reimbursements. Therefore, nothing was taxable either in this or in the succeeding year.

The Assessing Officer held that the assessee had offered to tax all sums received from India as royalty/FTS under the DTAA. However, there were certain amounts from CSC which had not been offered for taxation, not in any year till date. By way of example, it is stated that the amount for grant of software license as per form no. 3CEB of CSC and as per assessee's statement was Rs. 62,22,779; however, the assessee had offered to tax a sum of Rs. 61,81,410. It was further mentioned that the assessee had probably accounted for the amount net of tax deducted at source, but the difference may be due to some other reason also. CSC had claimed deduction of Rs. 62,22,779. There was difference of Rs. 41,369 on this account. There were payments by CSC, which pertain to the current year; however, the income had been deferred to the next year. The accounting for of the income was pending in some cases for two to three years from the date of the transaction. This might be due to fault in the recording of the transactions in the books by the assessee. The difference in the amounts was claimed by CSC and offered to tax by the assessee has been included in the income of the assessee. On this basis, the income of this year had been enhanced.

Service PE

The CIT(A) held that the payments under the technical services agreement for the employees visiting India to provide training were covered as FIS under Article 12 of the India US tax treaty and accordingly, no service PE was created. The tax department did not appeal against this conclusion of the CIT(A).

The Tribunal decision on the issue of Fixed Place PE highlights the need to closely analyse arrangements where employees of the foreign entity visit India. However, with respect, the decision has made certain important conclusions without a detailed reasoning of the factual matrix and without establishing that CIS had made available certain designated space to CMG. There is no reference in the ruling to the decision of the Delhi Special Bench in the case of Motorola Inc. v. Dy. CIT7 wherein it was observed that merely because the Indian company allowed the visiting employees of the foreign company to use certain facilities occasionally, it could not be said that the foreign company had at its disposal, as matter of right, certain space which could be characterized as a fixed place of business in terms of Article 5(1) of the tax treaty.It does not appear to examine the relationship between the service-level activities of CMG and those of CIS to determine whether the business of CMG could actually be said to be carried on from the premises of CIS. Further, it upholds the order of the CIT(A) in general but is silent as to whether the presence of employees seconded to CIS had a bearing on the Tribunal's conclusion. It also does not clarify whether economic dependence on the parent company, as observed by the CIT(A), could result into establishing a Fixed Place PE. Lastly, it does not throw light on how provision of certain free of cost hardware and software could lead to the conclusion that CMG has a PE in India.

All said and done, one would definitely worry as the decision could prove to be a dangerous weapon in the hands of the tax authorities who may allege the existence of a PE in case the Indian entity receives support and guidance from its foreign affiliates. It would be hard to find a situation where a subsidiary, especially a captive, does not receive support and guidance and hence the precedent is all the more worrisome.

Whether one agrees with the conclusion or not, it becomes more imperative to take a re-look at the specific roles of the visiting employees vis-à-vis the functioning and overall profile of the Indian entity (whether by way of dependence on the foreign entity or significance in the value chain) and view the same in a holistic manner. Employees expected to perform functions which are more than stewardship activities would typically be present in India for longer durations and hence, steps should be taken to shift the economic employment of the employees to the Indian entity so as to mitigate the PE exposure.

Attribution of profits to the PE

To attribute profits to the PE, the AO adopted a method which involved apportioning the total revenue earned by CMG from global operations based on the number of employees during the year in CMG and CIS.

The CIT(A) held that Profit Split Method was most suitable for determining the arm's length profit attributable to the PE. The approach applied by the CIT(A) entailed calculation based on the revenue from Indian operations. Further, substantial portion of the expenses were disallowed on various counts.

CMG inter alia put forth that, in the case of CIS, the transfer pricing officer made an upward adjustment to the mark-up charged by CIS to CMG by considering comparables as companies which assume normal business risk. Thus, there would be double taxation as on the one hand, profits had been attributed to the alleged PE of CMG and at the same time a transfer pricing adjustment was made in the hands of CIS.

The Tribunal held that no attribution of profits was required to be made on account of entrepreneurial services to manage risk related to service delivery. Also, that there could be no disallowance of expenditure for non-deduction of tax8 as the same is not in accordance with Article 7(3) of the tax treaty9.

The Tribunal observed that attribution of profits should be made in accordance with transfer pricing principles. As the charge for employees visiting India and those seconded to India was subsumed in the transfer pricing analysis of CIS, the Tribunal concluded that attribution was required to be made on account of free of cost assets and software provided by CMG to CIS.

payments for the hardware and software were in a lump sum and there was no separate consideration mentioned for the hardware and the software. It was the department which has split the consolidated payment into two - payment for hardware and payment for the software. Since the parties to the contract had not agreed upon a separate price for the hardware and the software, it was not open to the income-tax authorities to split the same and consider a part of the payment for software to be treated as royalty. [Para 173] The Bill of Entry for home consumption showed that a price had been separately mentioned for the software. It was not in dispute that the contract did not mention separate price for the hardware and the software. It was only the cellular operator, who was the importer of the GSM system as a whole, who placed a value on the software for purposes of paying import duties. The import duty is charged at the rate of 10 per cent plus 2 per cent on the value placed on the software. There was no evidence to show that the assessee was party to the fixation of the value for software for custom duty purposes. At any rate what was being imported was the GSM cellular system as a whole which included both the hardware and the software. The software was specific to the hardware and would not work in any other equipment. In such circumstances, it was not possible to infer, merely on the basis of the Bill of Entry and the custom duty payment on the software, that a separate consideration was agreed to between the parties for supply of the software. [Para 175]

In the instant case, there was only one supply contract which included the supply of both the hardware (GSM cellular equipment) and the software which was part of the hardware. A single lump sum consideration was mentioned in the contract. Therefore, there was all the more reason to hold that the lump sum payment could not be segregated into two, namely, one for the hardware and another for the software. [Para 176]

Attribution of income: Since (a) the assessee had no PE in India and (b) there was no business consideration in India, the question of attributing any income to either of those did not really arise. However, it was found that all the contracts were signed in India and, hence, a question might arise as to whether any income could be attributed to such activity. No income could be so attributed because either by way of business connection or because of the PE, what were to be taxed were only business profits. Since there was a DTAA (between India and Sweden), as per the well-established position in law that the DTAA should prevail over the provisions of the Act, the business profits, even if accruing to the assessee by way of signing of the contracts in India, would not be taxed because the assessee had no PE in India as required by article 5 read with article 7 of the DTAA. [Para 185]

The Commissioner (Appeals) was not right in holding that the assessee had a business connection in India from which income was deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 5(2) in respect of the supply of GSM cellular equipment to Indian cell operators. [Para 186]

The next contention put forth on behalf of the assessee is that the amount received from RIPL was in the nature of software royalty because it purchased certain software and transferred the same to it. In support of the contention that the receipt from RIPL is not royalty, the assessee relied on Engineering Analysis (supra). A proposition was bolstered that RIPL got copyrighted article from the assessee, which was different from the copyright in the software purchased. [Para 16] Insofar as the ratio in the case of Engineering Analysis (supra) is concerned, there is no dispute that it has been held by the Summit Court that ownership of copyright in a work is different from the ownership of the physical material in which the copyrighted work may happen to be embodied. Parting with copyright entails parting with the right to do any of the acts mentioned in section 14 of the Copyright Act. Where the core of a transaction is to authorize the end-user to have access to and make use of the 'licensed' computer software product, over which the licensee has no exclusive rights, no copyright is parted with. However, the facts of the instant case are entirely different. On a specific query, the assessee failed to point out as to the specific number of licenses purchased by the assessee from third party vendors and those transferred to RIPL. Rather it was fairly conceded during the course of proceedings and has been established that there was no direct transfer of software licenses to RIPL but it was a case of allowing user to RIPL from the centralized IT infrastructure maintained by the assessee in Switzerland. What is relevant is the amount of receipt by the assessee for rendering services and not the costs incurred in the purchase of software facilitating the provision of services. Here is situation in which the assessee purchased software from third party vendors and then licensed the same to RIPL for use. Rather all the software purchased by it were integrated by the assessee into its own centralized IT infrastructure for facilitating the provision of the IT services enlisted above to its group entities and RIPL is one of such beneficiary of the services. It is rather a case of the assessee only purchasing the software from third party vendors and the transactions qua such individual software coming to an end there itself. The ratio of Engineering Analysis (supra) can apply where the vendors demonstrate that what they transferred to the assessee was copyrighted article and not copyright. On the contrary, this is a second stage in which the software licenses, being in the nature of copyrighted article, were purchased by the assessee and then used in the providing various services, such as, Client Based Services (CBS), Business Applications for Sales, Marketing and Technology Users (BASMT), Business Applications for Parts and Service Users (BAPS), Business Applications for Operations Users (BAOP), Business Applications for Finance and Controlling Users (BAFC) etc. [Para 17]

The fact that the assessee utilized the software purchased from third party vendors for integrating them with its own software for making a common centralized integrated IT infrastructure so as to render the IT services is further fortified by the details of the alleged reimbursement submitted by the assessee. First table on the paper book has last two columns with captions `Weights for IT infrastructure cost allocation' and `Weighted average allocation'. On a specific query, the assessee submitted that the assessee company spent certain amount on IT infrastructure, independent of the software cost, which was allocated between all the 19 entities and the RIPL's share in it was determined at 17.09 per cent. This shows that apart from purchasing the software for the centralized IT infrastructure Centre, the assessee also incurred certain IT infrastructure costs for integrating them into its centralized system so as to render services to the worldwide entities, which was charged to RIPL at 17.09 per cent. This plentifully proves that the amount recovered by the assessee from RIPL is not towards transfer of any software so as to constitute software royalty. The contention of the assessee in this respect stands repelled. [Para 18]

The Assessing Officer has held that OIPL constitutes 'a fixed place of business' under Article 5(1) of the DTAA as the premises of OIPL in India and machinery/equipment installed therein are owned by the assessee. The Assessing Officer however, has not substantiated the said assertion by any cogent evidence/materials. On the other hand, the assessee statement that the assessee does not own, lease, or otherwise occupy any office premises or establishment in India, remains uncontroverted. The premises in India are leased by OIPL and the machinery/equipment are owned and operated by OIPL for its own business and it is OIPL which claims depreciation under section 32 on premises and equipment. [Para 29]

The issue of 'fixed place of business' and PE is no longer res-integra as held by the Supreme Court in the case of Hyatt International Southwest Asia Ltd. [2025] 176 taxmann.com 783 (SC) referring to the decision of Formula One World Championship Ltd. [2017] 80 taxmann.com 347 (SC) which held that for a place to be a Permanent Establishment (PE), two essential conditions must be satisfied (i) the place must be at 'disposal' of the enterprise and (ii) the business of the enterprise must be carried on through that place. Even on the aspect of 'disposal' test, the Assessing Officer has not established with any cogent evidence/materials that the assessee has any right of access or control over these premises, and that the premises are at the 'disposal' of the assessee. Neither the Assessing Officer nor the Commissioner (Appeals) have demonstrated anywhere in their order that a particular space or part of the premises of OIPL in India, was available/under control of the assessee for its business and that the employees of the assessee can walk into the said premise and occupy the space/table in its own right. Therefore, the crucial "disposal test," as established by the Supreme Court in the case of Formula One World Championship Ltd. (supra) and Hyatt International (supra) is not satisfied. Therefore, there is no fixed place PE under article 5(1) of the India-USA DTAA. [Para 30]

The assessee has a separate and distinct SDDLA with OIPL whereby the assessee, as a Licensor, has granted OIPL, the Licensee, right and authority to duplicate software products and to sublicense the same in India. For such grant of right, OIPL pays a royalty of 30 per cent of list price of the Licensed products. Sandeep Puri*

Royalties in general means the payment made to the owners of certain types of rights by those who are permitted by the owners to exercise the rights. The term originated from the fact that in Great Britain for centuries gold and silver mines were the property of the Crown and such 'royal' metals could be mined only if a payment ("Royalty") were made to the Crown.

Royalties thus reflect usage-based payments made by one party (the "licensee") to another (the "licensor") for ongoing use of intangible or tangible assets. Intangible assets are defined as identifiable non-monetary assets that cannot be seen, touched or physically measured, which are created through time and/or effort and that are identifiable as a separate asset. There are two primary forms of intangibles - legal intangibles (such as trade secrets (e.g., customer lists), copyrights, patents, trademarks, and goodwill) and competitive intangibles (such as knowledge activities (know-how, knowledge, collaboration activities, leverage activities, and structural activities). Royalties can be determined as a percentage of gross or net sales derived from use of the asset or a fixed price per unit sold. Further, there also exist other modes and metrics of compensation.

The cross border transactions have given rise to tax controversies, which are pending adjudications before the Tribunals and Courts in India.

The first leg of the controversy relates to the taxability of the foreign entity, granting the rights. When the user of the right, property or information is resident in one country say India and pays royalties to the owner thereof who is resident in another country say the USA, the amount paid by the user is generally subject to withholding tax in India, the source country. The basic challenge, which is pending before courts relates the characterisation of the certain payments. While the taxpayer contends that the payment received is in lieu of services and not grant of rights, the Revenue Authorities contends otherwise. The most talked about controversy here relates to transmission of data through undersea cables, satellites etc. Other could be where the taxpayer contends that there is transfer of rights in perpetuity and hence the transaction qualifies a sale. The most talked about controversy here relates to usage of off the shelf software products.

The second leg of controversy relates to the treatment of the cost incurred in the hands of the Indian user entity. For the purposes of this article, we are limiting the discussion to the transfer pricing challenges, which arise when the transaction is between two related entities of the group.

Take a simple scenario, a manufacturing enterprise or an inventor may have incurred substantial sums on the development of the property generating the royalties. However, the work of research and testing involves considerable capital outlays and does not always yield successful results. The issue lies in determining an appropriate arm's length return for using such property, which is rather complex. The Revenue Authorities generally raise the challenge from a variety of perspectives, such as (a) why user entity per se has taken up the right; (b) what is the technology granted and how it has benefited the Indian entity; and (c) how to determine the arm's length price.

In this article, we have taken a deep dive into these controversies.

CONTROVERSIES DISSECTED

One of the typical situations giving rise to the transfer pricing controversy involves a Foreign Multinational Group licensing technology/know-how to its Indian affiliate and charging a bundled Royalty. The Indian affiliate would deploy the technology in the manufacturing process and; thereafter would undertake selling and distribution function selling goods under the brand name of the Foreign Multinational Group. In lieu of the rights granted, Indian affiliate would pay a Royalty charge, of say 5%, which will be computed on its net sales. The entities would document their understanding through a written agreement.

The Revenue Authorities generally makes the following assertions upon encountering the above situation:

(a)

The taxpayer has not been able to provide substantial evidence of any tangible benefit arising from the use of such rights and as to why it entered into such an arrangement;

(b)

The taxpayer have not been able to demonstrate that its profits have increased, by use of technology or brand name and no cost benefit analysis was furnished;

(c)

The taxpayer has used Regulatory guidelines to justify the royalty rate and such treatment lacks judicial approval;

(d)

The taxpayer has failed to produce contemporary data, justifying the rate of royalty payout.

With the aid of some or all the assertions, Revenue Authorities at times adjudicate that value of such royalty payment charge is NIL.

Are there any transfer pricing implications for an existing Indian manufacturing and distribution company to become a contract manufacturer for its foreign parent entity?

Profit is a reward for the functions undertaken, assets deployed and risks borne (FAR). Thus this requires an analysis of the FAR of the Indian company in its existing operational form vis-à-vis its FAR in the proposed new form. Transfer pricing implications need to be determined for two stages – (i ) one time change stage, and (ii) going forward stage.

In the one time change stage analysis, if it is observed that the Indian company is reducing the scope of its manufacturing and distribution FAR in favour of its foreign parent entity, there is transfer of tangible or intangibles e.g. customers, distribution network, etc. and as a result its profits earning are also expected to reduce, it may require the Indian company to receive an arm’s length compensation (as an exit charge) from the foreign parent company for such change. However, in case of an Indian company where there is a history of operational losses being incurred and / or the future projections reflect possibility of operational losses or very low profits, the determination of arm’s length exit charge compensation may result in a Nil or a minimal amount. Evaluation on the need for, and the amount (if any) of arm’s length exit charge compensation is highly fact dependent and will need to be a specific exercise based on facts of each case.

From a going forward perspective, it is important to determine the arm’s length compensation to be received by the Indian company for acting as a contract manufacturer. The FAR for this purpose also needs to specifically consider what and whose is the source of raw material, source of manpower, source of technology, and other important inputs for the manufacturing process besides considering the level of capacity utilization.

Whether a captive back office service provider (compensated on a cost plus X% basis) should pay for various charges to the Head Quarter, and whether this could lead to round-tripping of costs?

In computing the arm’s length compensation for a captive back office service provider, it is important to include all the operational costs related to the activities and services of the service provider. Unless this is ensured, the cost base of the captive service provider may be artificially under-stated (if certain costs are directly borne by associated enterprises) and thereby artificially lower the arm’s length profit to be earned by it.

Some typical examples of costs borne by associated enterprises are discussed here. Cost of personnel deputed to work for (under the directions of) the captive service provider should be recovered, however cost of personnel visiting as representatives of the associated enterprise (in its role as a customer of services) should not be recovered from the captive service provider. Cost of senior group management visiting for stewardship purposes should not be recovered. Common IT and communication costs, common HR and administrative costs should be recovered if these result in specific benefit to the activities and operations of the captive service provider. Costs of any software provided which will enable the captive service provider to execute the required services should be recovered, however costs of a software platform where the service provider is required to merely deliver (not execute) the performed services may not be recovered.

To some extent this may lead to a round-tripping of costs however this may be necessary evil for appropriate determination of cost base and hence the cost plus X% compensation.

Whether the transfer of shares of an Indian company amongst two non-resident associated enterprises would attract Indian Transfer Pricing compliance?

This issue has been discussed in a recent ruling by the Authority for Advance Ruling (AAR) in the case of Amiantit International Holding Limited. In this Ruling, the AAR has held that while ascertaining Transfer Pricing compliance in India, the first question which has to be answered is whether the income is chargeable to tax in India or not. The Transfer Pricing provisions are not independent charging provisions. They merely mandate that income which is chargeable to tax in India is compliant with the arm’s length principle. Hence, where the income is not chargeable to tax in India, the question of arm’s length compliance does not arise. The Ruling in this case is consistent with the earlier ruling by the AAR in the case of Dana Corporation.

6.7 Section 80HHE provides for deduction in respect of profits and gains from software exports. As a measure to provide benefit to a supporting software developer exporting software through others, a new proviso to section 80HHE(1) has been inserted with effect from assessment year 1999-2000. The said proviso provides that where an assessee, being an exporting company engaged in the export out of India of computer software, issues a certificate in a prescribed form, that in respect of the amount of the export specified therein, the deduction under section 80HHE(1) is to be allowed to a supporting software developer, than the amount of deduction available to the assessee shall be reduced by such an amount which bears to the total profits derived by the assessee from the export, the same proportion as the amount of the export turnover specified in such certificate bears to the total export turnover of the assessee.

For this purpose,—

(i) exporting company has been defined as a company making actual export of computer software.

(ii) supporting software developer has been defined as an Indian company or a person (other than a company) resident in India developing and selling computer software to an exporting company for the purpose of export.

Further, a new sub-section (1A) has been inserted to provide that where the supporting software developer has developed and sold computer software to an exporting company in respect of which the said company has issued a certificate in the prescribed form in accordance with the provisions of section 80HHE(1) read with the proviso, a deduction will be allowed in computing the total income of the assessee to the extent of the profits derived by the assessee from the developing and selling of computer software to the exporting company in respect of which the certificate has been issued by the said company.

For the purposes of computing the profits derived by the supporting software developer as referred to in sub-section (1A), a new section 80HHE(3A) has been inserted which provides that

(i) where the business carried on by the supporting software developer consists exclusively of developing and selling of computer software to one or more exporting companies solely engaged in exports, the whole of the profits of such business shall be deemed as profits derived by the assessee;

(ii) where the business carried on by a supporting software developer does not consist exclusively of developing and selling of computer software to one or more exporting companies, the profit derived by the supporting software developer from sale of such software shall be the amount which bears to the profits of the business the same proportion as the turnover in respect of sale to the respective exporting company bears to the total turnover of the business carried on by the assessee.

The new sub-section (4A) provides that the deduction to the supporting software developer shall not be admissible unless he furnishes in the prescribed form along with his return of income -

(i) the report of an accountant, as defined in the Explanation below sub-section (2) of section 288, certifying that the deduction has been correctly claimed on the basis of the profits of the supporting software developer in respect of sale of computer software export to the exporting company; and

(ii) a certificate from the exporting company containing such particulars as may be prescribed and verified in the manner prescribed that in respect of the export turnover mentioned in the certificate, the exporting company has not claimed deduction under this section. The certificate issued by the exporting company shall be duly certified by the auditor auditing the accounts of the exporting assessee under the provisions of the Act or under any other law.

3.1 Introduction - The traditional notion of software has been a company hiring engineers who sit in a building writing code to create a software program used for a specific purpose and such program once developed is sent to customers in the tangible form of CD’s or DVD’s. This model equated well with the assembly line manufacturing process and an age-old model of tangible products.

However, the above is not how a majority of software is developed nowadays; the Internet has brought forth new business model – both business to business (B2B) & business to consumer (B2C) models.

Today there exists "web" companies which are valued at billions of dollars whose "crown jewels" are usually the intangible intellectual property they own or their patented business models or their proprietary technology web-service platforms. Examples of such web companies are Google, Facebook, eBay5 2 etc.

3.2 A simple web-based business model - In this case study we take a web-based business model related to the online advertising market (also called SEM – Search Engine Marketing), one of the fastest growing markets in the world. This is similar to the case study presented in Elizabeth King’s case study on Replication of Internet-Based Business Model52.

Search engines like Google5 3 derive most of their income from such markets which allow advertisers to bid on keywords in an auction-model on their technology platforms; when users search for the keywords which have been bid upon they are shown text ads sorted in the descending order of their bid. Such a market gave rise to a host of web companies who provide service to advertisers to efficiently and optimally bid on millions of companies – they are essentially providing SEM solutions to online advertisers.

We consider a USA company, USCo, which provides SEM i.e. Search Engine Marketing solutions using its unique and patented algorithmic techniques for efficient and optimal bidding; in simple terms the company takes control of advertisers online campaigns of its clients and bids on keywords in the online advertisement marketplaces offered by search engines like Google Adwords54 . USCo’s clients are typically two-fold: companies who wants to advertise online to boost traffic to its website and sales of its products & services, advertising agencies who provide full-service to their clients and provide both offline (TV, newspapers etc.) & online advertising solutions for clients.

USCo has a successful and established business model and handles over $500 million in advertising spend on the various search engines. Parts of USCo’s business model are patented. Further, USCo has developed proprietary software for its internal usage – to process, analyze & model the huge amount of data it churns daily. USCo has also developed online marketing & solicitation tools which it uses to market to, obtain, test and sign-up clients.

Now an Indian company, lets call it IndCo, wants to replicate USCo’s business model in India. Towards this the top management gets training in USCo and on doing so provides the USCo’s business model of online advertising solutions to clients & ad agencies in India.

To summarize:

1.USCo transfers the intellectual property of its proprietary software modified to suit local conditions.

2.USCo also provides the right to use of its marketing and solicitation online tools to IndCo, again these pages have to be modified slightly for local conditions.

3.USCo will perform routine service, maintenance and upgrades on the proprietary software given to IndCo.

4.USCo will provide legal and financial planning and advisory services to IndCo.

5.IndCo has been issued the rights to use USCo’s trademark and name in the Indian market.

A conjoint reading of the terms of the supply contract and the provisions of the 1957 Act, clearly showed that the cellular operator could not exploit the computer software commercially which was the very essence of a copyright. In other words, a holder of a copyright is permitted to exploit the copyright commercially and if he is not permitted to do so then what he had acquired could not be considered as a copyright. In that case, it could only be said that he had acquired a copyrighted article. [Para 162]

One cannot have the copyright without the copyrighted article but at the same time just because one has the copyrighted article, it does not follow that one has also the copyright in it. [Para 163]

Therefore, the payment by the cellular operator was not for any copyright in the software but was only for the software as such as a copyrighted article. It followed that the payment could not be considered as royalty within the meaning of Explanation 2 below section 9(1) or article 13.3 of the DTAA with Sweden. [Para 172]

Since the parties to the contract had not agreed upon a separate price for the hardware and the software, it was not open to the income-tax authorities to split the same and consider a part of the payment for software to be treated as royalty. The Bill of Entry for home consumption showed that a price had been separately mentioned for the software. It was not in dispute that the contract did not mention separate price for the hardware and the software. It was only the cellular operator, who was the importer of the GSM system as a whole, who placed a value on the software for purposes of paying import duties. The import duty is charged at the rate of 10 per cent plus 2 per cent on the value placed on the software. There was no evidence to show that the assessee was party to the fixation of the value for software for custom duty purposes. At any rate what was being imported was the GSM cellular system as a whole which included both the hardware and the software. However, it is possible that the non-resident entity may have a business connection with the resident Indian entity. In such a case, the resident Indian entity could be treated as the Permanent Establishment of the non-resident entity. The tax treatment of the Permanent Establishment in such a case is under consideration in this circular. During the last decade or so, India has seen a steady growth of outsourcing of business processes by non-residents or foreign companies to IT-enabled entities in India. Such entities are either branches or associated enterprises of the foreign enterprise or an independent Indian enterprise. Their activities range from mere procurement of orders for sale of goods or provision of services and answering sales related queries, to the provision of services itself like software maintenance service, debt collection service, software development service, credit card/mobile telephone related service, etc. The non-resident entity or the foreign company will be liable to tax in India only if the IT-enabled BPO unit in India constitutes its Permanent Establishment. The extent to which the profit of the non-resident enterprise is to be attributed to the activities of such Permanent Establishment in India has been under consideration of the Board.

A non-resident or a foreign company is treated as having a Permanent Establishment in India under Article 5 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements entered into by India with different countries if the said non-resident or foreign company carries on business in India through a branch, sales office etc. or through an agent (other than an independent agent) who habitually exercises an authority to conclude contracts or regularly delivers goods or merchandise or habitually secures orders on behalf of the non-resident principal. In such a case, the profits of the non-resident or foreign company attributable to the business activities carried out in India by the Permanent Establishment become taxable in India under Article 7 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement.

Paragraph 1 of Article 7 of Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements provides that if a foreign enterprise carries on business in another country through a Permanent Establishment situated therein, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other country but only so much of them as are attributable to the Permanent Establishment. Paragraph 2 of the same Article provides that subject to the provisions of Paragraph 3, there shall in each contracting State be attributed to that Permanent Establishment the profits which it might be expected to make if it were a distinct and separate enterprise engaged in the same or similar activities under the same or similar conditions and dealing wholly independently with the enterprise of which it is a Permanent Establishment. Paragraph 3 of the Article provides that in determining the profits of a Permanent Establishment there shall be allowed as deduction expenses which are incurred for the purposes of the Permanent Establishment including executive and general administrative expenses so incurred, whether in the State in which the Permanent Establishment is situated or elsewhere. What are the expenses that are deductible would have to be determined in accordance with the accepted principles of accountancy and the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

Paragraph 2 contains the central directive on which the allocation of profits to a Permanent Establishment is intended to be based. The paragraph incorporates the view that the profits to be attributed to a Permanent Establishment are those which that Permanent Establishment would have made if, instead of dealing with its Head Office, it had been dealing with an entirely separate enterprise under conditions and at prices prevailing in the ordinary market. This corresponds to the "arm’s length principle". Paragraph 3 only provides a rule applicable for the determination of the profits of the Permanent Establishment, while paragraph 2 requires that the profits so determined correspond to the profits that a separate and independent enterprise would have made. Hence, in determining the profits attributable to an IT-enabled BPO unit constituting a Permanent Establishment, it will be necessary to determine the price of the services rendered by the Permanent Establishment to the Head Office or by the Head Office to the Permanent Establishment on the basis of "arm’s length principle".

"Arm’s length price" would have the same meaning as in the definition in section 92F(iii) of the Income-tax Act. The arm’s length price would have to be determined in accordance with the provisions of sections 92 to 92F of the Act.

Decisions over-ruled in the budget 1. The Vodafone ruling:

The Supreme Court ("SC") in the case of Vodafone International Holdings B.V. v. UOI [2012] 341 ITR 1 (SC) has held that sale of shares outside of India by a foreign company to another is not liable to tax in India.

The Bill has sought to negate most of the parameters applied by the SC and has proposed retrospective amendments to the definition of the terms "capital assets" and "transfer". Similarly, amendments have also been proposed in section 9 (1) (i) of the Act by inter-alia providing that an asset or any share or interest in a company or entity outside India shall be deemed to have situated in India if the share or interest derives, directly or indirectly, its value substantially from the assets located in India. These amendments have been proposed with retrospective effect from 01 April 1962.

Additionally, in a first of its kind, a validation clause has also been proposed to be inserted to validate any notice sent or taxes levied in respect of income accruing or arising, through or from transfer of a capital asset situated in India, in consequence of the transfer of shares of a company registered or incorporated outside India or in consequence of agreement or otherwise outside India. In terms thereof, such notices shall be deemed to have been validly made and such notice or levy of tax shall not be called in question on the ground that the tax was not chargeable or on any other ground.

2. Taxability of software as "royalty":

Different High Courts ("HC") had taken divergent views on the issue, while the Karnataka HC had taken a view against the tax payers (i.e. software payments were held to be taxable as "royalty"), the Delhi HC had in the case of DIT v. Ericsson A. B. [2012] 66 DTR 1 (Del) decided the issue in favour of the assessee.

The Bill proposes to bring within the ambit of the term "royalty" transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred. The amendment is sought to be made with retrospective effect from 01 June 1976.

3. The other "royalty" story:

a. The Bill also proposes to amend/expand the definition of the term "royalty" to cover within its transmission by satellite as a "process". This is sought to be done with retrospective effect from 01 June 1976 to negate the decision of the Delhi HC in the case of Asia Satellite Telecommunication Co. Ltd. v. DIT [2011] 332 ITR 340 (Del) and other decisions on similar lines.

b. Similarly, the Bill proposes to cover within the ambit of the term "royalty" any right, property or information whether or not these are:

i. in the possession or control of the payer;

ii. used directly by the payer;

iii. situated in India.

This is to dilute the decision of the Mumbai Bench of the ITAT in the case of Standard Chartered Bank v. DDIT [2011] 11 ITR (Trib) 721 which has inter-alia held that since the assessee had merely used the equipment and did not have the possession or control of the equipment with themselves nor did they themselves use the equipment, the payment cannot be taxed as "royalty".

The amendment is with effect from 01 June 1976.

4. The Transfer Pricing controversy put to rest:

a. Various Benches of the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal ("ITAT") have held that the tolerance band of +/-5% provided for in Section 92C (2) of the Act is available as a standard deduction to the tax payers while computing the "Arm's Length Price" ('ALP'). The Bill proposes to settle the dispute against the tax payers by clarifying, with retrospective effect from 01 April 2002 that the tolerance band of +/- 5% is not to be taken as a standard deduction while computing the ALP.

b. The Karnataka HC in the case of GE India Technology Centre Pvt. Ltd. v. DRP and ACIT [2011] 338 ITR 416 (Kar) has held that the Dispute Resolution Panel ('DRP') cannot go beyond the proposed draft order and make enhancements on issues beyond the variations proposed in the draft order. The Bill proposes to enlarge the powers of DRP powers with retrospective effect from 01 April 2009, so to permit enhancement on any matter arising out of the assessment proceedings relating of the draft order notwithstanding that such matter was raised or not by the assessee.

Royalty payable after imports but known at the time of imports and was payable as condition of import is includible in assessable value - Warner Bros (FE) Inc v. CC (2018) 359 ELT 546 (CESTAT).

If buyer has paid royalties and licence fees separately in relation to imported goods, these are includible, unless these are already included in selling price. Royalty may include payments in respect of patents, trademarks or copyrights. However, following i.e. (a) charges for the right to reproduce the goods in India shall not be added and (b) payments made by buyer (importer) for right to distribute or resale the imported goods shall not be added if such payment is not a condition for export to India [Interpretative Note to rule 10(1)(c) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007].

License fee charged for countrywide use of software for use of (Oracle) software is includible in assessable value as it is condition of sale. Royalty and license fee payable on imported cinematographic film is includible in assessable value as it is related to imported goods and buyer is required to pay it directly or indirectly, as a condition of sale. - FD(DR) circular No. 86/2002-Cus dated 12-12-2002.

The Provisions of DTAA is not applicable – When?

It is important to mention here that the provisions of DTAA shall not apply in the situation where the payee or foreign company which has income chargeable to tax in India but it neither has PAN in India nor it furnishes the prescribed documents as required under the provisions of Rule 37BC of the Rules.

What if non-resident constitutes PE/Business Connection in India?

If the foreign company constitutes PE in India as defined in Article 5 of the respective DTAA or business connection in India as defined in section 9(1)(i) of the Act, then it shall be taxed in India as per the provisions of Article 7 of such DTAA r.w.s 9 of the Act read with rule 10 of the Rules wherein the foreign companies are liable to tax on net basis i.e. on its profits attributable to PE in India.

As per the provisions of section 44DA of the Act, the income by way of royalty or fees for technical services in the case of the foreign companies which carries on business in India through PE situated in India shall be computed under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession' in accordance with the provisions of the Act.

Further, such non-resident shall be required to meet with additional compliances like maintenance of books of accounts, tax audit u/s 44AB of the Act, compliances under other laws applicable in India, e.g., Companies Act, 2013, RBI / FEMA compliances, Goods and Services Tax, etc.

In view thereof, if the foreign company constitutes PE in India and books of accounts are not maintained as required under the provisions of Companies Act then the taxable profits shall be determined as per formulary approach prescribed under new draft rule 10 of the Rules.

Compliances in India under Income Tax Act

Return of Income

As per the provisions of section 139 of the Act, every company is required to file its Return of Income on or before the prescribed due date of filing Return of Income. The due date to file return of income in the case of company including foreign company is the 30th day of September of the assessment year (i.e. immediately succeeding the financial year) unless the company has entered into international transaction (as defined u/s 92B of the Act) with its Associated Enterprises ('AE').

As per the provisions of sec 115A(5) of the Act, the foreign company is not liable to file Return of Income in India if –

(a)

Its income consists of only interest or dividend income and

(b)

The due tax has already been deducted from such income

Transfer Pricing Provisions – Audit Report in Form 3CEB

In addition to the requirement of filing return of income by foreign company as explained above, if the foreign company has entered into international transactions with its AE which gives rise to income of foreign company chargeable to tax in India then it is subject to transfer pricing provisions in India and accordingly it should comply with the arm's length principle u/s 92 of the Act.

Accordingly, as per the provisions of section 92E of the Act, such foreign company who has entered into an international transaction with its AE shall obtain a report in Form 3CEB from a CA and furnish such report along with return of income on or before the due date as prescribed u/s 139(1) of the Act.
