Where assessee-company, incorporated in Malaysia, entered into an agreement with its Indian AE for use of assessee's SAP system and related services to keep it functional, etc., since assessee had merely given access of SAP system to AE for a certain specific purpose and by allowing such access, assessee had not transferred any right or license in respect of any copyright of any literary or artistic or scientific work to AE, provisions of clause (v) of Explanation 2 to s. 9(1)(vi) could not be applied to such a transaction so as to tax consideration received by assessee [CIT v. Colgate Palmolive Marketing SDN BHD [2023] 152 taxmann.com 124 (Bom.)].

Advertisement/publicity charges - Payment received on services rendered by assessee to the Indian concern was for advertisement, publicity and sales promotion keeping in mind their mutual interest and in that context, use of trademark, trade name or other enumerated service referred to in agreement with assessee were incidental to said main service and, therefore, such payments were not in the nature of 'royalty' but 'business income' [DIT v. Sheraton International Inc. [2009] 178 Taxman 84 (Delhi)].

Customised product - Mere passing of information concerning design of machine which is tailor-made to meet requirement of a buyer, by itself, does not amount to transfer of any right of exclusive user so as to render payment made therefor being regarded as 'royalty' [CIT v. Nayveli Lignite Corporation Ltd. [2000] 113 Taxman 206 (Mad.)].

Export commission - Where assessee entered into export agreement with AE in terms of which it was granted approval to sell motor vehicles manufactured using technology licenced by AE abroad, since by way of export agreement HMCL had not rendered any managerial, technical or consultancy services, payment of export commission could not be regarded as 'royalty' taxable in India [CIT v. Hero Motorcorp Ltd. [2017] 81 taxmann.com 162/248 Taxman 14 (Delhi)].

Forex fluctuations - Where interest/royalty/FTS income was claimed as exempt as per DTAA on accrual basis in earlier years, then forex fluctuation gain or loss arising on receipt of such income in subsequent period could not be considered as exempt since such gain could not be considered as a part of royalty and it should be taxed [Ballarpur Industries Ltd. v. CIT [2017] 84 taxmann.com 61 (Bom.)].

Hire charges - Where assessee, engaged in business of moving coal from various ports in India to State Electricity Board, Chennai, hired ships from various non-resident companies for transportation of coal, payments of hire charges made to said companies under time charter agreement amounted to 'royalty' [Poompuhar Shipping Corporation Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 38 taxmann.com 150/[2014] 220 Taxman 58 (Mad.)]. However, amount received by foreign company for hiring out dredgers to its Indian company would not be taxable in India as 'royalty' [CIT v. Van Oord ACZ Equipment BV [2014] 51 taxmann.com 356/[2015] 228 Taxman 199 (Mad.)].

Licence to use - Payment made to a non-resident in order to obtain licence to use database maintained by it is to be regarded as 'royalty' [CIT v. Wipro Ltd. [2011] 16 taxmann.com 275/203 Taxman 621 (Kar.)].

22.1-3 Distinction between copyright and copyrighted software Copyright is different from the material object which is the subject of the copyright. So, a transfer of the material object does not necessarily involve a transfer of copyright - Copyright Act by Iyengar.

For example, sale of a book (which is a copyrighted article) does not mean sale of copyright in the book. The customer gets only limited rights in the book. He cannot copy the book or any part of it.

Similarly, sale of software recorded on CD is sale of a copyrighted article. The buyer does not get copyright in software. He has only limited right to use the software product.

The assessee was a resident private limited company, engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling motor cars in India as well as abroad. It also provided warranty to the end customers who purchased the car and the assessee's sister companies maintained the cars sold by them according to the terms of the warranty promised by the assessee company, towards which the dealer companies incurred expenditure. As per the contractual obligation, the assessee company reimbursed such expenses incurred by its dealer - sister companies.

The Assessing Officer had held that the payments made by the assessee towards reimbursement of warranty expenditure to its group entities outside India was in the nature of payment made towards 'fees for technical services (FTS)' and, accordingly, taxable income in India.

The Assessing Officer had invoked the provisions of section 195 and disallowed the expenditure incurred by assessee towards purchase of software from tax resident of Japan and United Kingdom by treating it as taxable income in India in the hands of the assessee under the head 'royalty' as per provisions of section 9(1)(vi).

Commissioner(Appeals) upheld said order.

On appeal:

If courier service is provided through franchise, the franchisee will not be eligible for exemption available to small service providers as he is providing service under brand name of other.

The franchisor courier will be liable for service tax on amounts received from the franchisee - Speed and Safe Courier Services v. CCE (2008) 13 STT 257 (CESTAT) [It seems the franchisor was providing both courier as well as franchise services, but agreement indicated that it is a franchise agreement]. Business promotion expenses paid to parent company is not royalty - In Dy. DIT (IT) v. Marriot International Licensing Co. PV (2013) 35 taxmann.com 400 (ITAT), the Assessee was a foreign company. It had franchise agreement with one Indian company to establish and operate hotels in India under the name 'Marriot'. The Indian company was required to pay 1.5% of gross revenue to foreign company for 'International Marketing Activities'. It was held that this is not 'royalty'. [However, Indian company will be required to pay service tax under reverse charge mechanism].

Franchise service is not transfer of right to use goods and hence not deemed sale - In Malabar Gold v. CTO (2013) 40 STT 319 = 35 taxmann.com 569 = 63 VST 497 (Ker HC DB), it was held that franchise service is not subject to State Vat. It is not transfer of right to use trade mark [reversing decision in Malabar Gold v. CTO (2013) 38 STT 606 = 30 taxmann.com 606 = 58 VST 191 (Ker HC), where it was held that Vat is payable on franchisee services, even if service tax was paid] - same view in McDonalds India v. CTT (2017) 102 VST 482 (Del HC DB).

In Mahyco Monsanto Biotech v. UOI (2016) 58 GST 339 = 74 taxmann.com 92 = 95 VST 499 (Bom HC DB), it has been held that franchisee right to operate restaurant under 'Subway' mark in competition with other franchisees is not 'transfer of right to use goods'. Hence, service tax is payable, not Vat. However, transfer of seeds containing proprietary technology for further development of seeds is 'transfer of right to use goods'. Hence, service tax is payable.

Temporary or permanent transfer or permitting use or enjoyment of Intellectual Property Right (IPR) in respect of software falls under service group 99733.

Anti-virus software is covered under 'Information Technology Software' - K7 Computing v. CGST (2022) 135 taxmann.com 305 (Mad. HC).

The assessee acquired software from its foreign parent company for Rs. 3.20 crores for meeting its obligation under the agreement which was then supplied to HCL Technologies Limited for an amount of Rs. 3.20 crores for ultimate supply to National Insurance Company Limited. The said sale and purchase was routed through assessee's books of account and payments were made and received through assessee's bank account, albeit for both the sale and purchase the value of the software was Rs. 3.20 crores and the assessee did not earned any income/mark-up on it. The assessee earned Rs. 24 lacs from its foreign parent company for services during the year under consideration .

The assessee is contending that the assessee has not done any value addition to the software supplied by parent company to HCL Technologies Limited for making ultimate delivery to National Insurance Company Limited and the said software was directly downloaded by HCL Technologies Limited from the website of foreign parent company of the assessee based at Shanghai, China without intervention of the assessee to be ultimately supplied to National Insurance Company Limited under an contractual obligation as stipulated in the agreements . Thus, a claim is made out that no expenses were incurred by the assessee for supply of software as well no value addition being done by the assessee to said software, there arises no need of mark-up on said software value for the assessee.

The doctrine of commercial expediency is invoked and revenue was asked to stay away from the manner in which the assessee is entitled to conduct its business including transactions entered into by the assessee with its foreign parent company and with HCL Technologies Limited for purchase and sale of software without any mark-up/profits relying on doctrine of commercial expediency. The background of these agreements are that Request for Proposal was invited by National Insurance Company Limited for implementing and commissioning the 'Enterprise Architecture Solutions for Insurance' issued by National Insurance Company Limited.

The assessee-company is OEM-CI consortium partner of HCL Technologies Limited , the prime tenderer for implementing and commissioning the 'Enterprise Architecture Solutions for Insurance' issued by National Insurance Company Limited for which tripartite agreement was entered into by and between assessee, National Insurance Company Limited and HCL Technologies Limited.The prime tenderer for RFP floated by National Insurance Company Limited is HCL Technologies Limited while the assessee has entered into tripartite agreement with HCL Technologies Limited and National Insurance Company Limited. As it could be seen from Clause C and D of sub-contractor agreement that the foreign parent company of the assessee based in Shanghai , China is not a consortium partner in the tripartite agreement for supply and services/maintenance/ AMC of software and it is the assessee who has entered into all agreements in India. The assessee is a separate tax entity in contradistinction with its foreign parent company based in Shanghai, China.

In terms of paragraph 1 of article 7 of the subject treaty, the business profits of an enterprise of USA are taxable in India, only if it carries on business through a ‘Permanent Establishment’ (PE) in India. For this purpose, the meaning of ‘PE’ has to be found in the special inclusive definition in the treaty. The profits of the PE so taxable are the profits attributable to the said PE and arrived at by taking into account the deductible expenses in accordance with paragraph 3. As provided in paragraph 2, the profits attributable to the PE are required to be in accordance with the arms length principle.

To put it differently, if in a given case the profits of the PE have been determined, even in the normal course of the business, in accordance with the arms length principle, the question of the Assessing Officer carrying out a separate exercise in this regard does not at all arise; also not envisaged in the subject treaty.

Further, the methodology as per the TPR for determining the taxable profits is basically different; in that, it provides for applying the ‘arms length price’ to the gross income/receipts and to the expenses, separately, and determining the taxable profits on that basis.

The subtle but crucial distinction between the above referred two methodologies (that is, the one as envisaged in the treaty and the other as per the TPR under the Act) will be better appreciated if one bears in mind the old section 92 (which provided for adjustment of profits), which was substituted by sections 92 to 92F with effect from April 1, 2002 [which now provides for adjustment(s) of transfer price(s)].

As is thus seen, the underlying scheme under the Act of the TPR is not compatible but is inconsistent with the arm’s length principle as embodied in the subject treaty. Accordingly, article 7 lends no scope for invoking and applying the TPR in cases covered therein. In particular, in any view, the TPR cannot be invoked and applied in such cases rigidly or in toto.

According to the available information on international practice, the factual position is broadly as under:—

u There are discrepancies in the specifics of each country’s laws concerning the application of the arm’s length principle.

u Different countries may accept different methods of calculating the transfer price. For example, Japan requires that the three traditional methods (i.e. Comparable Uncontrolled Price method, Cost Plus method, and Resale Price method) be systematically discounted before allowing the use of alternative methods, whereas the US accepts the most appropriate method. Some countries may have immature transfer pricing regimes or apply the arm’s length principle in different ways.

As pointed further in this article, by virtue of article 27 of the subject treaty, which provides for the mutual agreement procedure, the above aspect would be required to be negotiated and agreed upon between the two treaty partners.

For the foregoing reasons, it appears that, it would not, to put it mildly, in any view, be prudent for the tax authorities in India to proceed on the premise that they could rigorously invoke and apply the TPR as per the Act, without having regard to the treaty provisions, or without consultations and specific concurrence of the treaty partner.

In terms of paragraph 1 of article 7 of the subject treaty, the business profits of an enterprise of USA are taxable in India, only if it carries on business through a ‘Permanent Establishment’ (PE) in India. For this purpose, the meaning of ‘PE’ has to be found in the special inclusive definition in the treaty. The profits of the PE so taxable are the profits attributable to the said PE and arrived at by taking into account the deductible expenses in accordance with paragraph 3. As provided in paragraph 2, the profits attributable to the PE are required to be in accordance with the arms length principle.

To put it differently, if in a given case the profits of the PE have been determined, even in the normal course of the business, in accordance with the arms length principle, the question of the Assessing Officer carrying out a separate exercise in this regard does not at all arise; also not envisaged in the subject treaty.

Further, the methodology as per the TPR for determining the taxable profits is basically different; in that, it provides for applying the ‘arms length price’ to the gross income/receipts and to the expenses, separately, and determining the taxable profits on that basis.

The subtle but crucial distinction between the above referred two methodologies (that is, the one as envisaged in the treaty and the other as per the TPR under the Act) will be better appreciated if one bears in mind the old section 92 (which provided for adjustment of profits), which was substituted by sections 92 to 92F with effect from April 1, 2002 [which now provides for adjustment(s) of transfer price(s)].

As is thus seen, the underlying scheme under the Act of the TPR is not compatible but is inconsistent with the arm’s length principle as embodied in the subject treaty. Accordingly, article 7 lends no scope for invoking and applying the TPR in cases covered therein. In particular, in any view, the TPR cannot be invoked and applied in such cases rigidly or in toto.

According to the available information on international practice, the factual position is broadly as under:—

u There are discrepancies in the specifics of each country’s laws concerning the application of the arm’s length principle.

u Different countries may accept different methods of calculating the transfer price. For example, Japan requires that the three traditional methods (i.e. Comparable Uncontrolled Price method, Cost Plus method, and Resale Price method) be systematically discounted before allowing the use of alternative methods, whereas the US accepts the most appropriate method. Some countries may have immature transfer pricing regimes or apply the arm’s length principle in different ways.

As pointed further in this article, by virtue of article 27 of the subject treaty, which provides for the mutual agreement procedure, the above aspect would be required to be negotiated and agreed upon between the two treaty partners.

For the foregoing reasons, it appears that, it would not, to put it mildly, in any view, be prudent for the tax authorities in India to proceed on the premise that they could rigorously invoke and apply the TPR as per the Act, without having regard to the treaty provisions, or without consultations and specific concurrence of the treaty partner.

The Court took the view that MSCo being an international company was entitled to insist on quality control and confidentiality in the services provided by MSCo. Stewardship activities involve briefing of the MSAS staff to ensure that the output meets the requirements of the MSCo. These activities include monitoring of the outsourcing operations at MSAS. The object is to protect the interest of the MSCo. These stewards are not involved in day-to-day management or in any specific services to be undertaken by MSAS. The stewardship activity is basically to protect the interest of the customer. Hence, contrary to the ruling of the AAR, the stewardship activities would not constitute a service PE under article 5(2)(l).

Moving ahead, the concept of a service PE finds place in the U.N. Convention19. It is constituted if the MNE renders services through its employees in India, provided the services are rendered for a specified period. In cases where the activities of the MNE entail it being responsible for the work of deputationists and the employees continue to be on the payroll of the MNE or they continue to have their lien on their jobs with the MNE, service PE can emerge. Applying the above tests to this case, the Court concluded that the employees deputed by MSCo. retain their lien on their jobs are on the payroll of MSCo. and on completion of tenure of two years repatriate back to his parent job. Hence, so far as the deputationists are concerned, a service PE under article 5(2)(l) does emerge.

Hence, the judgment makes it clear that activities in the nature of preparatory or auxiliary services, though carried out at fixed place, do not qualify as a PE. Similarly, the activities in the nature of back-office operations and inability to enter into or conclude contracts independently, would not give rise to an agency PE.

Whilst pronouncing its judgment, the Supreme Court held that definition of PE, as adopted by India, is an inclusive definition which covers, among others, service PEs, agency PEs, software PEs, etc. In passing such, the Supreme Court made reference to software PEs, where service providers may be required to act according to quality control specifications of their customers. However, this does not assist in determining the scope of software PEs and has, in fact, left room for uncertainty.

7. Under article 7 of the UN Model Convention, only that portion of business profits is taxable in the source country which is attributable to the PE. It specifies how such business profits should be ascertained. Under the said article, a PE is treated as if it is an independent enterprise (profit centre) de hors the head office and which deals with the head office at arm’s length. Therefore, its profits are determined on the basis as if it is an independent enterprise. The profits of the PE are determined on the basis of what an independent enterprise under similar circumstances might be expected to derive on its own. Article 7(2) Model Convention advocates the arm’s length approach for attribution of profits to a PE.

Therefore, there is a difference between the taxability of the PE in respect of its income earned by it in India which is in accordance with the Income-tax Act, 1961 and which has nothing to do with the taxability of the MNE, which is also taxable in India under article 7, in respect of the profits attributable to its PE. Under article 7, the taxability is of the MNEs. What is taxable under article 7 is profits earned by the MNE. Under the said IT Act, the taxable unit is the foreign company, though the quantum of income taxable is income attributable to the PE of said foreign company in India.

The EULA provided for a trial period which allowed HCL limited software access without payment of license fee. The obligation for full payment, per the terms of EULA, would only be triggered only if HCL opted for full license post this trial. Therefore, HCL was not required to pay the license fee at the time of import. The payments made by HCL to SAP India were in relation post-importation activities. Pursuant to the import of the CD containing the software, HCL paid license fee to SAP India for obtaining license key codes to unlock the full version of the software upon expiry of trial period. Hence, the license fee was not a condition of sale for the import of CDs containing software.

This apart, right to use the software is different from the sale of goods and HCL is only provided a non-exclusive right to use the SAP Software. Thus, there is no "sale".

As a result, the Tribunal held that the license fee paid by HCL to SAP India could not be included in the valuation of imported CDs containing software. Consequently, duty demand, interest and penalties were set aside.

Why does this case matter?

This judgment sheds clarity and sets a sound precedent that not every overenthusiastic attempt to automatically include license fee/royalty is appropriate – especially when these payments don't meet the strict statutory criteria under Rule 9(1)(c) of the CVR.

The judgment decisively burst several prevalent myths regarding the inclusion of license fee/royalty payments in customs valuation: Myth#1: License fee/royalty must always be included in value of the imported goods if the same is part of the agreements; Myth#2: License fee/royalty for obtaining additional licenses post-import of the goods, must be included for the purposes of Customs Valuation; Myth#3: Electronic delivery of software is treated the same as physical import for Customs purposes; and Myth#4: "Right to use" the imported goods is same as that of "sale of goods."

The Tribunal arrived at such conclusions on the basis of the specific terms mentioned in the EULA. In essence, the judgment highlights that assessing the inclusion of license fee/royalty in valuation of the imported goods is akin to reading fine print under a magnifying glass—every detail in the agreement can shift the outcome. Thus, each licensing agreement needs a careful, case-by-case look to decide if the license fee/royalty emanating therefrom becomes a part of customs valuation.

Beyond the Judgement: Practical Insights for Importers

This struggle isn't just about numbers or tax compliance. It's about language of the agreement. Misinterpretation could mean hefty penalties, but overzealous inclusion of license fee/royalty in the valuation of the imported goods could suffocate the cost structure of businesses. Every contract clause is dissected with the precision once reserved for engineering specs: Is this a 'condition of sale'? Does the license fee payment flow directly to the seller? Could it be included in the transaction value of the imported goods and consequently trigger customs duty?

Given the wide variety of contractual arrangements, it is essential to closely examine each agreement to determine whether any license fee/royalty is includible in the transaction value of the imported goods. If the contract or agreement is still in the drafting stage, it becomes even more critical to analyse these clauses thoroughly to ensure that the correct legal course is taken. Ultimately, it is best to review each of your agreements to ensure a sound risk management for imports.

2. Digital economy

Digital economy constitutes a shift of traditional business to online business that are enabled by information and communication technologies such as internet, mobile and sensor networks. Some of the key business activities in this space are enumerated below:

Cloud Computing: A new business model in the technology industry is the development of the virtual world a.k.a "Cloud computing". Cloud computing is a model for enabling convenient, on-demand access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources (e.g., networks, servers, storage, applications, and services) that can be accessed with minimal management effort or service provider interaction.

Online advertising: The latest form of marketing which uses the internet to deliver promotional marketing messages to its consumers.

E-commerce: A trading platform for trading in products or services using computer networks.

Under the Act, no specific regime has been prescribed on taxability of income from above-mentioned business activities. Therefore, both the tax payers and the Indian Revenue authorities are facing challenges in addressing the following tax issues:

-

How do enterprises in the digital economy add value in the value chain and make their profits?

-

Determination of place of accrual of income in the absence of a fixed place of business and consequent allocation of taxing rights to the resident country and the source country;

-

Characterisation of income earned by such enterprises;

-

PE implications and manner of attribution of income to such PE.

The definition of PE under the tax treaties entered into by India typically includes the concept of a fixed place PE. However, in the absence of any fixed place of business for any company operating under the digital economy model, the PE definition based on physical presence needs a re-thinking. Specifically in the context of e-commerce, the Commentary of the OECD states that a mere presence by way of a website cannot constitute a PE. Similarly, the interpretation of PE as per tax treaties also generally does not extend to websites, unless the servers on which websites are hosted are also located in the same jurisdiction. However, India (having an observer status to the OECD) has made a key reservation that a website may constitute a PE in certain circumstances, without elaborating on such instances.

Moreover, with the penetration of internet coupled with increase in confidence of on-line buyers, the trend of online advertising / website hosting have drastically been on the rise. The prima facie difficulty arises in respect of determination of source of income from such online advertising i.e. its "situs" and "place of business". It is pertinent to evaluate if mere presence of a search engine in a particular location other than the location of its effective place of management, through the internet or website can constitute PE? It is interesting to note that the Courts2 while explaining the concept of online advertisement, have held that consideration paid to non-residents for online advertising services qualifies as "business profit" and in the absence of PE of non-resident in India, the income cannot be said to be taxable in India.

For businesses engaged in cloud computing, the location of the server is the key to determine the place of PE. Facts and circumstances of each value chain would need to be determined including location-specific factors that increase the value attributable to the server location.

The OECD as part of its Action 1 of the BEPS project seeks to address the challenges in digital economy by shifting of place of taxation to market economies, rather than the home country where the entity is a resident. On applicability of the new measures, profits would be taxed where economic activities take place and value is created. In this context, the relevant limited recommendations of Action Plan 1 of BEPS are:

Wider definition of the term "PE" by curtailing exemptions for activities erstwhile being classified as "preparatory or auxiliary". Foreign e-commerce business having mere warehouses in India for storage and delivering goods sold online may going forward not be eligible for claiming exclusion from PE.

It also suggests modification in the definition of PE to address artificial arrangements through 'conclusion of contract' arrangements.

The report also suggests some additional safeguards which can be inserted in the domestic laws such as nexus rule in the form of significant digital presence, withholding tax on payment for digital transactions and an equalisation levy.

However, this argument is bound to fail in view of the very specific provisions under service tax laws. The Hon'ble Madras High Court in the case of Infotech Software Dealers Association has held that transaction in relation to canned/off-the-shelf software can be service in case the developer of software retains the copyright while right to use of software is given to the subscriber. The scenario has become grave for the dealers who prior to introduction of service tax were charging only sales tax on the value of software. Now in view of the specific category under service tax, they need to charge both sales tax and service tax. Since the sales tax and service tax are indirect taxes and to avoid litigation, the dealers tend to charge both the taxes and it is only the end - consumer who has to suffer in view of multiplicity of taxes.

As regards the customized/uncanned software, the contract for development of such software perhaps at the best may be viewed as a service contract. The customized software means software developed for a specific customer to meet his specific requirements. The software industry prior to the introduction of new category of taxable service in the name of 'Information Technology Software Service' was at an advantageous position, as no indirect taxes were applicable on the development of customized software treating it as a service contract. However, the advantageous position got diluted after the introduction of new category as above, as now development of customized software attracts service tax. The dilution has further been deepened after the judgment of the Hon'ble Madras High Court in the case of Infosys Technologies Ltd. in which it has been held that even customized software may qualify as goods.

The sales tax authorities after taking recourse to the judgment of the Hon'ble Madras High Court are issuing notices demanding tax on the transaction involving development of software. The judgment has opened a Pandora's Box of litigations in relation to customized/uncanned software.

Another area of litigation concerning software is supply of software through electronic downloads. In such a scenario, service tax gets attracted in view of the specific language of the taxable service under the category of 'Information Technology Software Service'. However, whether sales tax is also payable is another point where litigation surrounds the software industry. The Hon'ble Karnataka High Court recently in the case of Sasken Communication Technologies Ltd. has observed that intellectual property once put on a medium becomes goods and when transferred is leviable to sales tax. After this judgment, the industry players can hope that the sales tax authorities do not litigate on this issue.

The menace of double taxation is detrimental to the interests of users of goods/services as it results into high procurement costs, especially in those cases where credit of input taxes paid cannot be taken by the users. The domestic users only take a hit as the exporters of software generally enjoy the tax free status and, accordingly, no taxes are charged on the value of goods/services exported from India. Presently, the sales tax (local VAT) rate for software is either at 4% or at 5% and service tax rate is at 10%, which can significantly enhance the costs of procurements in case software suffers double taxation, specifically in cases where the credit of input taxes is not available either in full or in part.

Though the laws on sales tax and service tax are on the statute books for good number of years now, yet the provisions of these laws need alignment, which seems to be an uphill task in view of the fact that the Governments desire to garner more and more revenue and sometimes it happens by introducing provisions which put the taxpayer in a situation where he has no alternative but to resort to litigation.

2.2 Issues regarding Classification - Another controversy that surrounds the software revolves around its classification, especially in those cases where the software is not embedded in the hardware and is procured separately from the vendor of the hardware. The problem is generally faced by the importers of telecom equipments.

At present, the rate of customs duty on telecom equipments is generally at around 15% and on software it is at around 10% in case it is imported say on CD. Due to the difference in the rate of customs duty, the customs authorities always litigate on the genuineness of the imports and try to include the value of software in the value of hardware and, accordingly, make the value of software suffer higher rate of customs duty. This particular issue of telecom industry is yet to test the scrutiny of judiciary but apparently, both hardware and software are classifiable into different customs tariff classifications and different customs duty structure is also justifiable.

2.3 Issues regarding Withholding Tax - Another issue that hovers around software is whether the payments remitted by a resident to a non-resident for software can be said to be one for use of copyright or can be categorised as one for copyrighted article. The issue has over a period of time been interpreted differently by the Appellate Tribunals across India. In case, the amount is categorised as royalty, the Indian entity making the payment is required to do withholding of tax under section 195 of the Income-tax Act.

The Mumbai Tribunal in the case of Novel Inc. v. Dy. DIT [2011] 16 taxmann.com 186 has held that payments made by the Indian distributors to a non-resident for procuring rights to further sell the software to customers in India would not amount to royalty.

Unlike trade in goods, services do not cross the border or pass the frontier and, therefore, hard to regulate at that point. A ‘service’ is an intangible product and can be supplied easily by using information technology such as calls, fax and e-mail. The important characteristics of services are:—

(a) Services are process.

(b)Transaction in services may require personal contact between providers and consumers.

(c)Some services may have to be regulated.

Where ‘services’ itself moves without the provider or recipient having to travel to another country is referred to in terms as ‘Cross Border Provision of Services’5; whereas when the recipient of the service or ‘consumers’ moves to the country where service provider is established is known as ‘Consumption abroad’ or ‘Movement of consumer’6. Lastly, when the business itself moves to the country where services are to be provided it is considered to be commercial presence which is commonly referred as Permanent Establishment.

Of late, the outsourcing industry around the world has been confronted with the contentious question of whether outsourced services provided by companies — particularly by captive service providers/manufacturers — would lead to a Permanent Establishment (PE) of the non-resident service recipient to come into existence under the terms of the relevant tax treaty. India has been a major beneficiary in the outsourcing boom, and, hence, if Indian tax authorities were to hold that such activities are tantamount to a PE, the global profits attributable to the PE would be taxable in India at the rate of 42.23 per cent7. Further, the availability of a tax credit in the home jurisdiction for such tax paid in India would be uncertain, potentially leading to double taxation and wiping out the economic advantage of outsourcing to India. On the other hand, if no PE exists, no profits can be subjected to Indian corporate tax.

In India, tax liability is based on the structure of the outsourcing contract and the scope of activities being undertaken. The generally preferred models, like third-party service providers, captive centres set up as wholly owned subsidiaries or outsourcing to transition partners on a BOT basis are taxed differently under Indian tax laws. Companies establishing captive facilities and BOT arrangements have to consider issues relating to transfer pricing and permanent establishment.

B59A. An entity's activities significantly affect the intellectual property to which the customer has rights when either:

(a) those activities are expected to significantly change the form (for example, the design or content) or the functionality (for example, the ability to perform a function or task) of the intellectual property; or

For example, the benefit from a brand is often derived from, or dependent upon, the entity's ongoing activities that support or maintain the value of the intellectual property.

Accordingly, if the intellectual property to which the customer has rights has significant stand-alone functionality, a substantial portion of the benefit of that intellectual property is derived from that functionality. Consequently, the ability of the customer to obtain benefit from that intellectual property would not be significantly affected by the entity's activities unless those activities significantly change its form or functionality. Types of intellectual property that often have significant stand-alone functionality include software, biological compounds or drug formulas, and completed media content (for example, films, television shows and music recordings).

If the criteria in paragraph B58 are met, an entity shall account for the promise to grant a licence as a performance obligation satisfied over time because the customer will simultaneously receive and consume the benefit from the entity's performance of providing access to its intellectual property as the performance occurs (see paragraph 35(a)). An entity shall apply paragraphs 39-45 to select an appropriate method to measure its progress towards complete satisfaction of that performance obligation to provide access.

B61. If the criteria in paragraph B58 are not met, the nature of an entity's promise is to provide a right to use the entity's intellectual property as that intellectual property exists (in terms of form and functionality) at the point in time at which the licence is granted to the customer. This means that the customer can direct the use of, and obtain substantially all of the remaining benefits from, the licence at the point in time at which the licence transfers. An entity shall account for the promise to provide a right to use the entity's intellectual property as a performance obligation satisfied at a point in time. An entity shall apply paragraph 38 to determine the point in time at which the licence transfers to the customer. However, revenue cannot be recognised for a licence that provides a right to use the entity's intellectual property before the beginning of the period during which the customer is able to use and benefit from the licence. For example, if a software licence period begins before an entity provides (or otherwise makes available) to the customer a code that enables the customer to immediately use the software, the entity would not recognise revenue before that code has been provided (or otherwise made available).

B62. An entity shall disregard the following factors when determining whether a licence provides a right to access the entity's intellectual property or a right to use the entity's intellectual property:

(a)

Restrictions of time, geographical region or use—those restrictions define the attributes of the promised licence, rather than define whether the entity satisfies its performance obligation at a point in time or over time.

(b)

Guarantees provided by the entity that it has a valid patent to intellectual property and that it will defend that patent from unauthorised use—a promise to defend a patent right is not a performance obligation because the act of defending a patent protects the value of the entity's intellectual property assets and provides assurance to the customer that the licence transferred meets the specifications of the licence promised in the contract.

Introduction

Technology has always been at the cutting edge of the significant transformation that is taking place in the market place today. Mobile technology, analytics, cloud computing and wearables have emerged as new forms of technology, and even several traditional companies have started to add capabilities in these areas to cater to the growing customer preferences. In this digital revolution, leading the pack is the e-commerce segment, which is driving rapid growth of domestic IT-ITeS industry and is attracting unprecedented levels of global interest, funding and talent. Owing to such rapid revolution and growth, India ranks third in start-ups formed in the technology industry globally.

Keeping in pace with the growth in this industry, the controversies surrounding taxation of digital transactions are also ever on the rise. Governments and tax administrators of many countries are constantly evaluating the tax implications arising on operations of such entities, since transactions of the e-commerce players raises several contentious tax issues due to absence of national boundaries, physical presence of goods and non-requirement of physical delivery. In India, there are innumerable tax issues faced by the technology industry and in the ensuing paragraphs we have discussed the populist ones.

1. Withholding tax issues on cross border payments involving software

Transactions in the technology industry such as payments for purchase or usage of software, payments for online advertising, app stores, cloud computing are under the tax radar. Such transactions could involve:

-

Transfer of rights in a property (such as right to alter or reproduce work or issue copies of the work);

-

Few transactions could involve payment for services such as access / subscription to databases, standardised applications, e-library, online games, music, news etc.; and

-

Certain transactions could be a combination of both transfer of property rights and services. For e.g. customised software or configurable computing resources such as networks, servers, storage, applications along with services made available to the users through the internet.

The taxation and the related withholding tax implications on such payments to non-residents would be based on the characterisation of such income (business income or royalty or fees for technical services) under the Income-tax Act, 1961 ("the Act") read with the beneficial provisions of the tax treaty. Non-resident tax payers in several instances were seeking to characterise their income from such transactions as business income and offer the same to tax in India only where such income was attributable to a permanent establishment ("PE") in India. Hence, in order to curb such mischief, in the garb of a clarification, the Government brought in a retrospective amendment in the Act to widen the scope of definition of "Royalty". The amended definition of "Royalty" seeks to include transfer of any right to use a software including the granting of a license, irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred. This amendment significantly targets transactions involving payments for shrink-wrap or embedded software.

The issue of taxation of cross border software licensing transactions including payments towards access to databases, online applications etc. have been a significant bone of contention between the Indian Revenue authorities and the tax payers over the last decade.

Some of the key illustrative factors considered relevant by the Courts for determining the characterisation of income are listed below:

Nature of rights granted to the payee - Whether rights in the property is transferred or mere right of usage of property is conferred;

Nature of software - Customised vis-à-vis standardised software;

Whether the payment is towards the use or right to use a copyrighted article or a copyright in the article.

Degree of possession and control of the server / database / application;

Recourse to the service provider for the further requirement of any services;

Whether any specific configuration is carried out for the payee?

Whether any information is made available to the payee and right of further commercial exploitation is conferred on the payee?

Whether the payment is made for right other that right in the intellectual property?

Determination of taxability of transactions should be based on a holistic evaluation of the intention of the parties involved and the primary purpose for which the payment is being made. Issues on taxability of software payments along with taxation aspects of e-commerce transactions were extensively researched and opined upon by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development ("OECD") - Technical Advisory Group almost two decades back. However, India differed on most of the views of the OECD on this issue and currently maintains an enhanced observer status to the OECD. The views expressed by India are in variance with most of the developed countries on characterisation of income on software payments. The current action plans initiated by the OECD under the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting ("BEPS") also do not deal with such issues adding to the woes of the technology industry players.

Concentrix Services Netherlands B.V. v. ITO [2021] 127 taxmann.com 43/434 ITR 516 (Delhi)

Revenue contended that the protocol appended to the subject DTAA showed that the benefit of the lower rate of withholding tax would be available only if the country with which India entered into a DTAA were a member of the OECD at the time of the execution of the subject DTAA. None of the aforesaid countries, i.e., Slovenia, Lithuania, and Columbia, were members of the OECD on the date DTAAs was signed with India.Thus, clause IV(2) of the protocol appended to the subject DTAA would have no applicability.

On writ, Delhi High Court held that a bare perusal of Clause IV(2) of the protocol appended to the subject DTAA shows that it incorporates the principle of parity between the subject DTAA and the DTAAs executed thereafter. Such parity is available qua the rate of withholding tax or the scope of the conventions in respect of items of income concerning dividends, interest, royalties, fees for technical services, or payments for the use of equipment.

However, the principle of parity kicks-in, only if the third State with whom India enters into a DTAA is a member of the OECD. Further, India should have, in its DTAA, executed with the third State, limited its withholding tax rate, on subject remittances, at a rate lower or a scope more restricted, than the rate or scope provided in the subject DTAA.

Once the aforementioned conditions are fulfilled, then, from the date on which the DTAA between India and a third State comes into force, the same rate of withholding tax or scope as provided in the DTAA executed between India and the third State would necessarily have to apply to the subject DTAA.

Therefore, the beneficial withholding tax rate of 5% in India-Slovenia DTAA will apply from the date when Slovenia became an OECD member, i.e., from August 2010. However, India - Slovenia DTAA came into force in February 2005.

5. Income from cloud hosting and its ancillary services neither royalty nor FTS : ITAT

Racksapce US, Inc. v. Dy. CIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 92 (Mum. - Trib.)

The assessee was a tax resident of the USA. Assessee earned income from cloud services, including cloud hosting and other supporting and ancillary services provided to Indian Customers. The assessee filed the return of income and the notes stating that the cloud hosting services were not taxable as 'royalties' under Article 12 of the India-US tax treaty.

The Mumbai ITAT held that the agreement between the assessee and its customer was for providing hosting and other ancillary services to the customer and not for the use of or leasing of any equipment.

The Data Centre and the Infrastructure therein were used to provide these services belonging to the assessee. The customers do not have physical control or possession over the servers, and right to operate and manage this infrastructure or servers vested solely with the assessee. The agreement was to provide simpliciter hosting services and not give the underlying equipment on hire or lease. The customer did not know any server location in the data centre, webmail, websites, etc.

Thus, the income from cloud hosting services had erroneously been held as royalty within the meaning of Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi) as well as article 12(3)(b) of the India-USA DTAA by AO and DRP.

When the period for which the amounts of receivables received in advance enjoyed by the assessee were seen vis-a-vis the amount receivable beyond sixty days, it was apparent that the assessee had received significantly more advance rather than outstanding receivable beyond sixty days.

3.4-4 'Transfer of all or any rights' v. 'Transfer or grant of all or any rights' [Section 9(6)(b) & 9(6)(c)(i) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Explanations 2 & 4 to Section 9(1)(vi) of the ITA 1961)] Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(vi) defines the meaning of 'royalty' which includes "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence) in respect of a patent, invention, model, design, secret formula or process or trade mark or similar property", and Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi) clarified that the transfer of any right, property or information shall include transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

Under the ITA 1961, the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…" was used in Explanation 2(i) & 2(v) to section 9(1)(vi), whereas the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights" was used in Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi). However, under the ITA 2025, the former phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…", and the latter phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights". The corresponding provisions under the ITA 2025 are sub-clauses (i) and (vi) of section 9(6)(b) and sub-clause (i) of section 9(6)(c), respectively.

This explicit insertion of 'or grant' attempts to cover any form of allowing the use of rights, whether it is a full transfer (alienation of ownership) or a mere permission to use (grant). This appears to be an attempt to nullify the Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42 (SC). By explicitly including 'grant', the legislature intends to emphasise that payments for the use of software, patents, copyrights, and other intellectual properties, even if they do not involve a full 'transfer' of copyright or a 'parting with an interest' in the underlying rights, are brought within the ambit of royalty. The intent is to tax payments for the mere 'use' or 'right to use' such properties as royalty, irrespective of whether the transaction constitutes an outright sale of the underlying intellectual property or a mere licence. However, for non-residents, the tax implications of this expanded definition of royalty must always be considered in light of any applicable DTAAs that India has with other countries. While the ITA 2025 aims to broaden the domestic definition, it does not automatically override the DTAA provisions. The Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis was largely based on the DTAA provisions, and the amendment to Section 9(1)(vi) might not change the interpretation of DTAA articles if the DTAA's definition of royalty is narrower.

Note: Although this provision was not amended by the Finance Act, 2026, the above discussion highlights the changes introduced in the ITA 2025 compared to the ITA 1961.

3.5 The cap on the investment by an eligible investment fund has been increased from 20% to 25% [Section 9 and Schedule I of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 9A of the ITA 1961 Act)]

Section 9A of the ITA 1961 provides a special regime for offshore funds. It provides that in the case of an eligible investment fund, the fund management activity carried out through an eligible fund manager acting on behalf of such fund shall not constitute a business connection in India of the said fund. Further, an eligible investment fund shall not be deemed resident in India merely because the eligible fund manager undertaking fund management activities on its behalf is located in India. Thus, this exemption from the general rules for the determination of business connection and 'resident status' of offshore funds and fund management activity undertaken on their behalf is allowed on fulfilment of the conditions explained below:

(a)

The offshore fund should be an eligible investment fund.

(b)

The fund management activity of such a fund should be managed by an eligible fund manager.

The eligible investment fund means a fund established or incorporated, or registered outside India, which collects funds from its members for investing it for their benefit and fulfils the prescribed conditions. One such prescribed condition under the ITA 1961 is that the fund's investment in any entity does not exceed 20% of the fund's corpus, and that the fund does not make any investment in its associate entity.

Under the ITA 2025, this maximum capping on investment in any entity has been increased from 20% to 25%, and all other conditions remain the same.

10. Explanation 3(b) to section 65B(44) of Finance Act, 1994 introduced w.e.f. 1-7-2012 reads as follows - An establishment of a person in the taxable territory and any of his other establishment in a non-taxable territory shall be treated as establishments of distinct persons.

This Explanation has been given to definition of 'service'. In fact, this Explanation has nothing to do with definition of 'service' and is at a wrong place.

However, this Explanation is creating lot of difficulties (may be mainly because it has been placed at a wrong place). This Explanation is being interpreted to mean that HO in India and branch outside India are two different 'persons'. Hence, if the HO in India remits money to maintain branch outside India, it will be treated as 'import of service' i.e. branch outside India is providing service to Head Office in India.

Really, 'shall be treated as establishment of different persons' does not mean 'shall be treated as two different persons'.

Thus, Branch/office in India and branch/office of same business entity outside India will be treated as different 'establishments' and not 'different persons'.

Navigating the landscape of valuation for the imports

In the complex world of imports, businesses often consider the value of the physical goods to be paramount. However, they sometimes overlook that beyond the physical cargo lies something less visible yet crucial — the royalty/license fee payments. Royalties arise from licensing agreements which grant the importer rights inter alia to use manufacturing know-how, brand names, or software embedded within imported goods.

As the nature of contracts pertaining to imports/exports and associated license fee/royalty has evolved, the Customs valuation has also come a long way. Once upon a time, a physical shipment was all that customs authorities cared about for determining its value and imposition duties. Today's imports bundle licensed software, technology, trademarks, and other rights, making valuation of such shipments more complicated. While the goods themselves represent the tangible aspect for customs valuation, the accompanied intangible rights and their payments may significantly contribute to the overall value of the import transaction. This evolution sets the stage for courts to demystify when license fee/royalty should be included in the transaction value of the imported goods.

The recent judgement by CESTAT, New Delhi in the judgment of HCL Technologies Ltd. and SAP India Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs (Adjudication) [Final Order No. 51379-51462 of 2025 dated 29-9-2025] bring these complexities to the forefront. It deals with critical questions regarding includability of license fee in the value of the imported goods, specifically in the context of delivery of software through physical and electronic media.

Under the Lens: CESTAT's approach in the case of HCL Technologies Ltd.

Facts at a Glance

HCL Technologies Ltd. ('HCL') entered into an End-User License Agreement ('EULA') with SAP India Private Limited ('SAP India') to obtain non-exclusive and perpetual license to use propriety software, documentation and other information of SAP India. As per terms of the EULA, the software was to be delivered electronically. In the year 2006, SAP India raised substantial invoices on HCL for payment of license fee relating to rights provided under the EULA.

During the same time, HCL received some imported CDs containing SAP Software via courier, wherein a nominal value was declared under the courier bill of entry, for customs purposes. Perhaps, this is what caught the eye of the Customs Department – A CD with a software... only for pocket change?

An investigation was initiated against inter alia HCL for such imports. Upon conclusion of the investigation, the Customs Department rejected the declared value of the CDs under Rule 10A of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 ('CVR') [now Rule 14 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007] and sought to include the license fee in the valuation of imported CDs in terms of Rule 9(1)(c) of CVR.

The allegation of the Customs Department was that unless the license fee is paid, the software on the CD cannot be accessed or used; thereby, making the license fee integral to the transaction value of the imported CDs.

Tribunal's Verdict: Four Conditions for Royalty Inclusion in Customs Valuation

The Tribunal determined that for inclusion of royalties to the value of the imported goods, the following four key conditions under Rule 9(1)(c) of CVR needed to be satisfied:

1.

The license fee must relate to the imported goods;

2.

The fee must be payable directly or indirectly by the importer at the time of import;

3.

The license fee must be a condition of sale of the goods; and

4.

The fee must not already be included in the price actually paid or payable for the imported goods.

Guided by these conditions, the Tribunal took a closer look at the terms of the EULA entered between HCL&SAP India, and made the following findings:

The license fee was not related to the physical import of the CDs; rather, it was related to the intangible right to use the software in India. The EULA had itself provided electronic delivery as the mode of delivery of the software. Thus, the license fee was for usage of software rights and not for the import of physical CDs themselves.

The EULA provided for a trial period which allowed HCL limited software access without payment of license fee. The obligation for full payment, per the terms of EULA, would only be triggered only if HCL opted for full license post this trial. Therefore, HCL was not required to pay the license fee at the time of import.

Software Acquired for Internal Use

10. The cost of a software acquired for internal use should be recognised as an asset if it meets the recognition criteria prescribed in paragraphs 20 and 21 of this Standard.

11. The cost of a software purchased for internal use comprises its purchase price, including any import duties and other taxes (other than those subsequently recoverable by the enterprise from the taxing authorities) and any directly attri-butable expenditure on making the software ready for its use. Any trade discounts and rebates are deducted in arriving at the cost. In the determination of cost, matters stated in paragraphs 24 to 34 of the Standard need to be considered, as appropriate.

Subsequent expenditure

12. Enterprises may incur considerable cost in modifying existing software systems. Subsequent expenditure on software after its purchase or its completion should be recognised as an expense when it is incurred unless:

(a)

it is probable that the expenditure will enable the software to generate future economic benefits in excess of its originally assessed standards of performance; and

(b)

the expenditure can be measured and attributed to the software reliably.

If these conditions are met, the subsequent expenditure should be added to the carrying amount of the software. Costs incurred in order to restore or maintain the future economic benefits that an enterprise can expect from the originally assessed standard of performance of existing software systems is recognised as an expense when, and only when, the restoration or maintenance work is carried out.

Amortisation period

13. The depreciable amount of a software should be allocated on a systematic basis over the best estimate of its useful life. The amortisation should commence when the software is available for use.

14. As per this Standard, there is a rebuttable presumption that the useful life of an intangible asset will not exceed ten years from the date when the asset is available for use. However, given the history of rapid changes in technology, computer software is susceptible to technological obsolescence. Therefore, it is likely that useful life of the software will be much shorter, say 3 to 5 years.

Amortisation method

15. The amortisation method used should reflect the pattern in which the software's economic benefits are consumed by the enterprise. If that pattern cannot be determined reliably, the straight-line method should be used. The amortisation charge for each period should be recognised as an expenditure unless another Accounting Standard permits or requires it to be included in the carrying amount of another asset. For example, the amortisation of a software used in a production process is included in the carrying amount of inventories.

II. Illustrative Application of the Accounting Standard to Website Costs

1. An enterprise may incur internal expenditures when developing, enhancing and maintaining its own website. The website may be used for various purposes such as promoting and advertising products and services, providing electronic services, and selling products and services.

2. The stages of a website's development can be described as follows:

(a)

Planning - includes undertaking feasibility studies, defining objectives and specifications, evaluating alternatives and selecting preferences;

(b)

Application and Infrastructure Development - includes obtaining a domain name, purchasing and developing hardware and operating software, installing developed applications and stress testing; and

(c)

Graphical Design and Content Development - includes designing the appearance of web pages and creating, purchasing, preparing and uploading information, either textual or graphical in nature, on the website prior to the website becoming available for use. This information may either be stored in separate databases that are integrated into (or accessed from) the website or coded directly into the web pages.

3. Once development of a website has been completed and the website is available for use, the website commences an operating stage. During this stage, an enterprise maintains and enhances the applications, infrastructure, graphical design and content of the website.

4. The expenditures for purchasing, developing, maintaining and enhancing hardware (e.g., web servers, staging servers, production servers arid Internet connections) related to a website are not accounted for under this Standard but are accounted for under AS 10, Accounting for Fixed Assets. Additionally, when an enterprise incurs an expenditure for having an Internet service provider host the enterprise's website on its own servers connected to the Internet, the expenditure is recognised as an expense.

. During the last decade or so India has seen a steady growth of outsourcing of business processes by non-residents or foreign companies to IT-enabled entities in India. Such entities are either branches or associated concerns of the foreign enterprise or an independent Indian enterprise. Their activities range from mere procurement of orders for sale of goods or provision of services and answering sales related queries, to the provision itself of services like software maintenance service, debt collection service, software development service, credit card/mobile telephone related service, etc. An example of BPO services by an IT-enabled entity in India could be a case where a foreign company manufacturing computers abroad and also selling such computers to customers abroad, engages or sets up a call centre in India to process orders from or conclude contracts with customers abroad and also to answer sales related queries on telephone. Similarly, a foreign insurance company insuring risks in countries other than India may appoint or set up a call centre in India to attend to calls from customers outside India regarding acquisition of new insurance policy or revision of existing policy, to disseminate relevant information and accept insurance proposals from the customers, while actual policy issuance as well as collection of premium is done outside India by the foreign insurance company. Another example of such services could be the case of a foreign credit card company issuing credit cards to customers living in countries other than India, appointing or setting up a call centre in India to attend to calls from customers outside India seeking to acquire a new credit card, disseminate relevant information and accept the request for issue of a credit card from the customer, while the actual card issuance, delivery of the card and collection of charges are being done outside India by the foreign credit card company, and the charges paid to the Indian call centre for its services are at arm’s length/fair market price.

A non-resident company may outsource revenue generating business activities to an IT-enabled entity in India, such as the services of a travel agent, software developer, software maintenance, investment consultant, debt collection service, etc., and the IT-enabled entity in India may render the services either directly to the customers abroad or through the non-resident principal.

There may be certain other incidental activities outsourced which are incidental to the business of carrying on manufacture and sale of goods or merchandise or provision of services outside India, such as conclusion of contracts and procurement of orders to an IT-enabled entity in India.

The BPO entity in India carrying on the outsourcing activities for a non-resident company, may be its branch or subsidiary company or an independent company. Between PE and "business connection", there is little distinction. In content they are the same.

Status of BPO entity

8. The BPO entity in India carrying on the outsourcing activities for a non-resident company, may be its branch or subsidiary company or an independent company.

A branch connotes a physical presence of the foreign enterprise in India. It is an office with an independent administration. Where a non-resident has an office in India and employs staff to carry on its business, it is its branch. A branch office is not regarded as a separate legal entity. Its profits are the profits of a company owning the branch office. It is different from a subsidiary which has a legal entity of its own - CIT v. Stewarts & Lloyds of India Ltd. [1987] 165 ITR 416 (Cal.)—and which is regarded as a domestic company in the country where it is established. The subsidiary company may be a branch office of a foreign establishment under certain circumstances. If it is engaged in transactions with or on behalf of the foreign enterprise as an agent of the parent company in circumstances pointing out to a trading in a host country, it can be said to be performing functions on behalf of that enterprise in the same way as any could do - Fire Stone Tyre and Rubber Co. Ltd. v. Lewellin 37 TC 111. To that extent the subsidiary is the branch office of the foreign enterprise, in spite of it having independent and own legal status.

BPO entity - Taxability of income

9. For taxability of income attributable to the activities in India, the status of the BPO entity has to be first ascertained, whether it is a branch of the foreign enterprise or an independent entity, and then whether the branch qualifies as permanent establishment (PE) in terms of the Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) between India and the State of which the foreign enterprise is resident, or whether the independent entity has "business connection" in terms of the definition under section 9 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961 where there is no DTA. Between PE and "business connection", there is little distinction. In content they are the same.

4.3 Direct Tax Incentives – Circulars based on the recommendations of the Rangachary Committee - Central Board of Direct Taxes ('CBDT') released Circular No.1/2013 on January 17, 2013 and a Press Release on the same day for clarifying the intent of law on the direct tax benefits imparted to the Indian software industry through enactment of profit based incentives iterated in sections 10A, 10AA and 10B of the Income-tax Act. The Circular addresses various tax issues around the eligible tax holiday companies, deriving profits from eligible business where ambiguity prevails and, hence, litigation is rampant. On comparison of the recommendations of the Rangachary Committee report and the clarifications offered in the CBDT Circular, it becomes clear that the departmental Circular is premised on and completely endorses the recommendations of the aforesaid Committee.

4.3.1 The key takeaways from the Committee's report reiterated in Circular No. 1

4.3.1.1 ISSUE NO. 1 - Whether 'on-site' development of computer software qualifies as an export activity for tax benefit under sections 10A, 10AA and 10B of the Act?

4.3.1.1.1 THE CONTROVERSY- 'On-site' software development services are the services that are taken up on the premises of the client (a foreign company) due to exigencies of speed, uncertainty arising from new technology and confidentiality. The revenue denies the tax holiday benefit on the ground that no export has ensued from the eligible unit, the services being rendered from the premises outside India. Such view is also inflicted by CBDT's Circular No. 694 of 1994 which provides that the 'on-site' software development will be considered as an export only if the software is actually the product of the unit.

4.3.1.1.2 RECOMMENDATIONS OF RANGACHARY COMMITTEE- The Committee relied on the Explanation 3 to section 10A, Explanation 3 to section 10B and Explanation 2 to section 10AA. The cited Explanations create a deeming fiction that the profits and gains derived from on-site development of computer software outside India shall be deemed to be the profits and gains derived from the export of computer software outside India. The Committee also recommended suitable modifications in Circular 694 of 1994 relating to 'on-site' software development services, so as to qualify such services as export sales.

4.3.1.1.3 CLARIFICATION IN CIRCULAR NO. 1- The CBDT's Circular reiterates the view of the Rangachary Committee and modifies Circular No. 694, dated 23-11-1994 to clarify that the software developed abroad at the client's place would amount to 'deemed export' and would be eligible to tax benefits. However, it is necessary that there must exist a connection between the development of software abroad with the eligible unit set-up in India and work must be carried out through client's contract entered into with the eligible unit.

4.3.1.2 ISSUE NO. 2- Whether business receipts from deputation of technical manpower ('DTM') are eligible for deduction under sections 10A, 10AA and 10B?

4.3.1.2.1 THE CONTROVERSY- The revenue denied the profit based incentives on the premise that the deployment of manpower is for the limited purpose of sending trained manpower abroad and, hence, not an eligible activity under the prescribed tax holiday sections.

4.3.1.2.2 RECOMMENDATIONS OF RANGACHARY COMMITTEE- DTM that includes upgradation, testing, maintenance, modification, etc., of the software should be considered as eligible activity under the tax holiday sections, provided the DTMs are related to the software development activities of the eligible unit. The deployment contract would be an essential document to evidence the nexus between DTM and software development activities.

4.3.1.2.3 CLARIFICATION IN CIRCULAR NO. 1- The CBDT's Circular endorses the view of Rangachary Committee and states that benefit under sections 10A, 10AA and 10B should not be denied to DTMs at client's place abroad, provided it pertains to software development service undertaken pursuant to the contract between the client and the eligible unit.

The ITA 2025 has combined both provisions of Explanation 1(a) and the third proviso to Explanation 2A of section 9(1)(i) into section 9(9)(f). Sub-clauses (i) and (ii) of section 9(9)(f) correspond to Explanation 1(a) and the third proviso to Explanation 2A, respectively. It is to be noted that section 9(9)(f) uses the words "reasonably attributable" for both sub-clauses (i) and (ii). Thus, the word "reasonably" is now applicable in the context of SEP also. The deliberate inclusion of 'reasonably' in the ITA 2025 in the SEP context suggests a legislative intent for a potentially more nuanced or proportionate allocation based on overall business functions, assets, and risks. As a result, income attribution under SEP will no longer be distinct from attribution under ordinary business connection cases. Both will now be governed by the overarching principle of reasonable attribution, ensuring consistency and reducing the scope for disproportionate taxation.

3.4-3 Purchase of goods in India for export [Section 9(8)(c)(ii)(A) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Explanation 1(b) to Section 9(1)(i) of the ITA 1961)]

Explanation 1(b) to section 9(1)(i) of the ITA 1961 provides that in the case of a non-resident, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to him through or from operations which are confined to the purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export. In the corresponding section 9(9)(c)(ii) of the ITA 2025, the words used are "purchase of goods in India for the purposes of export out of India".

On a strict literal interpretation, the addition of "out of India" might seem redundant, since "export" universally means sending goods out of the country. However, the expression "export out of India" would primarily serve to explicitly remove any remote ambiguity. It could prevent an interpretation where "export" might be construed to include movement to a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) within India (which is treated as foreign territory for certain purposes but is geographically within India) or other domestic transfers that are deemed exports for other regulatory purposes but do not involve physical exit from India's customs territory. It would clarify that the exemption applies only when goods physically leave the Indian customs territory.

3.4-4 'Transfer of all or any rights' v. 'Transfer or grant of all or any rights' [Section 9(6)(b) & 9(6)(c)(i) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Explanations 2 & 4 to Section 9(1)(vi) of the ITA 1961)]

Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(vi) defines the meaning of 'royalty' which includes "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence) in respect of a patent, invention, model, design, secret formula or process or trade mark or similar property", and Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi) clarified that the transfer of any right, property or information shall include transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

Under the ITA 1961, the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…" was used in Explanation 2(i) & 2(v) to section 9(1)(vi), whereas the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights" was used in Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi). However, under the ITA 2025, the former phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…", and the latter phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights". The corresponding provisions under the ITA 2025 are sub-clauses (i) and (vi) of section 9(6)(b) and sub-clause (i) of section 9(6)(c), respectively.
