Guidelines for overseas business acquisition by Indian companies engaged in information technology, entertainment software, pharmaceuticals, bio-technology through ADR/GDR stock swap Guidelines were issued on 27th December, 1999 to liberalise the operational norms including approval mechanism for overseas business acquisition by the Indian Software Companies. In his Budget Speech 2000-2001, the Finance Minister had announced the intent to further liberalise the policy for acquisition of companies abroad and to extend the policy to wider spectrum of companies in the knowledge-based sectors to expand globally and transform into Multi-National Companies in areas where India has comparative economic advantage.

2. In partial modification of the guidelines issued on 27-12-1999, following parameters are set out for overseas business acquisition through ADR/GDR stock swap :

Coverage

3. The liberalised norms will extend to Indian companies engaged in areas/activities as indicated in Annexure to these guidelines for acquisition of overseas companies in their respective areas of business. The Indian companies in the specified sectors/areas are defined as those registered in India and 80% of the turnover is from these respective areas of the operation/business of the company in the three previous financial years. In the case of multi-product diversified company, not conforming to the 80% criteria, the liberalised norms would be applicable if they have an average annual export earnings of at least Rs. 100 crores in the three previous financial years in these sectors/areas.

Limit for acquisition

4. Overseas business acquisition by specified Indian Companies would be governed by the following guidelines :

(A) Overseas business acquisition abroad by the specified Indian companies under the automatic route

The financial limit to overseas business acquisition on an automatic basis without reference either to the Government or the RBI on a back to back basis i.e., through stock swap will be as follows :—

(i) US $ 100 million; or

(ii) Upto 10 times the export earning of the investing company during the preceding year as reflected in the audited balance sheet of the company.

For (ii) above if any other facility has been availed by the investing company for overseas investment through any other window including item (i) above during the financial year, the same would be adjusted and the entitlement would be for the balance amount.

The value limits indicated above would be an annual limit (financial year) for each company for one or more acquisitions.

Other criteria for qualifying for automatic route would continue to apply.

(B) Overseas business acquisition not governed by the automatic route

Cases not covered by (A) above, the specified Indian Company would send the proposal to RBI for consideration by the Special Composite Committee for Overseas Investment through ADR/GDR Stock Swap.

5. The criteria for automatic approval and other norms contained in the guidelines of 27th December, 1999 including the mandatory requirement of conforming to the FDI policy, an existing ADR/GDR listing abroad and reporting requirement, etc., would continue to be operative.

6. After issue of ADRs/GDRs for acquisitions, the particulars thereof, along with the copy of the documents submitted to the regulatory authorities in the host country should be transmitted to DEA and RBI within a month as post facto reports along with certification about compliance with the eligibility with reference to the definition of the company in the specified permitted category/sector and entitlement based on export earnings.

7. In respect of each overseas company acquired under the scheme, an Annual Performance Report, as per the existing procedure, citing the Identification Number allotted by RBI in respect of such overseas companies should be sent to RBI for the purpose of compilation of data and monitoring.

8. The above policy will be subject to review as considered necessary by the Government.

continues to remain legal employer and pays the salary, takes care of the social security benefits etc. The cost of the seconded employee economically belongs to the Indian entity but is paid by the foreign entity for non-tax reasons on behalf of Indian entity. In such a situation, the Indian entity is required to reimburse the cost of the employee to the foreign entity. Very often, ignoring the practical aspects of such arrangements, the tax authorities take aggressive positions and determine taxability involving one or more of the following: treating the reimbursement as subject to withholding tax in India – resulting into economic double taxation of the same income once as salary in the hands of the employees and then in the hands of the foreign company as fees for providing services;

disallowance of reimbursed salary cost in the hands of the Indian entity in the absence of withholding tax on such reimbursements; or

treating the foreign company as having a taxable presence (Permanent Establishment) in India in the form of its employees.

It is heartening to see how the tax tribunal in a few recent rulings4 has decided the aforesaid issues in favour of the taxpayer recognizing that such reimbursements if made subject to withholding tax would result in double taxation and have allowed reimbursements as business expenditure in the hands of the Indian entity where they were purely reimbursements and not regarded to constitute fee for technical services.

4.4 Provision of technical know- how – Whether contract manufacturing

Another controversial area is arrangements involving provision of technical know-how by a group entity to its Indian group entity enabling the latter to manufacture goods for group entities as well as third parties. Tax authorities tend to treat such arrangements as those of contract manufacturing and thus, disallow royalty pay-outs to the Indian entity treating it as a payment to self. In a few recent tribunal rulings5, the issue was decided in favour of the taxpayer distinguishing such arrangements from contract manufacturing.

5. CONCLUSION

The issues emanating from the aggressive approach adopted by the tax authorities, which adversely impact genuine cases, should be addressed both by the tax administration and the taxpayers, otherwise significant time and effort would go into litigation. It is certainly to be ensured that Indian tax revenue should not be lost due to improper characterization. However, it is most desirable that there is reasonable certainty with regard to taxability of remittances from India and of amounts which are deemed to be regarded as Indian sourced income. It calls for the tax administration to lay down clear and unambiguous rules and guidelines for source rules and where some provisions of law are open to interpretation, judicial precedents on similar issues should be followed. This will go a long way in reducing avoidable litigation and bring the much desired certainty in tax matters for multinational organisations. The taxpayers on their part also need to consciously ensure that their documentation is robust and adequately reflect the actual conduct and intent. There is certainly a need to establish trust and spirit of partnership between taxpayer and tax administration. Chanakya, the master of economics has given the guidelines to tax administration as "tax needs to be collected from people as the honey bee collects honey from flowers – without harming the flower itself".

However the ground reality is that GICs has been facing substantial litigation challenges from the revenue department, primarily on transfer pricing issues.

The Software Value Chain

A typical software development value chain entails various functions, starting from the Conceptualization and Design phases to Software Development, Testing, Bug fixing etc. and finally the delivery of the software module to the end customer and maintenance of the software after delivering the same. While an independent software entity would be responsible for all the phases, the role of a captive is usually limited to only a few of these phases. Particularly captives in majority of the instances are neither involved in the design or conceptualization phase nor are responsible for the delivery of the final product to the end customer. Their role is restricted to the specific portions of the software development process that is outsourced to them. Many of the GICs would typically receive a steady flow of work from their parent companies and they need not engage in any selling and marketing activities to bid for projects for themselves. Although they are responsible for the quality of services rendered to their related parties, they do not assume the majority of the risks pertaining to the business. In most cases, even if there is any re-work necessary, they are remunerated for the rework costs incurred. The most common compensation model for GIC is a cost plus remuneration model wherein they earn a fixed margin on their total operating costs and they are absolved from majority of the risks. For example in case of turmoil in the market condition, GICs would continue to earn a consistent margin.

Unlike the GICs, full-fledged software developers undertake all the functions, bear all the risks and might own/develop intangibles in the course of its business. This helps them to command a better price and earn higher profits in the market or losses depending on the market conditions such as demand vs. supply, type of market they are operating, economic conditions, etc. In contrast a typical GIC's functions would not involve the development or usage of any non-routine intangible that allows it to earn high profits for itself. Similarly, as GICs do not bear any entrepreneurial or business risk, even if the parent company is facing losses, GIC's margins will not be affected.In a nutshell, the business of a typical GIC does not witness much fluctuation and is insulated by a good measure from the risks and challenges that plagues a full-fledged software developer.

Hence, going by the economic rationale that higher risks would be compensated with higher expected return over a time period and vice versa, a full-fledged software developer would earn higher expected return in the long run, when compared to a typical GIC. However this fact has not been appreciated by the income tax authorities in India, as is evident from the several rounds of transfer pricing audits so far. The revenue authorities have compared low risk GICs with software developer who owns intangibles and are placed high in the value chain. GIC are limited risk bearers who need to be differentiated from full-fledged software development companies.

The Indian Transfer Pricing Audit Experience: Challenges

The GICs have been constantly under the scanner of the transfer pricing authorities. Over the years, they have faced extensive audit from both the Assessing Officers and Transfer Pricing Officers and have been questioned over their business model and profitability. As India continues its foray into the globalized world economy, transfer pricing will become a key concern area both from the perspective of investors and the Indian revenue authorities alike. Globally, transfer pricing authorities across economies have become more aggressive in a bid to protect their tax base and revenue. MNCs with cross border operations are thus facing increasing transfer pricing challenges from multiple geographical locations.

Section 9(6)(b) defines 'royalty' to include consideration for the use or right to use any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment. The classification of data centre services as 'royalty' has been a subject of judicial scrutiny. Indian courts, such as the Mumbai ITAT in Rackspace US, Inc. v. DCIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 92, have held that income from cloud hosting and ancillary services was neither royalty nor Fees for Technical Services (FTS). The Tribunal observed that the agreement was for providing hosting services simpliciter, not for the use or leasing of equipment, as customers did not have physical control or possession over the servers. If the foreign company retains control and operational responsibility for the data centre infrastructure and merely provides a service to overseas users, the income is unlikely to be classified as royalty. Furthermore, in case the users are overseas, the requirement that the royalty be for the use of a right/property in a business/income source in India would generally not be met.

The use of a data centre by a foreign company providing services to overseas or Indian users may not give rise to royalty income under a DTAA, given the specific interpretation of 'royalty' in these treaties and consistent judicial precedents. The definition of 'royalty' in most DTAAs entered into by India is typically narrower than the broad definition provided under section 9(6)(b) of the ITA 2025. DTAAs often require a more direct nexus to the use or right to use specific intellectual property or equipment, or the transfer of technical know-how. For payments to be classified as royalty for the 'use or right to use industrial, commercial or scientific equipment' under a DTAA, judicial pronouncements39 consistently emphasise that the payer (user) must have physical control or possession over the equipment.

Therefore, if the data centre services involve providing access to software, platforms, or infrastructure without transferring the underlying intellectual property rights or granting users control over or possession of the equipment, the income is unlikely to be characterised as royalty under the DTAA. It would typically be considered business profits, taxable only if a Permanent Establishment (PE) exists in India.

8.7-11d Computation of taxable income - The taxable income arising to the foreign company, for which the exemption under this entry is not available, will depend on whether the foreign company has a PE in India.

Business income connected to PE in India

If the foreign company has a PE in India and the business income earned in India is connected to that PE, the tax liability shall be computed in accordance with the ITA.

Business income not connected to PE in India

If the foreign company does not have a PE in India, its business income earned in India shall not be taxable in India.

8.7-12 Transaction with associated enterprises

Where an Indian entity provides data centre services to its associated enterprise (a foreign company), it may opt for the safe harbour framework under the transfer pricing provisions. If the Indian entity earns an operating profit margin of at least 15% of operating expenses from such international transactions, the transaction price will be deemed to be at arm's length, and no transfer pricing adjustment will be required. [see Para 12.2-2b]

It is clarified that under the Scheme, a GDR/ADR holder is entitled to hold or transfer GDRs/ADRs, or redeem them into underlying ordinary shares with the option to continue holding underlying shares, and thus has a right to the ordinary shares underlying the GDRs/ADRs. Therefore, if an ordinary shareholder of the issuing company acquires a right or entitlement by virtue of ownership of ordinary shares, the GDR/ADR holder also matures the same rights or entitlements owing to his rights over underlying ordinary shares. GDR/ADR holders, therefore, are entitled to same bonus and rights issue of shares as any ordinary shareholders of company. Similarly, if ordinary shareholders of a company 'A' become entitled to shares of another company 'B' as a consequence of a genuine business reorganisation, and which is duly approved by the High Court under section 391/394 of the Indian Companies Act, then the GDR/ADR holders of company 'A' also mature the same entitlement to shares of company 'B'.

4. Furthermore, when GDR/ADR holders mature an entitlement to shares in a company, the company would need to issue and place ordinary shares with the domestic custodian against which the overseas depository would issue corresponding GDRs/ADRs to the ADR/GDR holders.

5. It has, therefore, been decided to allow Indian companies to issue GDRs/ADRs in cases of bonus or right issue of shares or genuine business reorganisations duly approved by the High Court, in accordance with the provisions of the Scheme and the guidelines issued thereunder. Indian companies would be required to apply to the Department of Economic Affairs for obtaining approval for issue of GDRs/ADRs in all these cases. The Department of Economic Affairs would consider such requests on the basis of necessary supporting documents to assess that the proposed GDRs/ADRs issue is on account of the entitlements of GDR/ADR holders as stated above.

Section 9A of the ITA 1961 provides a special regime for offshore funds. It provides that in the case of an eligible investment fund, the fund management activity carried out through an eligible fund manager acting on behalf of such fund shall not constitute a business connection in India of the said fund. Further, an eligible investment fund shall not be deemed resident in India merely because the eligible fund manager undertaking fund management activities on its behalf is located in India. Thus, this exemption from the general rules for the determination of business connection and 'resident status' of offshore funds and fund management activity undertaken on their behalf is allowed on fulfilment of the conditions explained below:

(a)

The offshore fund should be an eligible investment fund.

(b)

The fund management activity of such a fund should be managed by an eligible fund manager.

The eligible investment fund means a fund established or incorporated, or registered outside India, which collects funds from its members for investing it for their benefit and fulfils the prescribed conditions. One such prescribed condition under the ITA 1961 is that the fund's investment in any entity does not exceed 20% of the fund's corpus, and that the fund does not make any investment in its associate entity.

Under the ITA 2025, this maximum capping on investment in any entity has been increased from 20% to 25%, and all other conditions remain the same.
